sections.heading: History
paragraphs: A hydrogen atom is the simplest element, made of just one proton and one electron. Hydrogen may be the most abundant element in the universe, but it was hard to discover. Hydrogen almost always bonds with other elements and, when it’s on its own, pure hydrogen is so light that it gets shot out of Earth’s atmosphere!

Henry Cavendish gets credit for discovering hydrogen, being the first to identify it as distinct element in a 1766 paper. He noticed the gas coming off metal shavings after pouring acid on them. He called the gas “inflammable air” because of how easily it caught fire and noted, in a later study, that the gas made water when burned. In 1783, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier named the gas hydrogen, from the Greek for “water forming”. While Cavendish gets credit for the discovery, scientists had actually produced hydrogen years before. Records indicate Irish chemist Robert Boyle did so as early as 1671!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: At standard temperature and pressure, hydrogen is a gas of diatomic (two atom) molecules (H2). It is colorless, odorless, and tasteless. It’s also highly combustible and clean burning.
At extremely low temperatures (less than -253°C), hydrogen is a liquid. The liquid form is primarily used as rocket fuel. NASA has the two biggest liquid hydrogen storage tanks in the world!

At extremely low temperatures and massive pressure (like 5 million atmospheres), hydrogen is predicted to be a metallic solid. Hydrogen makes up the majority of Jupiter and other gas giant planets. The pressure is so immense in the planet’s center, that the interior likely contains metallic hydrogen!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: As the most abundant element, hydrogen has a lot of uses. Great quantities of hydrogen are required to create ammonia (NH3), which is used primarily for fertilizer and for hydrogenation, a way of processing fats and oils. Hydrogen is also used in large quantities to make methanol (CH3OH), often used as a solvent, pesticide, or fuel. Hydrogen is also used in rocket fuel, welding, making hydrochloric acid, and purifying metallic ores.

In nature, hydrogen fuels most stars. The atoms collide and fuse, joining together to make new elements and releasing energy in the process. Scientists are studying that process, fusion, as a possible power source and a more efficient process for nuclear power plants, which currently rely on fission (splitting atoms).

Hydrogen fuel cells are a new and developing technology that will generate great amounts of electricity without harmful waste. Hydrogen gas is used as the fuel, releasing non-polluting water as a byproduct.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Although pure hydrogen is a gas, we find very little of it in our atmosphere. On earth, hydrogen occurs chiefly in water, but it is also present in organic matter, such as living plants, petroleum, coal, etc. It is found throughout our bodies in proteins, fats, carbs, sugars, and DNA.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Hydrogen occurs in three forms, or isotopes. Most hydrogen is in the form of hydrogen-1 or protium, having just one proton and one electron, with no neutrons in its nucleus.

Deuterium (hydrogen-2) is hydrogen’s other stable isotope. Also known as heavy hydrogen, deuterium atoms have one proton, one neutron, and one electron. Tritium (hydrogen-3) is an unstable, radioactive isotope of hydrogen. Tritium atoms have one proton, one electron, and two neutrons. Deuterium is pretty common, but tritium is exceedingly rare. While tritium can occur naturally, its primarily made as a byproduct in nuclear reactors. Both deuterium and tritium are used as fuels in nuclear fusion experiments, where just one gram of deuterium-tritium fuel makes more energy than 2,000 gallons of oil!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Unlike most elements, hydrogen was not formed in stars or supernova explosions—its nucleus, a single proton, was created during the big bang. It took nearly 400,000 years for those protons to slow down enough to bind with electrons, creating hydrogen atoms. The heavier elements formed from these original hydrogen atoms, combining in cosmic collisions to make atoms with more protons. Scientists use this same method of atomic collision to make man-made (or synthetic) elements in particle accelerators.

Hydrogen is the most abundant of all elements in the universe, accounting for about 90% of all atoms. It’s primarily found in water (H2O) and is prepared for commercial purposes in a variety of ways. Just like Henry Cavendish, we still isolate hydrogen by treating certain metals with acid. But electricity can also separate the hydrogen and oxygen in water to capture each gas, in a process called electrolysis. In the US alone, over 3 billion cubic feet of hydrogen is produced each year!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: When you think about helium, you might immediately think about balloons. But those joyful party decorations weren’t around when scientists and astronomers first observed the element during a solar eclipse in 1868. Pierre Janssen, a French astronomer observing the eclipse from India, wasn’t the only one to notice a yellow line around the sun, but he was the one to formally record and confirm the new spectrum line. Around the globe, Joseph Norman Lockyer observed the new gas while viewing the sun through London’s smog. Lockyer named the element helium after the Greek word for the sun, helios. Although their observations were a few months apart, Janssen’s and Lockyer’s papers arrived at the French Academy of Sciences on the same day, and they share credit for the discovery—but many of their scientific peers were skeptical that they’d actually discovered anything.

In 1882, Italian physicist Luigi Palmieri detected helium while analyzing material from a volcanic eruption, and that research laid the foundation for Scottish chemist William Ramsay to successfully isolate the gas in 1895 after finding it within a piece of uranium ore. Later that year, Swedish chemists Per Teodor Cleve and Abraham Langlet collected enough helium to accurately determine its atomic weight. Ramsay sent a sample to Lockyer, who celebrated the confirmation. Research doesn’t happen in isolation and helium’s discovery was certainly a team effort!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Helium is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic, gas. It is the first in the noble gas group in the periodic table, and like the other noble gases, it is very stable and doesn’t react with other elements. Helium has the lowest boiling point of any element—close to absolute zero—and it’s the only element that can’t be solidified or frozen at normal atmospheric pressure.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Beyond buoyant party décor, helium has many uses.
Want to learn a trade? Helium is used in arc welding for construction, vehicle assembly, and aerospace manufacturing.
Curious about energy? Helium helps cool nuclear reactors.
Injured your knee? Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines can’t work without helium and allow millions of patients each year to avoid unnecessary surgery.
Going scuba diving in Hawaii? A mixture of helium and oxygen is used as an artificial atmosphere for divers and others working under pressure.
Reading this on a cell phone or laptop? Helium is used in the production of computer chips, fiber optics, and semiconductors that support modern communications.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: As the smallest and lightest noble gas, helium doesn’t make friends—um, compounds—easily. It's happy with just its two electrons and isn’t interested in accepting extra electrons or joining other elements. That means it has no stable compounds under normal conditions.
If forced, helium can form weak bonds with other helium atoms under incredibly low temperatures, but because it is so stable on its own, a single atom is considered a helium molecule.

In the 21st century, scientists have been able to predict some stable helium compounds, which might exist within gas giant planets. To bond with other elements, helium must be subjected to high pressure. One of the most well-studied potential helium compounds pairs it with two sodium atoms, resulting in a unique crystal structure.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Helium is the second-most abundant element in the universe and exists in our air, but we can’t isolate and harvest the element. Because it is rare on Earth, we collect it through other means, including as a byproduct of mining natural gas.

In 1925, the United States created the National Helium Reserve, and by 1995, the reserve held more than 1 billion cubic meters of the gas. At that point, demand for helium had decreased too much to justify the storage costs, so the government phased out the reserve and began selling off the stored gas. By 2013, high-tech applications renewed demand for helium, and the Bureau of Land Management took over national helium storage.
Today, helium continues to come from wells in the American Great Plains; however, the small Middle Eastern country of Qatar supplies the most helium in the world.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1800, José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva, a Brazilian chemist, discovered the mineral petalite in a mine in Sweden. But it wasn’t until 1817 that Johan August Arfwedson realized that petalite contained a new element. Working in the lab of the famous chemist Jöns Jakob Berzelius, Arfwedson figured out that this new element had properties similar to sodium and potassium, but it was different in important ways, like how its compounds didn’t dissolve as easily in water. Berzelius named the element lithium, from the Greek word lithos, meaning "stone," because it was discovered in a solid mineral rather than from plants or animals.

At first, scientists couldn’t isolate pure lithium, even though they knew it was there. In 1821, William Thomas Brande managed to separate lithium using electrolysis, a method that relies on electricity to breakdown a compound. Brande’s discovery opened the door to learning more about lithium, but it would still take years before it could be produced in large amounts. In 1855, Robert Bunsen and Augustus Matthiessen found a better way to produce more lithium through electrolysis, which helped make lithium more accessible for industrial use.

Lithium’s first major use came during World War II when it was used in high-temperature greases for aircraft engines. Lithium-based greases have a high melting point and are less corrosive than other types. Demand for lithium skyrocketed during the Cold War, as it became crucial for producing nuclear weapons.

Lithium’s importance surged again in the 1990s when scientists developed lithium-ion batteries. These batteries revolutionized technology, powering everything from smartphones to electric cars. Today, lithium is more important than ever, as the world moves toward advanced, next-generation energy and battery-powered technologies.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Even though it is a metal, and looks silvery and shiny like a metal, lithium is soft enough to be cut with a knife and light enough to float in water!

Lithium is the lightest of all metals, with a density only about half that of water. At standard conditions, it is the lowest-density metal and the lowest-density solid element altogether. Like other alkali metals, it is highly reactive and therefore must be stored in vacuum or submerged in a non-oxygen-containing fluid, such as mineral oil. It reacts strongly with water, although not as violently as sodium does. And it adds a beautiful crimson color to a flame. Its red flame was observed in the lithium-containing mineral petalite and in lithium salts before lithium was ever isolated as an element.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Lithium's main use is in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, because of its high electrochemical potential. Lithium-ion batteries power electric cars, laptops, phones, and other mobile tech. The demand for lithium has greatly increased with the proliferation of these devices.

Lithium is also useful in nuclear fusion technology and for making special heat-resistant glass and glass ceramics. It continues to be used in high-temperature lubricating greases. Because it is extremely lightweight, lithium metal can be used to make lightweight alloys. Aluminum-lithium alloys, for example, are used in aircraft, bicycle frames, and high-speed trains.
In addition, lithium carbonate is a mood-stabilizing drug used to treat bipolar disorder, manic depression, and similar conditions.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Small amounts of lithium are found in nearly all igneous rocks and in many mineral springs. Lepidolite, spodumene, petalite, and amblygonite are the more important minerals containing it. In the past, lithium was mined from such mineral ores. But today, lithium is obtained from extreme salty water (brine) and salt flats. The salt, which contains some lithium chloride, is obtained by solar evaporation. Then the lithium is extracted through electrolysis. Much lithium is produced from the expansive salt flats in Argentina, Chile, and Bolivia. These countries have been called the “lithium triangle,” with approximately 75 percent of the world’s lithium reserves. In the United States, lithium is produced from salt deposits in Nevada.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Beryllium has an ancient history that dates back to 300 BCE, when the mineral beryl was first used. By the first century CE, early scientists noted how similar beryl and emerald were. Ancient texts even describe how to create artificial beryl and emerald! What they didn’t realize was that both of these gemstones contain beryllium.

In the late 1700s chemists explored what beryl and emerald were made of. They initially thought these minerals contained aluminum silicates, but in 1798, French chemist Louis-Nicolas Vauquelin discovered that the minerals contained a new element, but he could only isolate the oxide form. He called this new substance “glucine” because it had a sweet taste (we really don’t recommend tasting unknown substances), but it wasn’t until later that the element was officially named beryllium, after the mineral it was found in.

Thirty years later, two chemists working separately, Friedrich Wöhler of Germany and Antoinne Bussy of France, both independently figured out how to isolate beryllium. Both chemists discovered that they could use electrolysis to isolate beryllium by using potassium to strip the chlorine from beryllium chloride (a salt). Although they were able to isolate the metal, it only appeared as small grains and wasn’t easy to work with at first.

Over the years, beryllium became more important, especially during World War II. It was used in beryllium-copper alloys, which are super strong and tough, perfect for making tools and weapons. However, beryllium was later found to be toxic, and scientists had to develop safer ways to use it. Today, beryllium is used in aerospace, electronics, and even in nuclear reactors.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: The metal is silver-gray in color and has many desirable properties. It is one of the lightest of all metals. Despite that, it is much stiffer than steel. That means you can push and pull on it with great force without affecting its size and shape very much.

It also has one of the highest melting points among the light metals, so it stays solid even at high temperatures. At everyday temperatures, it resists oxidation damage in air. (A very thin protective oxidized layer appears on its surface, that’s all.). It has excellent thermal conductivity, allowing heat to move through it rapidly, and is not magnetic.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Beryllium metal is often used to achieve lightness, stiffness, and stability. It is used in computer parts, gyroscopes and other aircraft components, space-telescope mirrors, and a variety of other instruments.

Beryllium is especially useful for nuclear technology. When exposed to alpha radiation (where an unstable atom releases an alpha particle, made of two protons and two neutrons) beryllium emits neutrons. Neutrons are extremely valuable in a variety of fields, including nuclear physics, electronics, materials science, and medical research.

While beryllium can be made to emit neutrons, it does not easily absorb them. That makes it useful in neutron-rich environments, such as the walls of a nuclear reactor. There, it can contain neutrons without being affected or weakened by them. Beryllium oxide, too, is useful in high-temperature aspects of nuclear tech because of its very high melting point.

Beryllium can be mixed with other metals to make alloys. The alloy beryllium copper is used for springs, electrical contacts, spot-welding electrodes, and non-sparking tools. Beryllium alloys are also used as structural materials for high-speed aircraft, missiles, spacecraft, and satellites. They are used in cars as well, including windshield frames and braking discs.
Beryllium is also relatively transparent to x-rays and other forms of radiation. That makes it a valuable window material in x-ray devices and particle detectors.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Beryllium is found in some 30 minerals. Beryl and bertrandite are its most important commercial sources. Beryllium metal, with no other atoms attached, did not become widely available to industry until 1957. Today, it is made by using magnesium to remove fluorine atoms from the salt beryllium fluoride.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Boron compounds, like borax, have been used since ancient times. The Egyptians used borax in mummification and cleaning, while the Chinese used it in glazes for pottery. However, it wasn’t until the 1800s that scientists discovered boron as an element.

In 1808, three chemists, Sir Humphry Davy in England and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard in France, were able to isolate boron almost at the same time. They used similar methods, involving heating borax with potassium to create a dark powder, which was the element boron. However, the boron they isolated wasn’t pure. Pure boron wasn’t isolated until 1909 by American chemist Ezekiel Weintraub.

Pure boron is incredibly rare in nature, but it’s become important in modern technology. Boron is used in fiberglass, borosilicate glass (which is resistant to heat), and even in rocket fuel. It’s also used in nuclear reactors because it can absorb neutrons, helping control reactions.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Boron is a fascinating element because of its ability to form stable, covalently bonded molecular networks, much like carbon. This means boron can create strong connections with other atoms, allowing it to form a wide variety of compounds. Boron’s versatility makes it important in many fields of science and technology.

One group of compounds boron forms are called carbonates, which are useful in various chemical reactions and products. Boron also forms compounds known as metalloboranes and phosphacarboranes, which are incredibly complex and stable molecules. These compounds are used in fields like material science and chemistry, offering exciting potential for creating new materials with unique properties.

Overall, boron’s ability to create thousands of different compounds is due to its strong bonding abilities, allowing it to connect with various elements and form networks that have high stability. This versatility makes boron a key player in advanced materials, electronics, and chemical engineering.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Boron is an incredibly versatile element with a wide range of uses in everyday life and advanced technology. Borax, one of the most common boron compounds, is found in things like creams, body lotions, shampoos, and even bath bombs. It’s also the most economically important boron compound, used to make fiberglass insulation and as a key ingredient in disinfectants and detergents like sodium perborate bleach.

Boron has some exciting applications beyond household products. Amorphous boron is used in flares, creating a distinctive green color, and it’s also used in rocket igniters. Boric acid is essential in making textile products, and boron compounds help create borosilicate glass, known for its heat resistance. Scientists are also exploring boron compounds for treating diseases like arthritis.

In the world of high tech, boron-10 is a valuable isotope used in nuclear reactors to help control reactions and as a shield against nuclear radiation. It’s even used in neutron detection instruments! Another form, boron nitride, is nearly as hard as diamonds and is a great heat conductor, even though it acts as an electrical insulator.

Boron’s properties don't stop there—boron filaments are lightweight but incredibly strong, making them perfect for aerospace structures. It also has lubricating properties similar to graphite, and its hydrides are studied as potential rocket fuels.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Boron, like carbon, can form stable covalently bonded molecular networks. Carbonates, metalloboranes, phosphacarboranes, and other families that include boron make up thousands of compounds.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Boron has several crystalline and amorphous forms. The most common form is amorphous boron, a dark powder that is unreactive to oxygen, water, acids, and alkalis.

Three crystalline forms are 𝜶-rhombohedral, 𝜷-rhombohedral, and 𝜶-tetragonal. When exceptional circumstances arise, boron can form two amorphous forms—one a finely divided powder and the other a glassy solid.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Although boron isn't found free in nature, it occurs as boric acid in certain volcanic spring waters and as borates in boron and colemanite.

Two important sources of boron are the ores rasorite (kernite) and tincal (borax ore)—both of which are found in the Mojave Desert. Tincal, or crude borax, is the most important source of boron in the Mojave. Large borax deposits are also found in Turkey.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Carbon is sometimes called the “king of elements,” and for good reason: it’s everywhere you look! The element has been known to humans since prehistory, when it was found in the form of soot and charcoal. In fact, the word “carbon” comes from the Latin word carbo, which means “charcoal.”

In the fourth century BCE, diamonds—another form of carbon—began to be mined in India. But it would be a long time before anyone figured out that charcoal and diamond were different forms of the same element. In 1694, Italian scientists Giuseppe Averani and Cipriani Targioni took a step toward this discovery when they showed that it is possible to destroy diamonds with heat. They used a kind of magnifying glass to focus the sun’s rays until the diamond burned up!

Then, in 1772, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier showed that when charcoal and diamond were burned, they released the same amount of carbon dioxide. This finding indicated that charcoal and diamonds might be made of the same element—something that was confirmed by British chemist Smithson Tennant in 1796.

In 1954, a team of scientists at General Electric made the first artificial diamond. This process, which was initially expensive, has since become substantially cheaper. Today, synthetic diamonds can cost 75 percent less than natural diamonds, and something like 30 percent of diamonds sold in the United States are synthetic. Artificial diamonds are used in everything from jewelry to power tools and computers.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Carbon is a study in contrasts. Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring substance known to science, but other forms of carbon, like charcoal and graphite, are quite soft. While diamonds conduct electricity poorly, graphite conducts electricity and heat well. Diamond is transparent, which is why it’s desirable as jewelry, while graphite is opaque.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Carbon and carbon compounds have too many uses to count! Hydrocarbons—compounds of hydrogen and carbon—can be used to as fuels or to make plastics. Coal, oil, and natural gas power everything from power plants to automobiles and industrial manufacturing.

In its elemental form, carbon can be alloyed with iron to make metals like carbon steel. Graphite is used in pencils, in glass manufacturing, in batteries, and as a pigment, among other things. Charcoal makes both iron production and weekend barbecues possible!

Carbon can also be made into carbon fiber, which is a strong but lightweight material that’s used in everything from running shoes to bicycles and aircraft. Carbon nanotubes are a part of the fullerene family of molecules, which were first discovered in 1985. These molecules have enormous potential for use in medicine, pharmaceuticals, and electronics.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Among all the elements, carbon forms an incomparable number of compounds. Scientists have characterized more than one million carbon compounds, and new ones are discovered all the time.

In 1828, German chemist Friedrich Wöhler discovered that the biological compound urea could be produced from nonbiological chemicals, uniting the fields of organic chemistry, which focuses on carbon and carbon compounds, and inorganic chemistry, which deals with non-carbon compounds.

Hydrocarbons, which are used in fuels, plastics, and pharmaceuticals, are a common type of carbon compound. However, hydrocarbon fuels have a downside: when burned, they produce carbon dioxide, which when expelled into the atmosphere heightens greenhouse effects, a natural process through which heat is trapped near the Earth’s surface.

Other carbon compounds include alloys such as steel, the carbohydrates consumed by plants and animals, and minerals like marble and limestone. The carbon cycle is the process by which carbon moves between living things and throughout the environment—a complex exchange that makes life on Earth possible.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: A whole branch of chemistry (organic chemistry) is devoted to studying carbon. Organic chemistry evolved significantly after 1985, when buckminsterfullerine—an allotrope, or form, of carbon with a soccer ball-shape—was discovered. However, the three best-known carbon allotropes are amorphous carbon (which occurs in nature without a crystalline structure), graphite, and diamond.

In nature, you’ll find carbon in two stable (non-radioactive) isotopes: carbon-12 and carbon-13. Almost 99 percent of naturally occurring carbon is in the form of carbon-12. Carbon-14 is a naturally occurring radioisotope with a half-life of only 5,730 years. That half-life is right in the goldilocks zone for radiocarbon dating—not too short (or it would all be gone) and not too long (or it wouldn’t change enough to show aging)—making it ideal for figuring out the age of ancient artifacts.
In total, there are 15 known carbon isotopes. Carbon-8 is the shortest lived, with a half-life of much less than one second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Carbon can be found naturally in a variety of compounds and forms. The most common are graphite—whose top three producers in 2023 were China, Madagascar, and Mozambique—anthracite, a type of coal mined in China, Russia, and Ukraine; and diamond, which commonly comes from Russia, Botswana, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Nitrogen makes up a whopping 78% of the air we breathe, but for a long time, no one knew it existed! Back in the 1760s and 70s, chemists such as Carl Wilhelm Scheele, Henry Cavendish, and Joseph Priestley were trying to figure out what air was made of. They knew about oxygen, but there was still something else in the air that they couldn’t define. When they removed oxygen from the air, they found that the remaining gas couldn’t keep candles burning or support life. Mice placed in this mysterious air didn’t survive, so they called it names like "noxious air" and "burnt air." These properties provided clues, but no one realized they had discovered nitrogen.

The real breakthrough came in 1772 when Daniel Rutherford, a Scottish physician, isolated nitrogen from the air and suggested it might be a new element. While Rutherford didn’t fully understand what he had found, his work laid the groundwork for future discoveries. A few years later, in 1785, Henry Cavendish correctly determined that air was made of four parts nitrogen and one part oxygen, but he still didn’t use the word “nitrogen” to describe this mysterious gas.

The name "nitrogen" came about in 1790, thanks to French chemist Jean-Antoine Chaptal. He named the element "nitrogène," which means "nitre-forming." Nitre, or potassium nitrate (also called saltpeter), was important because it was used to make nitric acid and gunpowder. The word has roots in both Greek and Latin, and Chaptal's name stuck in English as well, entering the language as "nitrogen" in 1794. Another early name for nitrogen was "azote," meaning “no life” in Greek, because it couldn’t support breathing or combustion. This name is still used in many languages today.

Before the element itself was understood, nitrogen compounds had been used for centuries. Ancient civilizations knew about ammonium chloride, and during the Middle Ages, alchemists worked with nitric acid and nitrate salts. They even created a powerful acid called aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids, famous for being able to dissolve gold, the "king of metals." Nitrogen compounds also became essential for making gunpowder and fertilizers, giving nitrogen a starring role in agriculture and warfare.

By the early 20th century, scientists developed methods to produce nitrogen compounds on a large scale. The Haber-Bosch process, invented in the early 1900s, allowed industries to fix nitrogen (or capture it) from the air, creating synthetic fertilizers. This was a game-changer for farming, and today, about half of the world’s food production depends on these fertilizers. At the same time, nitrogen compounds became important in manufacturing explosives, playing a huge role in both World Wars. From ancient alchemy to modern industry, nitrogen has played a vital role in warfare, agriculture, and scientific advancements.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Nitrogen is a nonmetal that, in its gas or liquid state, is clear and odorless. N2 has a very strong covalent triple bond, one of the strongest bonds in all of chemistry. This has two main consequences:

First, it is very difficult to extract nitrogen from atmospheric gas, although it is possible. Some soil bacteria have evolved to do it, naturally fertilizing plants. And human industry does it by the “Haber-Bosch process”—a high-pressure, metal-catalyzed reaction of N2 with H2. The rest is done by lightning.

Second, there’s a ton of energy stored in N2’s strong triple bond. When nitrogen compounds convert or decompose to N2 gas, the triple bond breaks and releases a massive amount of energy. This is why many nitrogen compounds are valuable as explosives, like TNT (trinitrotoluene) and dynamite (with a nitroglycerin base).

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Nitrogen on its own has many uses. As a gas, it serves as an inert atmosphere (no oxygen) for preserving food, processing steel and stainless steel, and manufacturing electronic components. As a compressed gas, it is used to pressurize containers, like beer kegs and paintball guns. As a liquid, it looks like water. It is a cryogenic refrigerant with many uses, including freezing food for freshness. It also has medical uses, such as freezing blood, eggs, and sperm for preservation or freezing warts and cysts to remove them.

Nitrogen also has valuable compounds, particularly ammonia (NH3). It is an important fertilizer—a critical precursor to the production of nearly half of the world's food supply. It is also a common solvent and glass cleaner, but it has more specialized applications too, such as rocket fuel. Other nitrogen compounds are used as fertilizers and rocket fuels as well.
Nitrogen is also a key component of major biomolecules, including DNA and enzymes. It is likewise used in every major class of pharmaceuticals.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Commercially, ammonia is the most important nitrogen compound. It is useful on its own or as a precursor to making other nitrogen compounds. These include nitric acid (HNO3) and potassium and sodium nitrate (saltpeter and Chile saltpeter, KNO3 and NaNO3, respectively). These, like other nitrogen compounds, are used variously as food preservatives, fertilizers, explosives, propellants, and more.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Nitrogen, produced in stars, is the seventh most abundant element in the universe. It is the largest component of the earth’s atmosphere and one of the main constituents of the human body. However, it is not abundant in the earth’s crust. There, it makes up only 0.0019 percent, similar to lithium, niobium, and gallium.

The primary commercial source of nitrogen is air. Air is liquefied and then distilled to isolate nitrogen. That means the liquefied air is heated until one component evaporates and is collected. Then it is heated further until the next component evaporates, and so on.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Today we know that oxygen makes up a fifth of the air and is the critical element that lets us breathe. But how did we figure that out?

In 1668, English chemist John Mayow published results of the experiments he conducted on the study of air. He made some extraordinary insights. In one experiment, he placed either a burning candle or a live mouse in a glass, which he set upside-down in a wider vessel containing water, thus trapping the air. The candle would go out and the mouse would die. In each case, the water level rose within the inverted glass, taking up the space of something that had been consumed...

Some of this had been noted before by the likes of Leonardo da Vinci and even the ancient Greeks, but Mayow observed that, each time, the rising water displaced the same exact volume of air. That was a big clue. He figured out that one part of whatever made up the air was being consumed by the flame and the breathing mouse. He correctly calculated that the component in question amounted to one fifth of the air!

He also noted that when heated, the ore antimony would get heavier. He figured that it was bonding with that mysterious component of air. He even figured out that the purpose of the lungs is to extract this specific air component, reasoning that blood would then shuttle the component around the body to power our muscles and generate body heat. He was absolutely right! But it would be another century before scientists actually identified oxygen.

About a hundred years later in the 1770s, a trio of European scientists made the leap to identify oxygen as an element. In Sweden, Carl Wilhelm Scheele obtained oxygen by heating mercuric oxide. He determined that the emerging gas was the same one that was required for combustion. In England, Joseph Priestly also heated mercuric oxide, by focusing sunlight on it. He found that the emerging gas made candles burn brighter and made breathing easier. Mice breathing the gas became more active, and he personally felt “light and easy” for a while after breathing it.

Both Scheele and Priestly wrote to share their work with Antoine Lavoisier, in France. Lavoisier repeated several of Priestly’s experiments. He also noted that oxygen formed acids when combined with nonmetals, such as sulfur, phosphorus, charcoal, and nitrogen. He proposed naming it oxygen, from the Greek for acid (oxy) forming (gen). Soon thereafter, he helped determine that water was not an element but rather a blend of the elements hydrogen and oxygen.

This understanding laid the foundation for modern chemistry and our knowledge of how air and chemical reactions work. Oxygen plays a crucial role in industries like medicine, metalworking, and space exploration, transforming our knowledge of biology, chemistry, and the environment.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: As a gas, oxygen is colorless, odorless, and tasteless. As a liquid or solid, oxygen is a pale blue color.
As an element, oxygen is extremely reactive. It readily forms hundreds of thousands of organic and inorganic compounds and bonds directly with most other elements.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: A little over half of all oxygen produced commercially is used in the manufacture of steel. Oxygen is injected into molten iron to remove unwanted sulfur and excess carbon as SO2 and CO2.
Another quarter of the commercial oxygen supply is for the production of chemicals used to make products such as polyester, which is then used to make plastics and fabrics.

The remaining supply is used for a variety of applications—it is needed for welding and cutting metals; as a rocket propellent; for treatment of respiratory ailments; and for life support systems in aircraft, spacecraft and space suits, submarines, and scuba diving.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In addition to gaseous oxygen as O2, oxygen also forms another gas, ozone (O3). Ozone is formed by an electrical discharge or ultraviolet light acting on O2. Ozone's presence in the upper atmosphere helps prevent harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun from reaching the earth's surface. Ozone has a bluish color. Liquid ozone is bluish black, and solid ozone is violet-black.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Oxygen is the third most abundant element in the universe. It is second most abundant on earth, just slightly behind iron, a much heavier element that makes up most of the planet’s core. Oxygen is by far the most abundant element in the earth’s crust, making up 46 percent of its mass in the form of oxides of other elements. It makes up 89 percent of the mass of the ocean and 65 percent of the human body. By volume, diatomic oxygen gas, or O2, makes up 21 percent of our atmosphere. Oxygen is plentiful.

Fractional distillation is used to isolate oxygen for commercial and other purposes. Air is liquefied and then heated. At different temperatures, different atmospheric components will evaporate, so oxygen (and other gases) can be separated, recondensed, and collected. Another method involves flowing air over a specialized microporous material (zeolite) that absorbs nitrogen, leaving mostly oxygen.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: For centuries, a mineral called fluorspar (calcium difluoride) was added to metal ores to lower their melting points for smelting in metal refining. "Fluor" comes from the Latin word fluere, meaning "to flow." A solution containing fluorite and sulfuric acid was later discovered to produce a substance (hydrofluoric acid) that could be used in glass etching. The component of these compounds that would be come to be known as fluorine was proposed as an element in 1810. Fluorine is so reactive, however, that it does not occur freely in nature, and the element proved difficult and dangerous to isolate.

Many investigators tried to separate fluorine from hydrofluoric acid, with some experiments ending tragically. Most chemists studying fluorine in the 1800s were poisoned by their research—except for George Gore. He was never poisoned by his research, but he didn’t survive his research unscathed. Gore was able to isolate a small amount of the volatile element through an electrolytic process in 1869. However, when the fluorine gas that formed on one of his electrodes reacted with the hydrogen gas that formed on the other, he discovered the hard way that fluorine and hydrogen gas combine explosively, destroying most of his lab and nearly poisoning him, but he managed to escape unharmed.

Following 74 years of continuous effort by various scientists, chemist Ferdinand Frederic Henri Moissan finally isolated fluorine in 1886 (after being poisoned several times in his pursuit) through the electrolysis of potassium fluoride and hydrofluoric acid. He completely isolated the fluorine gas from the hydrogen gas and built his electrolysis device from pure platinum. Moissan was awarded the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 1906 for his work with fluorine, and in fact, his design has never been outdone and is still used in fluorine production.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Fluorine is a pale yellow, corrosive gas and the absolute worst at sharing. It’s the most electronegative element, meaning that when it bonds with other atoms, fluorine pulls all of the electrons towards itself. Fluorine is also the most reactive element. Finely divided metals, glass, ceramics, carbon, and even water burn in fluorine with a bright flame.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Until World War II, there was no commercial production of elemental fluorine. The Manhattan Project and nuclear energy applications, however, made it necessary to produce large quantities of the gas.

Fluorine is now used in producing uranium (from the hexafluoride) and more than 100 commercial fluorochemicals, including high-temperature plastics. Fluorine-carbon compounds, known as chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), were once used extensively in aerosols and refrigerants but have been phased out because of their negative impact on the environment.

Fluorine is also used in city water treatment (at one part per million) and in toothpaste to prevent tooth decay. Hydrofluoric acid is used to etch glass, including that of light bulbs. Fluorspar (calcium fluoride) crystals are used to make infrared lenses.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Noteworthy compounds include sodium fluoride, stannous(II) fluoride, and sodium monofluorophosphate, which are common toothpaste additives. Chemical reactions between fluorine and noble (virtually inert) gases have been confirmed in fluorides of xenon, radon, and krypton.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Fluorine is isolated through electrolysis of potassium fluoride and hydrofluoric acid as well as through the electrolysis of molten potassium acid fluoride.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1898, during a six-week period, British chemists William Ramsay and Morris Travers discovered three noble gases by evaporating liquid air and extracting the gases one-by-one (a process called fractional distillation). Krypton was the first gas to be identified, then Ramsay and Travers repeated the same experiment, this time changing the pressure to evaporate solid Argon. Because of the tweaked distillation process, the gas that evaporated first was neon which, when collected in an atomic spectrometer, glowed a brilliant red-orange light. The bright color shocked the scientists as Travers noted, "the blaze of crimson light from the tube told its own story and was a sight to dwell upon and never forget."

Neon as we know it, bright and descriptive on storefront signs and motel vacancy notices, did not come to be until the 1900s. In 1902, George Claude collected neon as a by-product of his air-liquefication business and in 1910, he sealed the neon in a tube (similar to the modern use) and tried to sell the tubes as an indoor lighting source. This business attempt was not successful because homeowners weren’t fond of the intense colors, but in 1912, Claude found success in using neon tubes for advertising.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Colorless and odorless, neon is the second-lightest noble gas. The notable reddish glow occurs when it is collected in a vacuum discharge tube.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The most common use of neon is in brightly lit signs used for advertising. Neon is also used to make high-voltage indicators and switching gear, lightning arresters, diving equipment, and lasers. These signs and buttons typically use electricity to get the gas to emit its bright red color. Liquid neon is also used for cryogenic freezing, a process that preserves items in extremely low temperatures.
In combination with other elements, neon has even more applications. For example, neon is used in the helium-neon lasers used for supermarket checkout scanners, printers, and more.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Neon is an inert gas, which means it does not react with other chemical elements and doesn't form compounds.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Neon also has six unstable isotopes in addition to its three stable ones. Neon's main isotope neon-20 is created by the nuclear fusion that happens in the core of stars.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Neon is rare on Earth, though common in the universe and solar system (stable isotopes of neon are found in stars). The atmosphere is the primary source of neon. It is collected by evaporating liquified air (fractional distillation).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Sodium has been an important element throughout human history, even though people didn’t know it by name for thousands of years. As far back as 6000 BCE, ancient civilizations discovered that salt (which is made of sodium and chlorine) could be used to preserve food. Before refrigerators existed, salt was one of the only ways to keep food from spoiling. Ancient Egyptians, for example, used salt to preserve fish and meat, which helped them store food for long periods. This simple mineral played a huge role in allowing early people to survive

Sodium wasn’t just valuable for food preservation—it was also considered a precious resource because of its role in salt. In ancient China, salt was so important that it was used as currency, and in the Roman Empire, soldiers were often paid in salt, which is where the word "salary" comes from. The trade of salt, rich in sodium, helped shape ancient trade routes, with salt caravans traveling across the Sahara Desert and sea salt being traded along the Mediterranean. Cities like Venice became wealthy due to their control over the salt trade.

Sodium remained a mystery for a long time, even though salt was essential to life. In 1807, British chemist Sir Humphry Davy made a major breakthrough when he became the first person to isolate sodium from salt. Using a process called electrolysis, where electricity is passed through a substance to break it down, Davy was able to separate sodium from the chlorine in salt. This was a huge discovery because it helped scientists better understand the chemical makeup of salt and the elements within it. Davy’s work with electrolysis didn’t just stop with sodium; he went on to isolate several other elements as well.

Throughout history, people fought over salt, and by extension, sodium, because it was so valuable. Salt became a source of conflict, as governments placed heavy taxes on it. In Europe, salt was so expensive that it led to wars and revolts. In France, the government’s control over and high taxation of salt led to protests and was one of the many issues that contributed to the French Revolution. In India, one of the key moments in the country’s fight for independence was the Salt March, led by Mahatma Gandhi, in protest of British taxes on salt.

Today, sodium is easy to find in many forms, but its role in salt has shaped human history for thousands of years. Whether preserving food or driving major historical events, sodium has had a huge impact on the world.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Sodium, like every reactive element, is never found free in nature. When isolated, however, it is a bright, silvery metal with a density just below that of water. So, it (barely) floats, but it also reacts violently in water. It is the third-least-dense elemental metal after lithium and potassium. It is a good conductor of heat and electricity. And the metal is soft enough to be cut with a knife quite easily.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Metallic sodium is vital in the preparation of various compounds in organic chemistry. The metal can also be used to improve the structure of certain alloys, descale metal, and purify molten metals.

Liquid sodium metal can be used as a coolant in certain nuclear reactors because it has excellent heat-transfer properties. It circulates in pipes through the reactor, absorbing heat from the nuclear reactions and bringing that heat to a boiler to make steam. The steam drives a turbine to make electricity. Sodium can also be alloyed with potassium (NaK) to make a metal that remains liquid at room temperature so the metal doesn’t harden in the pipes when the reactor is off.

The light emitted by sodium atoms includes two very prominent wavelengths, both yellow. Familiar yellow streetlights are sodium lamps. And yellow sodium lasers are used in adaptive optics at major astronomical observatories. The laser beam is pointed at the astronomical target, and a system rapidly analyzes changing atmospheric distortions to the beam. The system then makes minute adjustments to the shape of the telescope mirror to compensate, leading to sharper images.

However, sodium metal is far less useful than its compounds. Millions of tons of salt and other sodium compounds are produced each year. Salt is used for de-icing, in addition to food flavoring and preserving. Sodium carbonate is a used as a water softener. And sodium bicarbonate, or baking soda, is used in, well, baking. These and other sodium compounds are important to the paper, glass, soap, textile, petroleum, chemical, and metal industries. Soap, for example, is generally a sodium salt of certain fatty acids.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Sodium is the sixth-most-abundant element in the crust of the earth. It is most commonly found in the form of sodium chloride. This salt (ordinary table salt) dissolves easily in water and has therefore been absorbed into the oceans over time. Salt can also be found in many dried seabeds and lakebeds.
Sodium metal is obtained commercially by the electrolysis of sodium chloride.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1618, an English farmer named Henry Wicker noticed that his cows wouldn’t drink from a certain pool of water on his farm in Epsom, England. This was puzzling in part because England was suffering from a drought, so Wicker’s cows were thirsty! Although the water tasted bitter, Wicker noticed that it was helpful in healing scratches and cuts, and also that it could be used as a laxative. By evaporating the water, Wicker produced a salt that became known as Epsom salt. Epsom salts are still used today as a laxative and as a remedy for joint and muscle pain.

Wicker wasn’t aware that his Epsom salts were actually magnesium sulfate. That’s because it wasn’t until 1755 that Scottish chemist Joseph Black figured out that magnesium was a distinct element. Black was the first to understand the difference between magnesia (magnesium oxide, MgO) and lime (calcium oxide, CaO)—realizing that magnesia contained a new element even though its properties are very similar to lime (look at how they're positioned on the periodic table!). Black is also known for discovering carbon dioxide and for developing the materials-science concepts of latent heat and specific heat.

In 1792, Austrian scientist Anton Rupprecht heated magnesia with charcoal to obtain an impure version of magnesium metal. In 1808, chemist Sir Humphrey Davy of England managed to isolate a tiny but pure sample of the metal by electrolysis of magnesium oxide (using an electrical current to separate the magnesium and oxygen). In 1831, French chemist Antoine Bussy finally isolated a substantial amount of magnesium by reacting magnesium chloride with potassium.

Davy thought the element should be called magnium, but in the end, it became known as magnesium. The name comes from a Greek word for an area in modern-day Turkey, Magnesia, where a magnesium compound had been found.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Magnesium metal is tough, lightweight, shiny, and silver in color, although it tarnishes when exposed to air. Magnesium is highly flammable. It has been used in warfare partly because once it catches fire, it is extremely difficult to put out. In fact, adding water only makes the fire worse! The only way to stop a magnesium fire is by covering it with sand.
The bright light magnesium emits as it burns is why magnesium powder was used to produce a camera flash, in the early days of photography.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Like aluminum, magnesium is both strong and lightweight, so it is often used as a structural metal. Alloyed with other elements, magnesium can make metals that are strong and resistant to corrosion. That’s why magnesium alloys are essential in aircraft, missiles, and cars. The alloys are also valuable for objects for which weight is a concern, such as laptops, power tools, and luggage, and even in sporting equipment like bicycles. It's used to manufacture other metals, like steel and titanium, too.
Because it burns brightly and readily in air, magnesium is used in flares and fireworks. It has also been used in bombs and other weapons.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: In medicine, magnesium hydroxide (or milk of magnesia) is used as an antacid or laxative. Magnesium sulfate (Epsom salt) is used in baths to soothe sore muscles and treat topical skin irritations. In the past, magnesium bromide was prescribed as a sedative.

Magnesium compounds play important roles in diverse areas. For example, magnesium carbonate is used in everything from flooring to fireproofing, cosmetics, and toothpaste. Magnesium oxide is used in fertilizer and cement production, in wastewater treatment, and as an anticaking agent in canned food and frozen desserts.

The mineral magnesium silicate is known as meerschaum, which was once used in Turkey to make tobacco pipes. Later, in the 19th century, meerschaum pipes caught on in Europe, too. (Nicholas Cage fans will remember that a meerschaum pipe played a key role in the 2004 film National Treasure.)

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find magnesium in three stable (non-radioactive) isotopes—magnesium-24, -25, and -26. Of these isotopes, magnesium-24 is by far the most common, with about 80 percent of natural magnesium occurring in this form.

Scientists have discovered 19 radioactive magnesium isotopes, ranging from magnesium-19 to magnesium-40. The longest-lived of these isotopes, magnesium-28, has a half-life of around 20 hours, while the shortest-lived has a half-life of about 4 zeptoseconds. A zeptosecond is a trillionth of a billionth of a second, or about as long as it takes to drink a milkshake on a summer afternoon!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: By mass, magnesium is the fourth most abundant element on Earth after iron, oxygen, and silicon. It’s the seventh most abundant in the earth’s crust. It is found in large deposits in the form of magnesite, dolomite, and other minerals.

In the United States, magnesium metal is principally obtained by electrolysis of magnesium chloride from brines, wells, and seawater. China produces around three quarters of the world’s annual magnesium output.

Many foods, including almonds, cashew nuts, parsnips, bran, and chocolate, are high in magnesium. (If you needed an excuse to eat chocolate, now you have one!) Although magnesium is a vital element for humans, magnesium deficiency is a rare condition because most people have a substantial amount of the element stored in their bones.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The name aluminum comes from the Latin word alumen, which refers to alum, a type of aluminum sulfate. Alum has been used since at least the 5th century BCE! In ancient times, people used it mainly for two things: cleaning water and helping dyes stick to fabric. It was super useful for making sure water was clear and for keeping colors on clothes bright. Today, alum is also used in medicine and cosmetics, like in antiperspirants and to stop bleeding from small cuts, such as those you might get from shaving.

In the 1700s, scientists started to suspect that alum contained a new metal, which we now know as aluminum. In 1789, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier published a theory that alum contained this mystery metal. A few years later, British scientist Sir Humphry Davy tried to isolate aluminum by using electricity (a method called electrolysis), but that didn’t work. In 1825, Danish physicist Hans Christian Øersted finally managed to isolate aluminum—kind of. He heated an aluminum salt with potassium. The aluminum he got was still impure. Two years later, Friedrich Wöhler, a German chemist, improved Øersted’s process and succeeded in making pure aluminum! At first, it was just a gray powder, but by 1845, Wöhler figured out how to shape it into solid metal balls.

Interestingly, Davy was the one to suggest the name aluminum, but there was some confusion over how to spell it. Some early work used "aluminum" (ending in -um like platinum), while others used "aluminium" (-ium like most other metals). In the United States, people mostly preferred “aluminium” until around 1895, when “aluminum” became the more popular spelling. The debate wasn’t officially settled until 1925, when the American Chemical Society decided to go with “aluminum.”

Internationally, however, the debate continued. In 1990, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) declared that "aluminium" was the official name. But in 1993, they agreed that "aluminum" was also acceptable, meaning both spellings are correct today, depending on where you are.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Pure aluminum, a silvery-white metal, possesses many desirable characteristics. It is light, nonmagnetic, non-sparking, and electrically conductive. It can be shaped easily. It is the second most malleable metal and the sixth most ductile.
It does not rust. In air, it forms a thin, protective, corrosion-resistant oxide layer on its surface. This layer is shiny and reflective and does not tarnish as it would for silver.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Aluminum is a very lightweight metal. It has about one-third the density of steel. This makes it especially useful for applications where weight is a major concern. Aircraft and rocket frames are key examples, but cars, trucks, train cars, ships, and bicycles use aluminum, too. However, it is a soft metal, so it’s usually alloyed with small amounts of another metal to improve its strength for these transportation applications. The alloying metals include copper, magnesium, silicon, manganese, and zinc.

Aluminum is considered highly conductive, but its conductivity is only about 60 percent that of copper. Yet it is used in electrical transmission lines because of its light weight. It is also used in other electrical machinery (motors, generators, transformers, etc.).

Aluminum is inexpensive but more expensive than steel. So, in building construction, it is used when low weight or corrosion resistance is important, such as for doors, window frames, aluminum siding, gutters, and metal roofs.

It is extensively used for kitchen utensils, packaging (soda cans, aluminum foil), and lightweight components of consumer products. Many laptop computers, smartphones, and smartwatches have aluminum exteriors—often recycled from used soda cans. Aluminum is infinitely recyclable.
Aluminum is the second most widely used metal after iron.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: The aluminum compounds of greatest importance are the oxide, sulfate, and the soluble sulfate with potassium (alum).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Aluminum is the third most abundant element in Earth’s crust, after oxygen and silicon, and the most abundant metal. It makes up 8 percent of the crust by mass. The most common way to obtain it commercially is to mine it from bauxite, a sedimentary rock.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: “Silicon” comes from the Latin word silex, meaning flint. Sharp flints of silica (silicon dioxide, SiO2) are among humanity’s first known tools. For thousands of years, humans have put silica and other rock-crystal forms of silicon to different uses. They made beads and vases with it and the Egyptians knew how to make glass from silica by 1500 BCE.

In 1787, French chemist Antoine Lavoisier correctly suspected silica was an oxide of a new element, but the silicon and oxygen were bound so tightly that he didn’t know how to remove the oxygen to test his theory. In 1808, Sir Humphrey Davy of England tried to isolate silicon with an electric current (electrolysis). Even though he was able to isolate other elements this way, it didn’t work with silicon.

In 1811, French chemists Joseph Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard reportedly prepared an impure, amorphous (non-crystalline) silicon by heating potassium with silicon tetrafluoride. The idea was to use potassium’s reactivity to lure the tetrafluoride off the silicon, but they didn’t fully isolate or identify the new element. Chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius of Sweden followed Gay-Lussac and Thénard’s use of potassium. But Berzelius started with a different silicon compound and carefully purified the resulting material to finally derive amorphous silicon. In 1854, French chemist Henri Deville later prepared crystalline silicon. Others would follow in that important line of work.

Davy had proposed naming the unknown element silicium, ending in -ium because he believed it to be a metal, like lithium, sodium, or strontium. A Scottish chemist, Thomas Thomson, argued that it should instead be named silicon, believing it to be a nonmetal (like boron or carbon). Today it is considered something in between, a metalloid. Metalloids have some metal properties and some nonmetal properties.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Crystalline silicon has a metallic luster and appears bluish-gray color. Silicon is not very reactive and most acids, except hydrofluoric, do not affect it. Nonreactive usually means nontoxic; however, silicon can have some harmful properties. Miners, stonecutters, and others engaged in work where they breathe in silicon-containing dust may develop a serious lung disease known as silicosis and some silicates, such as asbestos, cause cancer.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Silicon is one of humanity’s most useful elements. Some of its applications require fairly little processing. Silicon in the form of sand and clay is used to make concrete and brick. In the form of silicates, it is used to make mortar and stucco, enamel, pottery, ceramic, and fiberglass. Combining silicon and oxygen atoms with organic chemicals creates the rubbery polymer silicone. Silicone is important as a sealant, lubricant, and adhesive. It is used to make many products, including electrical insulation, cooking utensils, and waterproof caulk.

Silica, as sand, is a key ingredient of glass. Glass is one of the most inexpensive materials and has very useful mechanical, optical, thermal, and electrical properties. Glass can be made in a great variety of shapes for a variety of purposes, such as containers, windows, insulators.

Silicon is used in many alloys as well. It enhances the properties of metals such as iron, aluminum, and steel. Other applications, particularly semiconductor applications, require more sophisticated processing. A semiconductor is what it sounds like: something in between a conductor like copper and an insulator like glass. Silicon is a natural semiconductor.

When silicon is extremely pure and then “doped,” it becomes spectacularly useful. Doping means substituting a few atoms (say, one out of every billion silicon atoms) with atoms of a different kind, such as boron, gallium, phosphorus, or arsenic. When suitably doped semiconductors are put together, they create a junction where electrical conductivity can be controlled. In a transistor, for example, applying a voltage to one area allows electricity to flow through a connected circuit. This creates an electrical switch with no moving parts. It is the basis for integrated circuits, which make up computer chips. The computer circuitry effectively reconfigures itself from moment to moment to meet the needs of different computer programs.

In addition to computer chips, semiconductor devices also include solar cells, x-ray detectors, and LEDs (for lamps, lasers, and display screens). Silicon has long been the core material for such devices.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Silicon comes in two main forms, or allotropes: amorphous and crystalline. In each, the atoms are organized differently, resulting in a different overall structure. Amorphous silicon, in which the atoms connect every which way, is a brown powder. It can be melted and poured to make solar panels. By contrast, the atoms in crystalline silicon are arranged in a perfectly regular pattern.

The most common silicon crystal looks metallic gray, tinged slightly blue. It has a crystal structure the same as a diamond. This makes sense because carbon and silicon are neighbors. Silicon sits directly below carbon on the periodic table. They both have four valance electrons (electrons that can be shared with another atom). So, it’s not surprising that carbon and silicon’s crystals would have the same structure.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Silicon is the eighth most abundant element in the universe by mass. It is made in the cores of massive stars and distributed through space when those stars explode. New stars, planets, and asteroids all obtain large amounts of silicon this way. Silicon is the second most abundant element in the earth’s crust, after oxygen. More than 90 percent of the crust—basically all kinds of rock, clay, soil, and sand—is made of silicon-oxygen minerals called silicates. Silica, found in quartz and sand, nicely exemplifies the relative amounts. It is made from one silicon atom and two oxygen atoms. Quartz is a major source of silicon used in industry.

Silicon is prepared commercially by heating silica and carbon in an electric-arc furnace. (That’s exactly what it sounds like—a furnace that heats with an electric arc.) Several other methods can be used, too, including one with aluminum instead of carbon. These methods are fine for making amorphous silicon, a brown powder that can be melted or vaporized easily. But, for more precise applications, high-purity crystals are needed. In the Czochralski process, a seed crystal is carefully dipped, lifted, and twisted in molten silicon. The crystal structure serves as scaffolding and molten silicon atoms to attach to the crystal in a very precise way, allowing the crystal to grow. Other methods also exist to create even higher-purity crystals for specialty applications.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Phosphorus has something of a smelly history. Phosphorus—which was the 13th known element and the first element discovered after ancient times—was first isolated from human urine by German alchemist Hennig Brand in 1669. Brand wasn’t trying to discover a new element, but rather to produce the philosopher’s stone, a mythical substance that was thought to turn base metals like copper, lead, and zinc into gold.

Brand let the urine evaporate and then heated the red-hot residue, producing a phosphorus vapor that he then condensed in water. This process yielded white phosphorus, which, although incapable of producing gold, glowed in the dark and could be used as a fire starter. Brand named the substance phosphorus mirabilis, which means “miraculous light-bearer.”

In the 18th century, chemists discovered that bone ash also contains phosphorus. In the 19th century, bird and bat guano became important sources of phosphorus, which by that point had become a key ingredient in fertilizers. Today, most of the world’s phosphorus comes not from urine, bone, or guano, but from phosphate rock, which was first used to produce phosphorus in 1850. The process of making phosphorus has gotten a lot more pleasant!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Phosphorus exists in at least four allotropes, or forms, that have wildly different qualities and that are denoted by color. White phosphorus is soft and waxy, and it looks a little like brie cheese. But you wouldn’t want to eat white phosphorus; this allotrope is toxic. White phosphorus is also the most reactive of phosphorus allotropes, and it is highly flammable. It can even ignite spontaneously! In the presence of oxygen, white phosphorus glows in the dark.

Red phosphorus is stabler than white phosphorus, although it’s more reactive than the other allotropes, capable of igniting at a relatively low temperature (around 300 °C). Violet phosphorus is still more stable than red phosphorus, but not as stable as black phosphorus. Black phosphorus is like graphite in terms of similar atomic structure and electrical conductivity.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: White phosphorus was first used to make matches. However, white phosphorus is toxic, which is why, beginning in the early 1900s, laws were enacted mandating use of the much less toxic red phosphorus instead. White phosphorus’ terrific flammability is why it has been used in weapons like firebombs and smoke grenades, and in tracer bullets.

The biggest use of phosphorus is in fertilizer, with up to 75 percent of phosphorus being used in this way. Phosphorus can also be used as a preservative, in steel production, and light-emitting diodes (LEDs). In the form of phosphoric acid, phosphorus is used to give certain foods and drinks a pleasantly bitter taste. If you’ve ever had Coca-Cola, you’ve consumed phosphoric acid!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Phosphorus can join with oxygen to form phosphate (PO43−), which is used in fertilizers. Phosphate also makes many salts that are commonly found in nature, and it can be used in special kinds of glass, like the ones used in sodium vapor lamps. Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) is used in everything from fertilizers to food preservatives, anti-rust chemicals, aluminum etching, and semiconductor manufacturing. Trisodium phosphate is an important cleaning agent that’s also used to remove minerals from water.

Some organophosphorus compounds—that is, compounds with a phosphorus-carbon bond—are used in pest controls and insecticides. These compounds can be extremely toxic. The nerve agent sarin is an organophosphorus compound. While some forms of phosphorus are highly flammable, certain phosphorus compounds are useful as flame retardants. Calcium phosphates are present in bones and tooth enamel.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Scientists have found 22 phosphorus isotopes, ranging from phosphorus-26 to phosporus-47. But only phosphorus-31 is stable (non-radioactive). The longest-lived phosphorus radioisotope, phosphorus-33, has a half-life of 25 days. The least-stable isotope, phosohorus-47, has a half-life of 2 milliseconds!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Today, most phosphorus comes from phosphate rock (although some still comes from guano). Phosphate rock is a kind of sedimentary rock with lots of phosphorus-bearing minerals inside. China, Mexico, and Morocco are the world’s top phosphorus producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Sulfur, with its unappealing rotten-egg smell, has been known to humankind for thousands of years. The element is mentioned in the Torah and in the Christian Bible (the term “brimstone” refers to sulfur). Sulfur has been known in China since at least the sixth century BCE, and the Romans mined sulfur on the island of Sicily. In the ancient world, sulfur was used in sulfur matches, in bleaching cloth, in making wine, and as a medicine, among other things.

The alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan, also called Gerber, thought that all metals contained sulfur. He theorized that base metals like copper could be transmuted into gold by the right process. Although Gerber, and the alchemists who followed him, were wrong about this, their work did give rise to modern chemistry in the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries!

In the 18th century, Antoine Lavoisier, who is considered one of the first modern chemists, suggested that sulfur might be an element. In 1809, French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thénard proved this. The Frasch process, developed in the 1800s, made it possible to extract large amounts of sulfur from underground.

In recent decades, the discovery of large elemental sulfur deposits has become increasingly rare. That’s why today, most sulfur is produced as a byproduct of oil and other hydrocarbon production. But you still don’t want to smell it!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Sulfur is a non-metal that comes in several allotropes, or forms, that have different qualities. The most common allotrope, octasulfur, is lemon yellow and crystalline. Solid sulfur is odorless, brittle, and insoluble in water.
When melted, sulfur takes on a blood-red color. Spooky! Sulfur can also catenate, meaning that it can bind to itself in chains.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Sulfur has too many uses to count! Much of the world’s sulfur is used in sulfuric acid, which makes possible the production of products that range from fertilizers to explosives (including the gunpowder used in firearms and fireworks), fuels, paints, detergents, paper, rubber, concrete, and antifreeze.

In 1839, Charles Goodyear discovered that combining rubber and sulfur in the presence of heat would cause the rubber to vulcanize, meaning stiffen. This discovery led to the invention of the modern automobile tire (and, indirectly, to the creation of the Michelin Man).

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Sulfur makes many compounds. In fact, it forms compounds with every element, except the noble gases. Sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is a highly corrosive substance that has many industrial applications. Organosulfur compounds, of carbon and sulfur, contribute to the bad smell given off by decaying plants and animals, but these compounds also come in many classes and have many applications.

Sulfur dioxide is an air pollutant produced by burning coal and heating oil and that can oxidize into sulfuric acid to be precipitated as acid rain. Other sulfur compounds, such as trifluoromethyl sulfur pentafluoride, play a key role in maintaining the Earth's climate.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Scientists have characterized 24 sulfur isotopes. Four of these isotopes are stable, or non-radioactive. Ninety-five percent of naturally occurring sulfur is sulfur-32. Sulfur-35 is the only sulfur isotope with a half-life of more than three hours (its half-life is around 87 days). This isotope is formed when cosmic rays strike atmospheric argon molecules.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: By mass, sulfur is the fifth most common element on Earth. Historically, sulfur was found around volcanoes and hot springs. It’s found throughout nature in a range of minerals, including iron pyrite (aka fools’ gold), gypsum, galena, barite, and others.

In the late 1800s, German-born American chemist Herman Frasch developed the Frasch process to extract sulfur from underground formations. By heating sulfur deposits with steam, the sulfur would melt and could be pumped to the surface.
Today, most sulfur is produced as a byproduct from refining hydrocarbons, including petroleum and natural gas. China, the United States, and Canada are the world’s top sulfur producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Chlorine in the form of common table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) has been known and used for many thousands of years. In Medieval times, Arabic alchemists experimented with various chloride salts and produced hydrogen chloride gas. When dissolved in water, the salt becomes hydrochloric acid, a strong and useful acid.

In 1774, Carl Wilhelm Scheele, a Swedish chemist, heated hydrochloric acid with a mineral now known to be manganese dioxide. One of the products of the reaction was chlorine gas (Cl2). Sheele observed the dense gas and noted its yellow-green color, its choking smell, and its bleaching effect on litmus, leaves, and flowers. He saw that it killed insects.

In 1809, French chemists Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis-Jacques Thénard tried to make chlorine gas react with charcoal. If the gas were an oxide of something, as Scheele had thought, the charcoal should peel the oxygen away to make carbon dioxide and some other material would remain. The following year, English chemist Sir Humphry Davy tried the same experiment and confirmed what the French researchers had found: the technique didn’t work. Chlorine gas, he correctly concluded, was not an oxide—it was its own element. He named it chlorine after the Greek word chloros, meaning yellow green.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Chlorine is a member of the halogen (salt-forming) column, or group, on the periodic table. It is extremely reactive, with the third highest electronegativity among all the elements, after fluorine and oxygen, and the highest electron affinity. This means it has an extremely strong tendency to pull electrons from another element when bonding and releases the most energy when doing so. It readily and directly combines with nearly all elements.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Most chlorine is used to manufacture chlorinated compounds for sanitation, paper-pulp bleaching, disinfectants, and textile processing. It is also extensively used in the production of petroleum products, medicines, antiseptics, bleach cleaners, insecticides, food, solvents, plastics, paints, and many other consumer products.

About 20 percent goes into polyvinyl chloride (PVC), the third most widely used synthetic plastic. By weight, PVC is more than 50 percent chlorine. It is used for flooring, pipes, bottles and packaging, inflatable products, car interiors, wiring insulation, synthetic rubber, and many, many other things.
As a disinfectant, chlorine kills bacteria. It is used to treat drinking water the world over. It is likewise used to make swimming pools safe to swim in.

While chlorine is a daily part of our lives, its gas form is extremely poisonous. At a modest concentration of 1000 parts per million in air, it is fatal after just a few deep breaths. It was first used as a chemical weapon in World War I.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: In nature, chlorine is found in the combined state only, chiefly with sodium as table salt. Salt dissolves readily in water and therefore finds its way into the ocean over geologic time.

Chlorine is the 21st most abundant element in the earth’s crust, often found as salts in evaporated seabeds. But it is the third most abundant element in the oceans after oxygen and hydrogen! In fact, it comprises nearly 2 percent of the mass of the oceans. Some inland seas, such as the Dead Sea and the Great Salt Lake, have even higher concentrations.

Chlorine gas, hydrogen gas, and sodium hydroxide are produced by passing a current through salt water. (This manner of using electricity to separate chemicals is called “electrolysis.”). All three outputs are commercially valuable.
