sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1785, British physicist Henry Cavendish studied the air in the atmosphere and found that it was made up of mostly nitrogen and oxygen. There was, however, a third gas that Cavendish could not identify. The gas was a mystery until 1984 when Sir William Ramsey and Lord Rayleigh used spectroscopy, the study of light and matter, to identify the colorless, odorless, and tasteless gas that we know as argon. Isolating the gas helped the chemists properly study its properties.
Named after the Greek word argos (“lazy”), this inert, or nonreactive, element was the first of the noble gases to be discovered.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Argon is odorless and colorless; however, it will glow a violet color if excited by a high voltage electric field.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: If you’re working in a sensitive environment and need a cool, calm, and collected gas that won’t react to other chemicals, argon is a great choice. One of the main applications for argon is for the gas inside incandescent light bulbs. Welders also use argon to protect their weld area, and healthcare professionals use argon lasers to treat retina issues in eyes.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Compounds involving this element are rare because argon does not react with other chemicals. However, some compounds of argon have been found in cold gases and plasmas. Scientists have also been able to create molecular ions (groups of elements) that include argon. Some of these same ions have even been found in space!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Argon comes from “common” air—the air in the atmosphere that surrounds us every day. Commercial companies collect argon from the air using a process called fractional distillation where air is liquified and then heated to a temperature that releases the gases (nitrogen, oxygen, and argon) one by one.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Potassium salts have been used since ancient times for various applications. The poisonous smoke from saltpeter (potassium nitrate, KNO3) was used in ancient India as a weapon. Saltpeter was later used to make gunpowder, starting in China during the first millennium CE. Alum (potassium aluminum sulfate, KAl(SO4)2), or some variant of it, was likely used in ancient Egypt and Rome. It was later used in the Middle Ages for dyeing, having been produced in Africa and exported to Europe. And potash (potassium carbonate, K2CO3) was used in the bronze age (3300–1200 BCE) for bleaching textiles and making glass, ceramics, and soap.

Potassium itself was discovered in 1807 by English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy. He used an electric current on “caustic potash” (potassium hydroxide, KOH) to isolate the potassium. This method of using electricity to drive a chemical separation is called electrolysis, and potassium was the first of many elements to be discovered with it. Davy noted that his potassium formed metal globules, which, when dropped in water, would float and catch fire. Dancing around the water’s surface, they burned with a purple flame.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Potassium is a soft metal that’s easily cut with a knife. Pure potassium is silver in color, but it oxidizes (tarnishes) in air within minutes. Therefore, it must be kept in a non-oxygen-based liquid, such as mineral oil.

It is one of the most reactive metals and one of the most electropositive (meaning its more likely to give its electrons when bonding with other elements). It is also the second-lightest metal after lithium, light enough to float in water. As with other alkali metals (those in the first column of the periodic table), it decomposes in water. In potassium’s case, it spontaneously catches fire in water.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Potassium is essential for plant growth, and natural soils usually contain potassium. However, in farming, plants are completely harvested each year, so the potassium must be replaced by adding fertilizer. Ninety-five percent of potassium production is for fertilizer.

Important potassium salts include its chloride (for fertilizer and medicine), nitrate (for fertilizer and gunpowder), hydroxide (for soaps and detergents), and carbonate (for glassmaking). Others are used as food additives, inks and dyes, and compounds for processing certain metals, among other uses.
An alloy of sodium and potassium (NaK) is used as a heat-transfer medium.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Potassium is the eighth most abundant element in the earth’s crust. It is plentiful, though not easily extractable, in rocks such as feldspar and granite. Potassium and its salts are more easily obtained in minerals found in large deposits in ancient lakebeds and seabeds. These minerals include large deposits of sylvite (potassium chloride, KCl), as well as carnallite, langbeinite, and polyhalite.
Potash is found and mined all over the world. The largest known deposit is found at a depth of 3000 ft in Saskatchewan, Canada.
Potassium metal is isolated by electrolysis of its hydroxide (Davy’s technique) and by heated reactions between its compounds and other elements, such as carbon, silicon, and sodium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Calcium has been part of human history for thousands of years. As far back as 7000 BCE, ancient civilizations were using lime (calcium oxide, CaO) as a building material and a plaster for statues. The Romans were especially known for using lime in their cement, concrete, and mortar, calling it calx. But while they used calcium in all sorts of ways, the element itself wasn’t discovered until much later.

It wasn’t until 1789 that French chemist Antoine Lavoisier figured out that lime contained a new element. Lavoisier was a pioneer in chemistry, and he was the first to suggest that calcium was hiding inside lime as part of an oxide (an element combined with oxygen).

In 1808, British chemist Sir Humphry Davy took on the challenge of isolating calcium. Using a method called electrolysis, which involves using electricity to break down substances, Davy was able to separate calcium from the calcium oxide. This wasn’t easy though! He had to build on earlier experiments done by Swedish chemists Jöns Jakob Berzelius and Magnus Martin af Pontin, who had also been trying to isolate calcium. Davy eventually succeeded by electrolyzing calcium oxide together with mercury oxide. After the oxygen was removed, he boiled off the mercury, leaving pure calcium behind.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: The metal is ductile and has a silvery color. Chemically, it is one of the alkaline earth elements; it readily forms a white coating of nitride in air, reacts with water to produce calcium hydroxide and hydrogen gas, and burns with a yellow-red flame.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The primary use of calcium is in the form of lime, as a building material. Similarly, gypsum or calcium sulfate, the fine white powder found in abundance at White Sands National Park in New Mexico, is used in plaster of Paris, which is used to make casts to set broken bones.
Various calcium compounds are also used in food supplements and pharmaceuticals. Calcium compounds are a key ingredient in toothpaste and in antacids.

Isolated calcium metal is valuable as a deoxidizer (or desulfurizer or decarburizer, for sulfur and carbon) in the production of other metals, such as chromium, thorium, uranium, and zirconium. It is also used in steelmaking. It forms useful alloys with aluminum, beryllium, copper, lead, and magnesium. The alloy with lead is used in car batteries.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Calcium forms a lot of important compounds, like calcium oxide, carbonate, carbide, chloride, cyanamide, hypochlorite, nitrate, and sulfide.
Calcium phosphate is the primary component of bones. There is about one kilogram of calcium in a typical human being, and 99 percent of that is found in our bones.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: By mass, calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the earth's crust, after oxygen, sodium, aluminum, and iron. It is an essential constituent of bones, teeth, and shells. Never found in nature uncombined, calcium occurs abundantly as limestone (calcium carbonate), gypsum (calcium sulfate), and fluorite (calcium fluoride). Indeed, limestone is largely made from old corals, shell fragments, and fossilized debris.

In the United States and Canada, calcium is typically obtained by heating lime from limestone with aluminum to remove the oxygen. Russia and China typically use electrolysis of calcium chloride to remove the chlorine.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Scandium’s discovery was predicted years in advance, when Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published his groundbreaking periodic table—the one on which the modern periodic table is based! In 1869, Mendeleev's table predicted the existence of 10 as-yet-unknown elements. Mendeleev predicted one of these elements would have an atomic weight between 40 (calcium) and 48 (titanium). He called it “ekaboron” (meaning “like boron”) and it turned out to be the transition metal scandium.

Swedish chemist Lars Fredrik Nilson separated the oxide of scandium from a mineral called euxenite in 1879, a decade after Mendeleev’s prediction. Nilson named element 21 after the Latin word for Scandinavia. Scandium has qualities that closely matched what Mendeleev predicted for the element, thereby validating the periodic table’s predictive powers. This is still important for research today and helps guide discoveries. No crystal ball required!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Scandium is a soft, relatively light, silvery metal that, when exposed to air, takes on a yellow or pinkish tint. Scandium’s qualities are more like those of yttrium, which shares the same column, than to those of titanium, which shares the same row.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Scandium is often alloyed with aluminum because scandium-aluminum alloys are stronger than aluminum alone. These alloys also have a higher melting point, which allows them to be welded. The alloys are used in everything from aerospace components (early applications included in Soviet missiles MiG fighter planes) to sporting equipment (such as baseball bats and bicycle frames). If anyone asks you what a Soviet fighter plane and a baseball bat have in common, the answer is scandium! Scandium is also added to mercury vapor lamps to help make light that looks like sunlight.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: In water, scandium precipitates as scandium hydroxide (Sc(OH)3), which is why it’s so widely dispersed throughout the Earth’s crust. Scandium oxide (Sc2O3), also known as scandia, is the form of scandium that’s the most commercially available and serves as the starting point for scandium metal.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Naturally occurring scandium only exists as the isotope scandium-45. Scientists have documented 25 radioactive isotopes of scandium. The longest-lived isotope, scandium-46, has a half-life of around 84 days; the shortest-lived has a half-life of only nanoseconds. A nanosecond is one billionth of a second!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Scandium isn’t especially rare—it’s the 35th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust—but because it’s widely dispersed in small amounts, it is expensive to produce. Most of the world’s scandium supply comes from mines in China, Russia, and Malaysia, where it is extracted as a byproduct of uranium processing.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Titanium was discovered in 1791 in Manaccan Cornwall, Great Britain, by William Gregor, a clergyman who spent his free time collecting and analyzing Cornwall’s minerals. While examining a sample of black sand that he’d found in a Manaccan valley, Gregor spotted a strange substance that he called “maccanite.” He thought it must be a new element, but other scientists paid little attention to his discovery.

Gregor was vindicated four years later, when German chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth found an unknown element in a mineral sample that came from Hungary. Klaproth called the element “titanium,” after the Titans of Greek mythology, who were said to live beneath the earth. Not long after that, Klaproth heard about Gregor’s research and acquired a sample of maccanite, which he also found to contain titanium. Gregor was given credit for the element’s discovery, although Klaproth’s name for the element stuck.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Titanium is a shiny white metal. It isn't very dense, but it is strong, resistant to corrosion, and able to tolerate high temperatures.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because titanium is as strong as steel but much less dense, it’s used in things that need to be both strong and lightweight, like bicycles, airplanes, and spacecraft. Titanium is also used in golf clubs, which need to be tough enough to survive being thrown by frustrated players.

Titanium resists corrosion, which makes it useful for propellors and other parts of ships that are exposed to saltwater. Titanium metal connects well with bone, so it’s often used surgically for things like hip replacements and tooth implants.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Almost all the titanium used is in the form of titanium oxide. This compound is used to make things bright white, from house paint to toothpaste, or even cake icing. Because titanium oxide is good at absorbing UV light, it’s also used in sunblock.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, titanium is found in five stable (non-radioactive) isotopes (titanium-46, -47-, -48, -49, and -50). Approximately 74 percent of titanium is titanium-48.
Scientists have discovered 21 radioactive titanium isotopes. The half-lives of these isotopes range from 63 years to less than half a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Titanium can be found in minerals like anatase, brookite, ilmenite, perovskite, rutile, and titanite. You can also find it in many iron ores.

Although there is a lot of titanium in nature, titanium is more expensive than aluminum or iron because it’s difficult to process. Researchers didn't figure out how to make pure titanium metal until 1910! Large-scale titanium production only became possible in the 1940s, when Luxembourgish metallurgist William Kroll developed a new technique to produce the metal at commercial scales.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Most elements have to settle for being discovered once, but vanadium enjoys the honor of being discovered twice! Spanish mineralogist Andrés Manuel del Río was the first to find element 23. In 1801, del Río identified the new element in a sample of Mexican “brown lead” ore (which would later be known as vanadinite). But French chemist Hippolyte Victor Collet-Descotils said that del Río’s element was only chromium, and del Río took the other scientist’s word for it.

In 1831, Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström rediscovered element 23 while studying steel. Sefström named the element vanadium after Vanadis, which is another name for the Norse goddess Freyja. Later that year, German chemist Friedrich Wöhler determined that the element Sefström had discovered was, in fact, the same element that del Río had found three decades before. While del Río would be recognized as vanadium’s discoverer, the element would keep the name Sefström had chosen.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Vanadium is a bright white, corrosion-resistant metal. It’s relatively soft and ductile, meaning that you can stretch it without breaking it. Vanadium resists corrosion from acids and salt water.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Most vanadium—about 80 percent—is used in a steel alloy called ferrovanadium, which is much stronger and more corrosion-resistant than steel made without vanadium. Vanadium steel is used in everything from automobile and bicycle frames to tools and knives.
Because vanadium doesn’t absorb a lot of neutrons, vanadium alloys are often used in nuclear reactors, which rely on continually colliding neutrons to create energy.
The element is also used in vanadium redox batteries, which are a type of rechargeable battery. It’s used as a pigment in ceramics and glass, too.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Most vanadium-containing steel alloys use vanadium pentoxide (V2O5). Vanadium pentoxide is also a catalyst for producing sulfuric acid, which is used in everything from fertilizer manufacturing to oil refining and wastewater processing.
Many silver vanadium oxide compounds are used in batteries.

Vanadyl sulfate (VOSO4) is used in food supplements and experimental medications for people with diabetes or other disorders. Vanadium sulfate is often marketed as an aide for bodybuilders, although scientists are unsure whether the supplement is actually effective.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Because of its many oxidation states, vanadium has a complex chemistry. In nature, vanadium is found in one stable isotope (vanadium-51) and one unstable isotope (vanadium-50). But scientists have observed 24 radioactive isotopes of vanadium that have been created synthetically in a lab.
The longest-lived synthetic vanadium isotope is vanadium-49, with a half-life of 330 days, but most of vanadium's isotopes have a half-life of less than ten seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Vanadium appears in some 65 different minerals, including vanadinite, roscoelite, carnotite, and patronite. It’s also found in phosphate rock, certain iron ores, and sometimes in crude oils, too. However, most vanadium now comes from magnetite (an iron ore).
China, South Africa, and Russia are the biggest vanadium producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In the 1760s, German minerologist Johann Gottlob Lehmann discovered a bright red mineral in the mines of the Ural Mountains. The mineral, which he called Siberian red lead, quickly became an important pigment. In 1798, French chemist Louis Nicolas Vauquelin separated chromium from a sample of Siberian red lead. He named the new element after the Greek word chroma, meaning color. Chromium soon became important for tanning, the process of treating animal hides to make leather.

Before long, scientists including Michael Farraday and Robert Bunsen found that chromium resists acids and corrosion. Mixing chromium into iron led to the invention of stainless steel, which you’ll find in kitchen knives and appliances. Chromium can also make things shiny, like car parts and furniture legs.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Chromium is a hard, shiny, silvery-blue metal that resists corrosion. Humans are thought to need very, very small amounts of chromium in their diet, but too much can be dangerous.
Chromium’s hardness and corrosion-resistance are reasons why the element is often alloyed with other metals.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Today, around 90 percent of all leather is still tanned using chromium. However, this process produces toxic waste, so researchers are looking for other tanning methods.
Most chromium is used to make stainless steel or to give objects a shiny appearance.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Many chromium compounds are brightly colored. They can be blue, yellow, red, purple, green, or somewhere in between.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Chromium has four stable isotopes (chromium-50, -52, -53, and -54), with chromium-52 being the most common in nature.

Pure chromium is hard to find in nature. Instead, most chromium comes from chromite ores. Some forms of chromium, like trivalent chromium, are safe enough that you can find them in vitamins or nutritional supplements. Other forms of chromium, like hexavalent chromium, are toxic and can cause cancer.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most chromium comes from something called chromite, which is a mineral that’s made up of iron oxide and chromium. South Africa produces around two fifths of the world’s chromium. India, Kazakhstan, and Turkey also produce a large amount of chromium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: People have been using manganese for thousands of years, even if they didn’t always know that they were! The cave paintings at Lascaux, some of the oldest known works of art, were created in part with manganese dioxide pigments. In Ancient Egypt, glassblowers discovered that adding manganese to glass, which was naturally greenish, would make the glass transparent.

In the late 1700s, a group of Swedish chemists led by Torbern Bergman became convinced that manganese was an element separate from magnesium. Johan Gahn purified manganese for the first time in 1774, proving that manganese was indeed its own element.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: On its own, manganese metal is brittle and looks a lot like iron. There are four allotropes, or forms, of manganese, all of which are metallic. The qualities of these allotropes vary, but one form is flexible, soft, and easily cut.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Today, over 90 percent of manganese produced worldwide is used to make steel. The earliest steels had impurities that made them brittle and hard to work with. However, British industrialist Robert Forester Mushet discovered that by adding manganese to molten iron, the steel became much more malleable and easier to work with. Manganese steel, which contains even more manganese than ordinary steel, is extremely strong. It’s used for things like railway tracks, rifle barrels, and mining equipment.

Soda cans are made of aluminum alloyed with manganese to make the metal corrosion resistant. Alkaline batteries also use manganese, and manganese compounds are mixed into fertilizers. Manganese is an essential nutrient. Much as the element makes steel stronger, manganese also makes for strong bones! That's why manganese is often mixed into livestock feed.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Manganese forms many compounds. Manganese oxide, sulfate, and gluconate are used in fertilizers. Manganese dioxide is used in certain kinds of batteries, paints, fireworks, and porcelain.
A variety of manganese compounds are used to give glass different colors.

Potassium permanganate can be an oxidizing agent and has been used as a preservative for flowers and fruits. The next time you give someone a bouquet of roses, consider giving them a little potassium permanganate, too!

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Manganese-55 is a stable (non-radioactive) isotope found in nature. Manganese-53 is also found in nature, but because it is radioactive, it’s quite rare, making it useful in radioactive dating (which involves using isotopes to tell how old something is).

Several radioactive manganese isotopes have been created in laboratories. The longest-lived, manganese-53, has a half-life of 3.7 million years. The shortest-lived isotopes have half-lives of less, or much less, than one minute.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Manganese minerals are found all over the world, with pyrolusite and rhodochrosite being the most common. South Africa is the largest producer of manganese ores, followed by China, Australia, and the Gabonese Republic.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: It isn’t quite clear when iron first started to be used around the world, but the first evidence of ancient iron use came in the form of a bead discovered in an Egyptian tomb dating back to 3200 BCE. But this iron didn’t come from Earth—it came from space!

In ancient times, people had no idea that iron was so abundant on Earth. They mined it from meteorites, which could be up to 90% iron. Meteoric iron, in contrast to terrestrial iron, is extremely rare, making the iron more valuable than gold and once believed to be a gift from the gods.

Once the Iron Age came about, 1200–600 BCE, the smelting and mining of earthly iron became widespread, and people used it to create tools and weapons out of iron. Iron became more and more commonly used as civilizations learned how to heat it with carbon to make steel, a much harder metal than iron alone.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Iron is nontoxic, brittle, hard and fusible. Pure iron is very chemically reactive and rapidly corrodes, especially in moist air or high temperatures.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Arguably its most important role, iron is critical to plant and animal life by supporting the function of hemoglobin, a protein that uses iron to carry oxygen on red blood cells. Heme and non-heme iron are dietary forms of the element. Heme iron, found in meat, fish, and poultry is more readily absorbed by the body. Non-heme iron is found in both plant foods and meat and is less efficiently absorbed.

In terms of manufacturing, iron is most used to make steel with different properties. Cast iron (containing 3-5% carbon) is used for pipes and valves. Magnets can also be made of iron and iron alloys. Iron catalysts are also used to convert synthesis gas or syngas, a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide, into liquid fuels.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Iron has a broad set of applications, spanning from medical to manufacturing.
Medical iron compounds include ferrous gluconate and ferric pyrophosphate, which are used to treat anemia. Ferric salts are applied to wounds to aid healing.

When iron combines with chlorine, it makes ferrous chloride and ferric chloride. These are used in the dye industry to help fix colors and stabilize chemicals. They're also used to absorb moisture in various industries.
When iron mixes with sulfuric acid, it forms ferrous sulfate and ferric sulfate. Ferrous sulfate is important for making other iron compounds and is used in ink, fertilizer, and pesticides.

When iron combines with oxygen, it makes ferrous oxide, ferric oxide, and ferrosoferric oxide. These are used in glass and makeup pigments, to polish metals and diamonds, and in computer memory chips.
All of these compounds, iron chlorides, iron sulfates, and iron oxides, are used to clean water and treat sewage.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Iron has four allotropes (different physical forms of the same element) known as alpha, beta, gamma, and omega. The alpha form is magnetic but loses magnetism when heated into the beta form at 700°C.
Naturally occurring iron includes four stable isotopes—iron-54, -56, -57, and -58. Ten other isotopes are known to exist.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Iron is abundant in the universe! It’s found in large quantities in the sun and many types of stars. It is also a major component of siderite, a type of meteorite.

Back on this world, iron is the fourth most abundant element by mass in the Earth’s crust. The core of the Earth is thought to be largely made up of iron. While the most common iron-containing ore is hematite (frequently seen as black sands along beaches), several other minerals contain iron. Some examples include magnetite and taconite (that's on Tuesday, right?).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Cobalt blue has been used for centuries in pottery glazes, jewelry, vases, and paints. It was used across ancient civilizations and has been found in the ruins of Pompeii, porcelain from the Tang and Ming dynasties, and ancient Egyptian statues.

In 1730, Swedish chemist Georg Brandt became interested in a dark blue ore that was found in some local copper. He eventually proved that it was a new metal. Cobalt was the first metal to be discovered in the modern era, with all previously known metals having no recorded discoverers.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Cobalt has been known and loved through the ages for its brilliant blue color, but pure cobalt metal is a gray steel color. The blue color comes from cobalt-containing salts, like cobalt aluminate. Beyond its beauty, cobalt is known for its strength and magnetism at high temperatures.
Cobalt is a silver-white, hard, lustrous, and brittle metal.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Beyond having been used for centuries to produce brilliant blue colors, cobalt has some pretty impressive properties, like a high melting point and mechanical strength that make it very useful. When combined with other metals, cobalt produces superalloys (mixed metals) that stay strong even at high temperatures.

One of Cobalt’s superpowers is that it remains magnetic even at very high temperatures. Adding it to other metals makes strong magnets that can get very hot and sometimes that’s useful. For example, samarium cobalt stays magnetic up to 800°C! Cobalt's magnetism is important for recording and storing information on magnetic tapes and hard drives.
Cobalt is also used in newer batteries and to make strong coatings on drills and saws, aircraft turbines, and prosthetic bone replacements.
Cobalt is also part of an important vitamin—vitamin B-12. The vitamin, also known as cobalamin, is essential for making red blood cells, maintaining the nervous system, and stabilizing DNA.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Cobalt compounds include cobalt oxide, cobalt potassium nitrite, cobalt aluminate, and cobalt ammonium phosphate.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: One stable cobalt isotope exists in nature—cobalt-59. The other twenty-two isotopes are radioactive, with half-lives ranging from five years to less than a second.
Cobalt-60 is the most long-lived radioactive isotope and is important, medically, as a radiation therapy for cancers.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Cobalt occurs in minerals called cobaltite, smaltite, and erythrite. It is often associated with nickel, silver, lead, copper, and iron ores, from which it is most frequently obtained as a by-product (cobalt is what’s left over after the main metal is mined).
Important ore deposits are found in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, China, Canada, Australia, the Republic of Zambia, and Brazil.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: As the fifth-most common element on Earth, it comes as no surprise that nickel made its way into human civilizations early on. In fact, although the element wasn’t scientifically discovered until 1751, nickel has been found in 2,000-year-old bronze alloys. It also gained attention in the 15th century, when miners in Germany thought the silvery-white metal with a golden tinge contained copper—earning it the nickname devil’s copper or Kupfernickel. When Swedish chemist Axel Cronstedt isolated an element from the Kupfernickel mineral in the mid-18th century, he drew from its history and called the element nickel.

In the 19th century, “nickel silver” was common in plating assorted goods. The lustrous metal was combined with copper and zinc to give the appearance of silver, without containing any actual silver. The United States began using nickel mixed, or alloyed, with copper for coins in 1857. In 1866, the five-cent shield nickel, composed of 25% nickel and 75% copper, became the country’s standard 5-cent piece.

Today, we know that nickel is found everywhere—from the Earth’s core to the meteors entering our atmosphere, and throughout the earth’s crust. It is still used for plating and in coins, but the most common usage is in stainless steel and, increasingly, in the rechargeable batteries of electric vehicles.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Nickel is a silvery metal that is twice as abundant as copper and resistant to corrosion, even at high temperatures. It is often used as a plate to protect other metals from corrosion. It is hard, malleable, ductile and somewhat magnetic. It conducts heat and electricity.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Nickel is extensively used for making stainless steel and other corrosion-resistant alloys. Tubing made of copper-nickel alloy is used in desalination plants for converting sea water into fresh water. It is used extensively to make coins and nickel steel for armor plates and burglar-proof vaults.

Nickel gives glass a greenish color. Nickel plating is often used to provide a protective coating for other metals, and finely divided nickel is a catalyst for hydrogenating vegetable oils. It is also used in ceramics and in the manufacturing of some types of magnets and batteries.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Compounds of nickel have several commercial and industrial applications. Nickel chloride, nickel nitrate, and nickel sulfamate are used in electroplating baths. Nickel sulfate is used in electroplating catalysts, ground-coat enamels, and fixatives for dyeing and textile printing. Other compounds are found in fuel cells and storage batteries or used in the cores of electrical equipment.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are five naturally occurring, stable isotopes of nickel. At least 34 other isotopes are known.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: A considerable amount of nickel came to Earth from outer space—arriving as meteors landed across the globe. Ontario, for example, is responsible for about 15% of the worlds production of nickel thanks to meteoric nickel dating back millions of years. Nickel can also be extracted from terrestrial minerals such as pentlandite and garnierite.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Copper’s story is one of discovery and invention. Thousands of years ago, around 9000 BCE, early humans stumbled upon a shiny, reddish-brown metal. They quickly realized that the metal was easy to shape, allowing them to make tools and jewelry. As one of the first metals that humans ever worked with, copper sparked curiosity about how metals could be used in everyday life.

As civilizations advanced, so did their understanding and use of copper. People figured out how to melt copper ore and cast it into different shapes—a process called smelting. By combining copper with tin, they created bronze, a stronger alloy that marked the beginning of the Bronze Age, where tools and weapons became more durable. This scientific breakthrough in alloy-making transformed societies and set the stage for more exciting innovation.

One of the coolest developments in copper’s journey happened in ancient Egypt, when scientists developed Egyptian Blue, the first synthetic pigment. This brilliant blue color, derived from copper, was used to decorate tombs, temples, and statues. Copper’s role expanded beyond practicality, sparking creativity and artistic expression. No longer limited to tools and weapons that advanced work and warfare, copper became a medium for fostering art and culture.

In more modern times, copper continues to play a huge role in science and technology. During the Industrial Revolution, copper became essential for conducting electricity, leading to the rise of telegraphs, motors, and eventually the electronics we use every day. Today, researchers are still discovering new uses for copper—from next generation energy systems to medical technology. It’s amazing that such an ancient metal is still helping us push the limits of science and innovation!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Copper is a reddish metal with a bright metallic luster. It is easy to bend, and a good conductor of heat and electricity (second only to silver in electrical conductivity).

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Copper is used mostly in its metal form. About 60% of the copper produced is used for electrical wiring and cable. Copper is an excellent material for wiring because of its electrical conductivity (helps current flow), ductility (shape can change easily), corrosion resistance (won’t break down), low thermal expansion (shape doesn’t change with heat), and tensile strength (won’t break under tension).

In your lifetime, copper is likely to support you in many ways—from your smartphone and home plumbing to the wiring in your solar panels, your electric toothbrush, pots and pans, spare coins, television, and electric car. If you own a musical instrument, have a dental filling, or go for an ultrasound, you can thank copper. It’s even likely you’ll rest in it after burial (a coffin) or cremation (an urn).
Copper has wide use as an agricultural poison and can kill algae for water purification. Copper compounds, such as Fehling's solution, are widely used in analytical chemistry tests for sugar.

Copper is an essential element for the human body. We need around 1.2 milligrams of copper a day, to help enzymes transfer energy in cells. But, like Paracelsus said, "dose makes the poison" and too much copper can hurt us.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Common copper compounds include copper acetate, cuprous oxide, cupric oxide, cupric chloride, copper oxychloride, cuprous chloride, cupric nitrate, copper cyanide, and copper naphthenate.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Copper occasionally occurs natively, and is found in many minerals such as cuprite, malachite, azurite, chalcopyrite, and bornite. Large copper ore deposits are found in the US, Chile, Zambia, Zaire, Peru, and Canada. The most important copper ores are the sulfides, oxides, and carbonates. From these, copper is obtained by smelting (heating and melting), leaching (draining from), and by electrolysis (passing electric current through it).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Zinc has been used by humans for thousands of years. But for a long time, people didn’t know what they were working with!

Archaeological finds show that zinc was used to make brass as early as 1300 BCE in Greece and, later, Rome. However, it is likely that zinc only came to be separated and purified as a distinct metal starting around 1100 CE in India.

In 1746, German chemist Andreas Marggraf separated zinc from calamine—a zinc ore historically used in medicines. You may have used calamine lotion for poison ivy and other rashes. Marggraf documented the process in detail, which is why he generally gets the credit for discovering zinc in the West (even though four years earlier, British chemist William Champion had patented a process for separating zinc).

Although researchers are confident that the word “zinc” comes from the German zink, nobody is quite sure why the element took this name. One theory holds that zink comes from zinke, meaning “jagged” or “tooth-like,” perhaps in reference to the pointy appearance of zinc crystals.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Zinc is a metal that reacts with acids and alkalis; its chemistry is a lot like nickel and copper (which are also first-row transition metals). Zinc is a bluish-white metal that is hard and brittle at most temperatures. It has a relatively low melting point. Zinc tarnishes in air and its compounds tend to be colorless.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Most zinc is used in the process of galvanization, which involves applying a coating of zinc to prevent steel or iron from rusting (more than 50 percent of metallic zinc is used in galvanization). Galvanized metal is used in everything from automobiles to buildings, boats, and bridges.

Zinc is also used to produce brass (an alloy of copper and zinc), along with other metal alloys, such as aluminum solder. And zinc oxide is used in paint pigments, semiconductors, fire retardants, rubber, pharmaceuticals, and more.

Although zinc has historically been prescribed as a medication, today there are few medications that contain zinc. However, zinc is a vital trace element for humans, and you’ll still find it in vitamins and nutritional supplements.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find zinc in five stable (non-radioactive) isotopes: zinc-64, -66, -67, -68, and -70. Zinc-64 is the most common of these (about half of natural zinc is in this form).
Scientists have characterized about 25 unstable, or radioactive, isotopes whose half-lives range from 244 days (for zinc-65) to much less than one second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Zinc is produced from ores such as zinc blende (aka sphalerite) and other ores. In 2022, China was the largest producer of zinc, followed by Peru and Australia, although zinc is mined in countries around the world. Iron, aluminum, and copper are the only metals produced in greater quantities than zinc.
Up to 30 percent of the zinc produced globally comes from recycling. Some elements are too valuable to use just once!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev, creator of the periodic table, predicted the existence of element 31 based on trends in his table. Based on its position within the table (between the known elements aluminum and indium), he named the undiscovered element eka-aluminum and correctly deduced many of its properties, including its density and low melting point—all before the physical element was actually discovered!

Gallium was discovered not long after, in 1875, by chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran. He identified the element within a sample of the zinc ore sphalerite by observing its two violet lines on a spectrometer—a device that uses light diffraction to show the unique “color fingerprint” of each element. In the same year, de Boisbaudran obtained a sample of the free metal by chemically separating it from hydroxide. His name for the element comes from the Latin word Gallia, meaning Gaul, a region that once encompassed his homeland of France.

Gallium’s discovery was a landmark confirmation that the periodic table was more than just a way to classify the elements—it was a predictive scientific model. Mendeleev’s table showed that the elemental properties followed periodic trends, even for the elements we hadn’t yet discovered.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Elemental gallium has a beautiful, silvery appearance. The metal expands by 3.1 percent when it solidifies and fractures conchoidally, similar to how glass breaks in an unpredictable pattern.

Gallium is one of four metals—the others being mercury, cesium, and rubidium—that is liquid near room temperature. It melts in a person’s hands at the normal body temperature of 98.6 °F. Gallium’s liquid range is among the widest of all metals, and it has a low vapor pressure even at high temperatures.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Gallium readily alloys (or combines) with most metals and since its discovery has been widely used in alloys that require low melting points. For example, gallium alloys are used in thermometers as a safe and environmentally friendly alternative to the highly toxic element mercury.
Beginning in the 1960s, gallium’s application in semiconductor production caused a shift in commercial use, and today 98% of available gallium is consumed by the semiconductor industry.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: 95% of gallium consumed worldwide is in the form of the compound gallium arsenide. The next most common is gallium nitride, formed when gallium reacts with ammonia.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Gallium does not occur as a free element in nature but as trace amounts of gallium(III) compounds in zinc ores, such as sphalerite, and in the aluminum ore bauxite. It is extracted as a byproduct of smelting these ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Germanium was one of several chemical elements whose existence was predicted in 1869 by Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev.

The element germanium was discovered a little over 25 years later, at a mine near Freiberg, Germany. There, a miner found an unusual stone that wound up in the hands of German chemist Clemens Winkler. Winkler analyzed the mineral and found that something like 7% of its mass didn’t belong to any known element. In 1886, Winkler separated out a new element from the mineral. The element's properties matched up almost exactly with what Mendeleev had predicted for element 32, making the discovery an important proof of Mendeleev's idea that elements follow a repeating pattern in the periodic table.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Germanium is a whitish-grey metalloid (meaning that it has some properties of a metal and some non-metallic properties). In its pure state, germanium is crystalline and brittle.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Initially, there were few uses for germanium. That changed in the aftermath of World War II, when researchers figured out that germanium was a semiconductor (a material that has conductivity somewhere between that of a conductor and an insulator). Semiconductors are important components in modern electronics. Components like diodes and transistors quickly came to depend on germanium to function.

Later, silicon—which is cheaper to produce than germanium—replaced germanium in many electronics. Although germanium isn’t as popular as it used to be, it’s still used in things like camera lenses, microscopes, and thermal imaging cameras. In countries other than the United States, it’s used to help make polyethylene terephthalate (PET), a common polyester. Germanium can also be used in detectors that identify radiation sources, like at airport security—something to think about the next time you watch your shoes disappear into a scanning machine!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Germanium forms relatively few compounds. Germanium oxide is transparent to infrared light, which makes it useful in infrared spectroscopes and in other optical equipment like camera lenses. Some germanium compounds aren’t toxic to mammals, but kill bacteria, which makes them useful in medications.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are five naturally occurring germanium isotopes: germanium-70, germanium-72, germanium-73, germanium-74, and germanium-76. All these isotopes are stable (non-radioactive), except for germanium-76, which is slightly radioactive.

At least 27 radioactive germanium isotopes have been made in laboratories. The most stable of these isotopes, germanium-68, has a half-life of 271 days. The least stable, germanium-60, has a half-life of 30 milliseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Germanium is a rare element. Most commercially produced germanium is a byproduct of zinc ore processing. China is the largest producer of the world’s germanium. Canada, Finland, Russia, and the United States are also major germanium producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Arsenic is one of the most notorious elements in the periodic table, known since ancient times as a powerful poison. Its name comes from the Syriac word zarnikh, meaning "yellow" or “gold colored,” referring to a yellow mineral, orpiment, that contains arsenic. In ancient societies, the arsenic-bearing mineral was highly desired as a pigment. The Ancient Egyptians even used arsenic to gild metals.

In ancient times, arsenic had a number of practical uses, but it also gained a dark reputation. During the Bronze Age, it was mixed with copper to create arsenical bronze, a strong metal used for tools and weapons. However, arsenic's real claim to fame was its use as a poison. Because it was tasteless, odorless, and caused symptoms that resembled common illnesses, it earned the nickname "king of poisons" and "the inheritance powder." Arsenic poisoning would remain undetectable until the development of the Marsh test in the 1830s.

Although arsenic has been around for thousands of years, it wasn’t recognized as an element until much later. In 1250, Albertus Magnus, a German Dominican friar, philosopher, and scientist, isolated the element by heating soap with an arsenic compound. This marked the first step toward understanding arsenic as a separate element. In 1649, the German chemist Johann Schröder published two methods for preparing arsenic, describing more clearly how to purify the element. Even though arsenic had been known and used in different forms for thousands of years, these scientists' work that helped distinguish arsenic as its own chemical element, setting the stage for its later uses in medicine and industry.

In the 19th century, arsenic was widely used in products like green dyes for wallpaper, and in insecticides to kill pests in crops. The popular dyes Paris Green and Scheele’s Green, which contained arsenic, were eventually replaced as people learned more about how dangerous arsenic could be. By the 1940s, arsenic-based insecticides were phased out in favor of safer alternatives.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Arsenic is a metalloid, meaning that it has some qualities that are like those of a metal and some qualities that aren’t. Arsenic comes in three allotropes, or forms. The first, commonly called grey arsenic, is the most stable: it’s grey and metal-like, although it’s also brittle and relatively soft. The second, yellow arsenic, is soft and waxy, and it’s also unstable and toxic. The last form, black arsenic, is brittle and glassy.
Because arsenic isn’t a metal, it doesn’t melt when heated, but sublimes (meaning that it turns directly from a solid into a gas, without becoming a liquid first).

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: In the past, arsenic was used in pesticides or herbicides, but regulations have reduced this use. Arsenic continues to be an important component of the chemicals used to treat wood. Today, arsenic is often mixed into lead alloys, which are used in everything from bullets to car batteries, semiconductors, electrical circuits, and light-emitting diodes (LEDs).

Although arsenic is often thought of as a poison, small amounts of the element can act as a stimulant on the human nervous system. That’s part of the reason that the element has been used, at times, as a medicine. Recent studies have found that arsenic nanoparticles may be effective at attacking cancer cells!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Chromated copper arsenate is often used to make wood repellant to termites, fungi, and other pests. Gallium arsenide is used in semiconductors and other electronics.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Arsenic has one stable (non-radioactive) isotope, arsenic-75. At least 33 synthetic (laboratory-made) arsenic isotopes have been identified. The most stable of these, arsenic-73, has a half-life of a little over 80 days. Twenty-eight arsenic radioisotopes have half-lives of less than one day.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: You’ll find arsenic in minerals, with arsenopyrite being the most common. Today, most of the world’s arsenic is produced as a byproduct from processing lead, copper, cobalt, and gold ores. The United States stopped producing arsenic in 1985. In 2022, Peru was the world’s top arsenic producer, followed by China and Morocco.

Research has found that many groundwater sources around the world have dangerously high levels of arsenic. This arsenic comes from human and from natural sources. Around 150 million people around the world are now thought to be exposed to arsenic-laced drinking water, which can cause all kinds of health issues.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Selenium was discovered by Baron Jöns Jacob Berzelius, a Swedish chemist who is also credited with discovering cerium. Now considered one of the founders of modern chemistry, Berzelius stumbled upon the element quite by accident in 1817, when he noticed a reddish mud collecting in vats used to manufacture sulfuric acid.

He began experimenting on the substance and initially thought it was tellurium, in part because it apparently smelled like radishes when heated. Berzelius ultimately named this element selenium, after the Greek word selene (moon), as a complement to tellurium, which is named after the Latin word for the Earth.

In 1873, an English engineer named Willoughby Smith made a surprising discovery while testing materials for underwater telegraph cables. He was working with selenium, that still wasn’t well understood at the time. He was surprised when he noticed that selenium’s ability to conduct electricity increased when it was exposed to light. This was the first clear observation of photoconductivity, and it opened the door to a whole new way of thinking about light and electricity. Thanks to this simple observation, selenium became one of the earliest materials used in light sensors, solar cells, and even early photocopiers. It was a big moment for science, sparked by curiosity and a little bit of luck.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Selenium exists in several allotropic forms and can be prepared with either an amorphous or a crystalline structure. Amorphous selenium is either red (as a powder) or black (in vitreous form). Crystalline monoclinic selenium is a deep red; crystalline hexagonal selenium, the most stable variety, is a metallic gray.

Selenium exhibits both photovoltaic action (where light is converted directly into electricity) and photoconductive action (where the electrical resistance decreases with increased illumination). It can convert AC electricity to DC.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Selenium is a semiconductor, meaning it conducts some electricity (just not as well as conductors do). It becomes a significantly better semiconductor when light is shining on it; selenium is used in solar cells because it can produce electricity directly from sunlight.
As sodium selenate, the element can decolorize glass and make the red glass needed for traffic lights. It has many other uses, such as in photography, livestock feed, and drug production.

Humans need to consume trace amounts of selenium to stay healthy. It’s found in organ meats like kidneys and liver, but if liver pate doesn’t sound appealing, rest assured that it’s also in nuts, chicken, eggs, spinach, fish, and many other common foods.
Selenium is best enjoyed in moderation; consuming far too much can make your nails fall off. A toxic dose can also lead to brain damage, hair loss, and strong garlic breath.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Selenium forms few inorganic compounds, including selenious acid (H2SeO3), selenium dichloride (SeCl2) and selenium oxychloride (SeOCl2). Hydrogen selenide and other selenium compounds are extremely toxic and resemble arsenic in their physiological reactions.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Selenium is found in many foods and is a byproduct of refining metal sulfide ores. Today, most of the world's selenium comes from the muds produced during the electrolytic refining of copper.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Carl Jacob Löwig and Antoine Balard both discovered bromine independently, in 1825 and 1826, respectively. Löwig found the element in a sample of mineral spring water from his hometown of Bad Kreuznach, Germany. Publication of his findings was delayed, however, and in the meantime, Balard found bromine in seaweed from the salt marshes of Montpellier, France.

Balard originally named his discovery mulide, from the Latin word for “brine,” reflecting the salty marshes of the seaweed. He later changed the name to bromide, from the Latin for “stench," for similar reasons.

Even though bromine was discovered in the 1820s, it wasn’t produced in large quantities until 1858, when large salt deposits were found in Stassfurt, Germany. These salt deposits made it easier to produce bromine as a by-product of potash, and its production started to pick up.

Bromine was first used for early photography—making the light-sensitive silver layer needed for daguerreotypes. The process originally relied on iodine, but neighboring bromine proved to be better at increasing light sensitivity of photographic plates, helping to create sharper images.

By the American Civil War, doctors were using a bromine solution to treat gangrene, even before we fully understood how infections worked. Later, bromine compounds had more medical uses, like being used in sedatives and to treat seizures, but eventually, other drugs replaced them.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Bromine is the only nonmetallic liquid element and one of two elements (the other being the metal mercury) that is a liquid at standard temperature and pressure. It readily vaporizes to a stinky, reddish-brown gas at room temperature that can irritate the eyes and throat. It is also readily soluble in water or carbon disulfide, forming a red solution. When spilled on the skin, it produces painful sores. Bromine presents a serious health hazard, and maximum safety precautions should be taken when handling it.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Before lead was banned in gasoline, much of the bromine in the United States was used in the production of ethylene dibromide, a lead scavenger used in antiknock compounds, which prevent fuel from combusting in the engine at the wrong time.
Bromide salts were once commonly used as a sedative before shorter-acting drugs were available. They remain pharmaceutically useful in antiepileptics.
Bromine is also used today in water purification compounds, dyes, sanitizers, and photographic film, much like it's first commercial use in daguerreotypes.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Bromine unites readily with many elements and can take on a bleaching action, meaning it can decolorize other substances. The compounds potassium bromide and sodium bromide were used medically in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. During World War I, bromide compounds were used as poison gas.
Organic bromine compounds are also an important component of fire retardants, and more than 50% of bromine use worldwide is for this application.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Because it is so reactive, bromine does not occur as a free element in nature. Like other elements in the halogen group, it can be extracted from halide salts. It is commercially sourced from saltwater evaporation ponds as well as seawater, which contains about 85 ppm of bromine.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1898, chemists William Ramsay and Morris Travers evaporated liquid air, removing all its components. The residue that was left was the noble gas, krypton. This same fractional distillation method helped scientists discover three noble gases in the same year!

In 1960, scientists decided to define a meter using the light from the element krypton-86. They measured the meter as the distance of 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of krypton light in a vacuum, replacing an older definition that used a metal bar. This new way of measuring was much more precise! The krypton-based definition lasted until 1983, when scientists switched again, this time defining a meter as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 seconds. This change helped us measure distances even more accurately!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like most noble gases, krypton is colorless and odorless. It is characterized by several lines on the emission spectrum (the spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic radiation). The strongest spectral lines that make up krypton are green and yellow. Solid krypton is white and has a face-centered cubic crystal structure.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The most popular use of krypton is in light sources—especially in light bulbs for flashlights and cameras. Although krypton is mostly inert, it is reactive enough to combine with fluorine, which creates a useful krypton-fluoride combination used in some lasers.
Krypton is used in nuclear fusion experiments and experimental particle physics. Because krypton is a product of nuclear reactors, it is also used to detect nuclear production.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Krypton is mostly nonreactive like its noble gas counterparts, but it does react with fluorine under extreme conditions.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: The krypton we find in the Earth’s atmosphere has five stable isotopes. Krypton also has about 30 unstable isotopes and isomers. An additional isotope, krypton-78, has an extremely long half-life—9.2x1021 years! Because the isotope lasts so long before it decays, scientists consider it stable.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Krypton is one of the noble gases that has remained on Earth since its formation, and we can obtain it from the air by using fractional distillation. The concentration of krypton in the atmosphere is about 1 ppm, but the amount in space is a little more uncertain. Scientists believe there are high amounts of krypton in space based on measurements that use meteoric activity and solar winds.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: A grayish mica called lepidolite was discovered in the 1760s. It would subsequently be shown to contain lithium and potassium, and 101 years later, rubidium.

In 1861, rubidium was discovered by two famed German scientists—Robert Bunsen, inventor of the Bunsen burner, and Gustav Kirchhoff, a pioneer in electric circuits and “blackbody” radiation from hot objects. Both were experts in flame spectroscopy, a way to analyze a sample based on what colors are emitted when the sample is burned. Each element has a unique color signature. They saw that lepidolite emitted multiple bright ruby-red colors that had not been seen before. They figured out that it was a new element and named it rubidium. (Rubidium and ruby have the same Latin root, rubidus, referring to the deep-red color.)

Isolating rubidium from lepidolite proved quite complicated and challenging. But Bunsen and Kirchhoff succeeded… sort of. Rubidium spontaneously ignites and oxidizes in air, so they managed to isolate it from one compound only to immediately create a new one, an oxide. Still, they were able to measure the atomic weight, the density, and the melting point all to within a hair of their modern values. Pure rubidium metal wasn’t obtained until 1928.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Rubidium melts to a liquid metal at a little above body temperature. It is a soft, silvery-white, and ductile, being very pliable. It is the second-most electropositive element (readily donating electrons in bonding) after cesium, making it highly reactive.

It would be exciting (and dangerous) to have a sample of pure rubidium metal because of two major oxidation reactions. First, it ignites spontaneously in air. Second, like potassium and cesium (above and below it on the periodic table), it reacts violently in water. It bonds with a hydrogen and oxygen atom from the H2O, making RbOH, and sets fire to the remaining hydrogen! Therefore, storing rubidium is tricky. It must be kept in mineral oil or in an inert atmosphere.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Rubidium isn’t produced in great quantities, and its most important use is probably for physics research. However, there are some practical applications. For example, some atomic clocks use rubidium instead of cesium. Although cesium is considered a better timekeeper, rubidium atomic clocks paired with GPS have excellent accuracy at lower cost. They are frequently used in the telecommunications industry.

Rubidium is useful in medicine, too. It is processed in the body like potassium (which lies directly above it on the periodic table) and is faintly radioactive, so it can be used to track where potassium is absorbed. It can also be used to locate brain tumors because it collects in tumors more than in regular cells. Rubidium can also be used to make special types of glass and gives fireworks a red-purple color.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: The largest source of rubidium comes from the mineral pollucite. Pollucite ore is particularly abundant at Bernic Lake in Manitoba, Canada. The ore is primarily used as a source of cesium, but rubidium is also obtained as a byproduct. Similarly, rubidium is recovered as a byproduct of lithium extraction from lepidolite. It can also be sourced from other potassium minerals and brines.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Strontium is named for the town of Strontian, Scotland. A Scottish doctor, Adair Crawford, recognized that a particular ore found in the Strontian lead mines behaved differently than other ore. Another Scot, chemistry professor Thomas Charles Hope, examined the ore in greater detail in 1791. He confirmed and built upon Crawford’s observations, concluding that it contained a new element. English chemist Sir Humphrey Davy isolated the element in 1808 using electrolysis (electrical current to drive a chemical separation reaction) to split up strontium chloride.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Strontium is a soft, reactive metal. Freshly cut, it has a silvery, slightly yellowish appearance, but it rapidly turns more yellowish as it oxidizes in air. If it’s cut into small enough pieces, the pieces spontaneously ignite in air.
Natural strontium is a mixture of its four stable isotopes.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: You may not have known it, but you've probably played with strontium a lot! Strontium carbonate and other strontium salts are used to make bright red fireworks and flares. It is also used to make magnets. Strontium aluminate is the key ingredient in glow-in-the-dark toys because it is phosphorescent, another way to say it glows. When something phosphoresces, it absorbs light and slowly reemits it at a different wavelength, giving off a color.
Strontium chloride is also used in toothpaste for sensitive teeth and in refining zinc.

Strontium atoms have a natural transition between two states that can be exploited to make atomic clocks. Most existing atomic clocks use cesium atoms, but strontium is slightly more accurate. That means strontium atomic clocks are able to define, with great precision, what “one second” really is.

In addition to its chemical and atomic properties, two strontium isotopes have valuable nuclear properties. The human-made isotope strontium-89 is used to treat bone cancer. Because it behaves chemically like calcium (being in the same column on the periodic table), it goes where calcium goes—into the bones. It especially goes to the parts of bones where new cells are forming. Because cancer makes cells grow so quickly, strontium-89 finds its way to bone tumors, killing them because of its radioactivity.

The isotope strontium-90 is produced in nuclear reactors and can be obtained from nuclear waste. It is strongly radioactive, emitting high-energy particles that heat up the surrounding matter. In a device called a “radioisotope thermoelectric generator” (RTG), that heat can be used to make electrical power—like a powerful battery. With a half-life of 29 years, strontium-90 makes for a long-lived RTG. It can power important devices in remote locations where it’s not easy to replace or recharge batteries, like spacecraft, navigational or research buoys in the middle of the ocean, isolated lighthouses, and remote research stations.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are three different forms, or allotropes, of solid strontium metal. As the temperature is raised beyond 235°C, and then 540°C, the atoms rearrange themselves. They connect to one another at different angles. This gives the three allotropes a different look and feel. (Diamond and graphite—allotropes of carbon—provide a striking example of this.) If the temperature is increased past the melting point at 777°C, the last allotrope melts to a liquid.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: As of 2015, the leading producers of strontium were China, Spain, and Mexico. Even though strontium deposits are plentiful in the United States, domestic mining ended in 1959. The main sources are two whitish crystals, the minerals celestine and strontianite. Celestine (strontium sulphate, SrSO4) is more common and more available, while strontianite (strontium carbonate, SrCO3) is more rare and more useful. The sulphate form is often mined and chemically converted into the more useful carbonate.
To obtain strontium metal by itself, strontium oxide can be reacted with aluminum or strontium chloride can be separated by electrolysis.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Yttrium may be the element with the most difficult name to pronounce—although “ytterbium” and “praseodymium” are also in the running! The element is one of four named for the town of Ytterby, in Sweden, along with ytterbium, erbium, and terbium.

Yttrium owes its discovery to Carl Axel Arrhenius, a Swedish soldier and amateur chemist who, in 1787, discovered a strange black rock near an old quarry in Ytterby. Arrhenius determined that the rock was an unknown mineral, which he named ytterbite. In 1794, Johan Gadolin at the Royal Academy of Åbo identified a new oxide in Arrhenius’ mineral, calling it yttria. It was the first known rare-earth metal compound. Although the idea of a chemical element didn’t yet exist, Gadolin’s description of yttria, which contained yttrium, was so detailed that he gets credit for discovering element 39.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Yttrium has a silver color. It’s a soft, relatively stable metal, but small pieces can ignite at relatively low temperatures.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: For decades, the most important use of yttrium was in cathode tubes, which gave televisions their color. Specifically, yttrium was used to produce a red color. However, because modern TVs don’t have cathode tubes, yttrium is used less often in this way.

Yttrium aluminum garnet is used to make artificial diamonds, and it’s also used in lasers. Scientists are also using yttrium in fuel cells, which can allow cars to run on fuels like hydrogen, instead of gasoline.

In recent years, yttrium has received a lot of attention as a superconductor. Superconductors are materials that don’t have electrical resistance, making them useful for applications like MRI machines. Superconductors need to be extremely cold to function, which limits their use and makes them expensive. It was a big deal when, in the 1980s, researchers discovered that yttrium barium copper oxide was a superconductor with a relatively high operating temperature.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Most yttrium used in commercial contexts is in the form of yttrium oxide. Yttrium oxide is used to make yttrium iron garnets, which are used to filter microwaves and for other electronics applications. Yttrium can also be added to metal alloys to make them better at resisting corrosion and oxidation.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, yttrium is found exclusively in the form yttrium-89, its only stable (non-radioactive) isotope. At least 32 synthetic (laboratory-made) isotopes of yttrium have been observed. The least stable of these, yttrium-106, has a half-life of around 150 nanoseconds. A nanosecond is equal to one billionth of a second, so not much time at all! The most stable synthetic yttrium isotope, yttrium-88, has a half-life of around 107 days.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: You’ll find yttrium in every rare-earth mineral. Commercially, most yttrium comes from monazite sands. India, Madagascar, and South Africa have major monazite sand deposits. In the past, Australia, Brazil, China, India, and the United States have all been major yttrium producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The mineral zircon, coming from the Persian word zargun (meaning "gold-like"), has been around for ages—even getting shout-outs in the Bible under various aliases, like hyacinth, jacinth, and ligure. But it wasn't until 1789 that a German scientist, Martin Klaproth, realized the rock contained a brand-new element. He called it zirconia, and the race to isolate the metal was on!

A few folks tried and failed, including Sir Humphry Davy in 1808, but it wasn't until 1824 that Jöns Berzelius cracked the code. Using a mix of potassium and zirconium fluoride, he finally isolated zirconium metal. This new metal was in an impure form, though.

Fast forward to 1925, when the crystal bar process was invented by Anton Eduard van Arkel and Jan Hendrik de Boer, enabling commercial refinement of the metal. This method stuck around until 1945 when William Kroll came up with a better, cheaper solution: the Kroll process. Then, zirconium really “took off”—right into space! It was the perfect element to use in space shuttles and other high-stress applications.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Zirconium has a very high boiling point, making it perfect for high-heat applications. It’s also shiny and has a silver-white color, which is why it’s sometimes used to make wedding rings and other jewelry! Move over, gold!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Zirconium is very important for nuclear energy. Because it is so strong and resistant to corrosion, zirconium is used to form the cladding (a protective skin) on the fuel rods that act as a power source in nuclear reactors.
Because it’s such a tough element, zirconium compounds are also used in ceramics, jet engines, lamp filaments, and even space shuttle parts!

Zirconium and titanium are similar, and because of that, they’re competitive: titanium has been used for a long time in dental implants, but zirconium is looking like a better choice. Zirconium is more resistant to corrosion and less likely to cause a bad reaction in the body.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Zirconium can occur in powder and metal forms, both of which have commercial uses.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: The main ores found in zirconium are zircon (ZrSiO4), which is mined in the United States, Australia, and Sri Lanka; and baddeleyite (zirconium oxide, ZrO2), which is mined in Brazil. Major producers of zirconium include Australia, China, Indonesia, South Africa, and Ukraine.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1801, English chemist Charles Hatchett discovered niobium in a mineral sample he received from the United States. He originally named it columbium after Columbia, a term used for the US (think Washington D.C.—district of Columbia).

Because the element's properties were so similar to tantalum (directly below it on the periodic table), many scientists questioned if it was actually a new element. Between 1864 and 1866, various European chemists (Christian Wilhelm Blomstrand, Henri Étienne Sainte-Claire Deville, and Louis J. Troost) clarified the differences, proving definitively that these were two unique elements, with Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac being the first to isolate the element in its pure form.

In 1864, German chemist Heinrich Rose named element 41 after Greek mythology's Niobe, daughter of Tantalus (tantalum's namesake) given the elements' similar properties. In 1949, the name niobium was selected as the element’s official name and was adopted by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) in 1950.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Niobium is a crystalline, solid that is ductile (easily stretched without breaking) and hard. It is a shiny, white metal at room temperature and is slow to oxidize. But niobium can form a blue film when exposed to room temperature air.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Niobium is primarily used in steel production, where it is added to increase steel's strength and make it easier to weld.

To a lesser extent, niobium alloys are used for space applications, particle accelerators, and electromagnetic radiation detectors. Even though these applications only represent 10% of niobium's use, they still use a massive amount of the element. For example, together the Large Hadron Collider and the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor rely on over 1500 tonnes of niobium-alloy superconducting wires to operate.
Since it is hypoallergenic (being unlikely to cause an allergic reaction), niobium is also used for jewelry, optical lenses, and other medical applications.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Niobium is primarily found in the mineral columbite. Brazil and Canada are the top producers of columbite, but the mineral is also found across the globe in Australia and Nigeria.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Most molybdenum today comes from the mineral ore molybdenite (molybdenum disulfide, MoS2). But prior to 1778, molybdenite was often confused with graphite (a form of carbon) and the lead ore, galena (lead sulfide, PbS). In fact, the element's name comes from the Greek word molybdos, meaning lead, and molybdenite was often used like graphite. It was a darkening agent like pencil “lead” and a dry lubricant like powdered graphite.

In 1778, Carl Wilhelm Sheele, a Swedish chemist, determined that molybdenite was neither graphite nor lead sulfide. He suggested it contained a new element and named it molybdenum, after the ore. Sheele then handed his research off to Peter Jacob Hjelm, who found a way to isolate molybdenum in 1781.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Molybdenum metal is shiny, silver-white, and very hard. It has one of the highest melting points among readily available metals. It is very resistant to being stretched or compressed and is less likely to expand with heat.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: About 80% of commercially available molybdenum is used in alloys. Its high melting point, resistance to oxidizing except at high temperatures, lack of elasticity, and lack of thermal expansion (swelling with heat) make it ideal for strengthening other metals. It is particularly valuable for alloying with steel to increase strength, hardness, and resistance to corrosion. Most high-strength steels contain up to 8 percent molybdenum. It also makes valuable heat- and corrosion-resistant nickel alloys. Molybdenum alloys are used in engine parts, power tools, heating elements, and electrodes. Alloying with molybdenum also improves electrical conductivity.

Molybdenum disulfide powder is still used as a dry lubricant, just as it was hundreds of years ago. It can withstand high temperatures that would break down oil-based lubricants. Other uses for molybdenum include catalysts and pigments.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Though rare—58th in abundance in the earth’s crust—molybdenum is found in concentrated pockets, which increases its availability. It is mostly obtained from molybdenite ore. Wulfenite and Powellite are minor commercial sources. Molybdenum is also recovered as a byproduct of copper and tungsten mining operations.

Getting molybdenum metal out of molybdenite is a complex, multi-step chemical process. The process involves oxidizing (replacing the sulfide with oxide), treating and extracting with ammonia, and reacting with hydrogen gas to displace the oxide. Multiple heating steps are needed along the way. Once isolated, it is sold as a gray powder.
