sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In the late 1800s, Dmitri Mendeleev’s pioneering periodic table predicted the existence of element 43. That prediction led to something of a scientific treasure hunt, with many teams of researchers vying to be the first to find the element. After all, who wouldn’t want to be the first person to discover an element?

In 1925, a German team reported that they discovered element 43, naming it “masurium.” But because other scientists couldn’t replicate the researchers’ results, doubt remained about whether the element had really been discovered.

It wasn’t until 1937 that Italian scientists Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè officially discovered element 43. They did this using the discarded parts of a cyclotron—a kind of particle accelerator that is used to smash atoms into pieces. Segrè acquired the cyclotron parts from American physicist Ernest O. Lawrence (proving in the process that one person’s trash really is another person’s treasure). Because technetium was the first artificially produced element, Perrier and Segrè named the element after the Greek word teknet, meaning “artificial.”

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Technetium is a silvery-grey metal that looks like platinum and tarnishes slowly in moist air. The element’s chemistry is a lot like that of rhenium, its neighbor in the periodic table.
Technetium can be mixed into steel to help prevent rusting. However, because technetium is radioactive, its applications in steel production are limited.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The most important technetium isotope is technetium-99, which is made in nuclear reactors when uranium-235 fissions, or splits apart. When technetium-99 breaks down, the isotope emits a gamma ray (an electromagnetic wave like an x-ray, but with a shorter wavelength). Doctors can inject technetium in a patient and, by monitoring the gamma rays, “see” how well certain organs are working. Technetium-99 is used in millions of medical procedures each year.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Technetium is the lowest-numbered element in the periodic table whose every isotope is radioactive. The longest-lived technetium isotope, technetium-97, has a half-life of some 4.2 million years. That might sound like a long time, but not compared to the age of the Earth!

Technetium’s relatively short half-life is why scientists had such a hard time discovering the element. Among the 30 other technetium isotopes that have been identified, almost all have half-lives of less than one hour.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Technetium can be produced in particle accelerators. However, most technetium comes about as a byproduct of nuclear fission reactions, when radioactive elements, like uranium, split apart. For this reason, although technetium’s name comes from the word for “artificial,” technetium occurs naturally among uranium ores.

Most commercially produced technetium comes from spent nuclear fuel rods. But technetium isn’t found just on Earth. By analyzing the light that comes from space, scientists have figured out that certain kinds of stars make technetium, too!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Ruthenium is an unusual element in that it has been discovered twice! In 1807, Polish chemist Jedrzej Andrei Sniadecki analyzed platinum ores from South America, hoping to find a new element (the same way that William Hyde Wollaston and Smithson Tennant, who’d discovered rhodium, palladium, osmium, and iridium, had done). Sniadecki succeeded in discovering a new element in May 1808, but French chemists criticized his results, which they couldn't replicate. As a result, Sniadecki retracted his claim.

In 1827, Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius and German chemist Gottfried Osann evaluated platinum samples from the Ural Mountains in Russia. Osann claimed to have found three new metals in the samples, which he called pluranium, polinium, and ruthenium. But Berzelius was skeptical of Osann’s claims.

It wasn’t until 1844 that Russian chemist Karl Claus definitively discovered ruthenium in the platinum samples (although nobody ever found Osann’s pluranium or polinium). Claus decided to keep the name for the element that Osann had chosen, which comes from the Latin word for Russia.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Ruthenium is a hard, shiny, silvery-white metal that looks like platinum. Ruthenium is one of the rarest elements on Earth!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: About half of ruthenium is consumed by the electrical industry, where it’s used for electrical contacts, in chip resistors, and in electrodes. Another 40% of ruthenium is used by the chemical industry, especially as a catalyst (which helps make chemical reactions happen). Ruthenium can also be alloyed with platinum to make the platinum harder, or it can be alloyed with other metals to improve their durability and corrosion resistance.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Ruthenium(III) chloride is among the most common commercially available forms of ruthenium. Ruthenium bonds readily with carbon. Some ruthenium compounds have recently been used in solar panels to convert the sun’s energy into electricity.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find ruthenium in several stable, or non-radioactive, isotopes—seven of them, to be precise: ruthenium-96, ruthenium-98, ruthenium-99, ruthenium-100, ruthenium-101, ruthenium-102, and ruthenium-104.
Scientists have discovered 27 radioactive isotopes, with half-lives ranging from around one year to less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Ruthenium is part of the platinum group of metals. As a result, it’s usually found in ores alongside other platinum group metal elements—like osmium, iridium, and, you guessed it, platinum.
Most ruthenium is produced as a byproduct of nickel processing. The biggest ruthenium producers are South Africa, Russia, and Zimbabwe.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Rhodium was discovered in 1803 by British chemist William Hyde Wollaston. Wollaston had already discovered the element palladium, but for some chemists, discovering one element isn’t enough!

Wollaston had been experimenting on a sample of platinum ore that had been smuggled out of Latin America and acquired by his business partner, chemist Smithson Tennant. Tennant and Wollaston were working to develop a way to purify large amounts of platinum.

By dissolving the platinum ore in the acid mixture aqua regia—whose name means “royal water”—Wollaston was able to carry out a process that eventually yielded rhodium metal. Wollaston named the element after the Greek word “Rhodon,” meaning “rose,” in reference to the reddish tint of the sodium rhodium chloride he produced.
As it happened, Tennant discovered the elements osmium and iridium in the same ore sample that Wollaston had found rhodium. Forget two birds with one stone—it's more like three elements, one ore!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Rhodium metal is silvery white and hard, and it looks a lot like platinum. However, rhodium has a higher melting point and lower density than platinum.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: For a long time after rhodium was discovered, no one was quite sure what to do with it. As a result, it wasn’t used much. That changed in the 1970s, when Volvo developed the three-way catalytic converter, which helps remove harmful chemicals from automobile exhaust. Today, around 85% of rhodium is used in catalytic converters.
The next biggest use of rhodium is in the glass industry, which uses rhodium as a coating that can protect glass and make it more reflective.

In the chemical industry, rhodium is used as a catalyst in the production of nitric acid and acetic acid. Rhodium also plays a role in the production of menthol, which you’ll find in everything from chewing gum and cigarettes to toothpaste. You can thank rhodium for your fresh breath!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Unlike other elements, rhodium doesn’t turn into an oxide when heated: rhodium will absorb oxygen from the atmosphere, but then release it again once it cools off.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, rhodium comes in just one isotope—rhodium-103. Scientists have made around twenty unstable, radioactive, rhodium isotopes, with half-lives ranging from over four years to much less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Rhodium is one of the rarest elements, and it’s not easy to separate from the elements that often are found alongside it, such as gold, palladium, platinum, and silver. Most rhodium—more than 80% produced annually—comes from platinum ores mined in South Africa. Russia and Zimbabwe also produce rhodium.
Worldwide, only around 20 tons of rhodium are produced each year. Rhodium is also obtained by recycling, oftentimes from catalytic converters in vehicles.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: If you discovered a new element, what would you do? Wouldn't you want to tell people about it right away? Not British chemist William Hyde Wollaston...

In 1802, Wollaston was primarily focused on figuring out how to process large amounts of platinum ore. During his research, Wollaston inadvertently discovered a new element—palladium—in some platinum ores from South America. Wollaston named the element after the recently discovered asteroid—Pallas, which in turn had been named after Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom, warfare, and handicraft.

Announcing his discovery would have revealed his methods for purification and compromised his business that relied on that process to purify platinum. Instead of claiming the discovery, Wollaston anonymously sold some samples of palladium, teasingly advertising the metal as “new silver” and tempting other scientists to identify it—perhaps in an attempt to solicit peer review.

Irish chemist Richard Chenevix wrongly concluded that the metal was an alloy of platinum and mercury. Despite being wrong, Chenevix was awarded the Royal Society's most prestigious award, the Copley Medal, for his work. Knowing the award was undeserved, Wollaston anonymously offered a reward to anyone who could reproduce Chenevix's experimental claims.
Ultimately, Wollaston revealed himself and announced his discovery of palladium in 1805, disclosing his process for isolation and proving that the substance was in fact its own element.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Palladium is a shiny and silvery white metal that looks a lot like platinum. It’s not terribly toxic, as far as metals go. Relative to the other platinum group metals, it has a low melting point, and it isn’t very dense. Because palladium doesn’t interact with oxygen at room temperature, it won’t tarnish.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Most palladium is used in catalytic converters—the part of a car’s exhaust system that turns harmful emissions, like carbon monoxide, into less harmful ones, like carbon dioxide. Palladium helps clean the air we breathe!

That’s not all palladium is used for, though. Palladium can absorb up to 900 times its weight in hydrogen gas, which makes it useful in separating and purifying hydrogen. Increasingly, palladium and other platinum group metals are being used in fuel cells, which can turn hydrogen into electricity.

Other uses for palladium include ceramic capacitors, which are used in laptop computers and smartphones. If you’ve ever seen someone sporting a piece of white gold jewelry, you’ve probably seen palladium: white gold is often produced by alloying gold with palladium.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find palladium in seven isotopes. Six of these are stable (non-radioactive): palladium-102, palladium-104, palladium-105, palladium-106, palladium-108, and palladium-110. Palladium-106 is the most common isotope, with around 27% of palladium occurring in this form. Palladium-108 gets second place at around 26.5% of naturally occurring palladium.

Palladium-107 is unstable (radioactive) but it still has a very long half-life (around 6.5 million years) compared to other radioactive elements. Scientists have created many radioactive palladium isotopes, with half-lives ranging from 21 hours to less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most palladium comes from South African ores, although Russia and Zimbabwe are also major palladium producers. Palladium ores often contain other platinum group metal elements, such as platinum, rhodium, and ruthenium. Because palladium is often used in automobiles’ catalytic converters, which can be recycled, recycling is also a major source.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Humans have been fascinated by silver since prehistoric times. Archaeologists have found evidence of silver being separated from lead as far back as 3000 BCE! By the time of the Greeks and Romans, silver was a huge part of the economy, with coins and jewelry made from this shiny metal. Silver mines were so rich with metal that miners could simply extract silver from the rock by hand! Silver production came to a screeching halt with the fall of the Roman Empire and didn’t pick back up until hundreds of years later.

By the 1500s, silver became even more important with the rise of the Spanish empire. The Spanish "piece of eight" became the world’s most famous currency, used by explorers, traders, and especially pirates! The Spanish peso became the first world currency and served as the basis for the Japanese yen, Chinese yuan, and US dollar. The discovery of silver in the Americas set off a silver rush that changed global trade forever.

But silver isn’t just about wealth and trade—it’s packed with myth and mystery, too. In ancient folklore, silver was said to have magical powers, like being able to detect poison or cross into the magical world of fairies. The idea of a "silver bullet" comes from legends about its ability to defeat supernatural creatures, like werewolves and witches. Now, we use the phrase to describe anything that’s a perfect solution to a tough problem. Throughout history, silver has been more than just a metal; it’s been a symbol of protection, purity, and power.

Today, silver is still a major player in the world economy, with about one-fifth of it being recycled. Whether it’s in coins, jewelry, technology, or tales of magic, silver’s shine has captivated the world for millennia!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Pure silver has a brilliant white metallic luster. Silver isn’t very strong, which is why ancient societies didn’t use it in metallurgy, but instead used it as a form of money or in art. Silver is a little harder than gold, and it’s very ductile—meaning it can be easily stretched—and malleable. It can be hammered or pressed into shape without cracking. Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of all metals; electricity flows easily through silver, making it ideal for electronics.

Polished silver is the best-known reflector of visible light, but silver quickly interacts with sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide in the air, making the metal tarnish. Silver is mildly toxic, and inhaling silver dust can make you sick.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Silver has many uses. Sterling silver—an alloy containing 92.5% silver mixed with another metal—is used in jewelry (or “bling,” as the ancients would have it).
Silver is used in dental fillings, solder and brazing alloys, electrical contacts, and high-capacity batteries. Silver is also used in solar panels, TV screens, and automobile parts.

Thanks to its antimicrobial properties, silver is frequently used on high-touch surfaces—such as door handles, medical equipment, and even bank pens—to help reduce the spread of germs. Silver nanoparticles can also be used in clothing to kill odor-causing bacteria and keep you smelling fresh.
Although silver seems rare, it’s just about everywhere you look!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Silver forms many compounds that have lots of varied uses. Silver fulminate is a powerful explosive. Silver nitrate, bromide, and iodide are sensitive to light and played important roles in the history of photography.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, silver is found almost equally in one of two isotopes—silver-107 or silver-109. These isotopes are produced in stars and supernovae. Scientists have identified 28 unstable, or radioactive, isotopes of silver.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most silver comes from lead, lead-zinc, copper, gold, and copper-nickel ores. Today, Mexico, China, and Peru are top silver producers. Recycling is trendy in the silver world, with a fifth of global supply coming from recycled silver.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In the early 1800s, doctors in Germany made medicines out of a substance called calamine to help with ailments like swollen joints. But sometimes these medicines, that were supposed to be white, turned yellow! In 1817, Friedrich Stromeyer, a curious doctor, figured out that the color change only happened when the calamine had a certain material in it. He separated out the material and discovered it was a new element! He called it cadmium, after the Greek word for calamine—kadmeia.

However, at around the same time that Stromeyer made his discovery, two other German scientists—K.S.H. Hermann and J.C.H Roloff—also discovered cadmium. Although Stromeyer generally gets the credit for discovering the element, historians aren’t sure who technically discovered cadmium first!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Cadmium metal, which is soft and shiny, looks a lot like silver. Cadmium melts at a low temperature. It’s also ductile, meaning that it can stretch without breaking. Cadmium metal doesn’t corrode easily, which is why the element gets used in electroplating. However, cadmium is poisonous and can cause illnesses like cancer.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Almost all cadmium is used in rechargeable batteries. These batteries can power tools, portable computers, and household appliances, among other things. Because cadmium doesn’t corrode easily, it can be used for electroplating, which involves protecting a metal by coating it with a thin layer of a different metal.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Cadmium can be bought as an oxide, chloride, or sulfide. Cadmium sulfides range in color from yellow to maroon, which is why they’re often used in paints or dyes. Mixing a little cadmium into another metal can help make the metal stronger, or better at conducting electricity, or easier to melt, among other things.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are eight isotopes of naturally occurring cadmium, two of which are radioactive.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Cadmium can be found in ocean water and in the Earth’s crust, although it’s relatively rare. Most cadmium comes from processing zinc, copper, and lead ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Indium was discovered in 1863 through the teamwork of Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Richter at the Freiberg School of Mines in Germany. Reich was investigating a zinc-containing mineral that he believed might also contain the recently discovered element thallium. He obtained a solid, yellow substance from the mineral sample that he thought was thallium sulfide. However, his spectroscope—a device used to look at the color “fingerprint” of an element—showed a line pattern that wasn't just different from the unique pattern of thallium—it didn't match any known element!

Because he was color blind, Reich asked Hieronymus Richter to take a look at the pattern on the spectroscope. Richter could see that one of the lines was a brilliant violet. This eventually gave rise to the name indium for the new element, from the Latin word indicum, meaning violet. Together, Reich and Richter isolated indium and announced its discovery.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Just like neighboring tin, indium is a silvery-white metal with a brilliant luster. It is extremely malleable and ductile and soft enough to cut with a knife.
The pure metal gives a high-pitched "cry" when bent as its tiny crystals rub against each other.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The first large-scale use of indium was as a stabilizing agent in alloy coatings applied to aircraft engine parts during World War II. Today, indium alloys with low melting points are used in devices like heat-triggered fire sprinklers and semiconductors. Indium has been called the “metal vitamin” because of how greatly small amounts can improve the properties of other metals.

Since the 1990s, indium has most commonly been used to make indium tin oxide (ITO), which conducts electricity, "wets" glass (meaning it bonds more strongly to glass surfaces than it does to itself), and is transparent. These characteristics make ITO the perfect film for liquid-crystal display (LCD) screens and touch screens, earning indium designation as a technology-critical element. Because of its anti-corrosive properties, ITO is also used in energy-saving reflective finishes on the windows of tall buildings and as a component of high-absorption solar panels.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Indium is most often found as a small component of zinc sulfide and (less commonly) lead ores. Most indium is obtained as a byproduct of smelting these ores. Indium is about as abundant as silver or mercury, but until 1924, only a gram or so constituted the world's supply of this element in isolated form. Today, about 900 metric tons of indium are produced annually.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The discovery of tin and its impact on metalworking marked a major turning point in human history. Around 3500 BCE, metalworkers in what is now Turkey discovered that adding tin to copper created a stronger metal—bronze. This discovery led to the Bronze Age, when people started using bronze to make tougher tools, weapons, and even jewelry. Bronze, made from about 10% tin and 90% copper, was much harder than pure copper. This combination of metals advanced technology and allowed civilizations to thrive.

By 1000 BCE, large deposits of tin were discovered in England, becoming one of the most important sources of tin in the world. The tin was traded across the Mediterranean, fueling the bronze production that powered early European and Middle Eastern civilizations. The importance of tin in trade and industry was so significant that it motivated the Roman invasion of Britain in 43 CE, as the Romans sought control over the lucrative mines.

By the 1300s, tin was being used as a protective coating for other metals, a process known as tinning, to prevent corrosion. This process eventually led to the development of tinplate in the 1600s, which involved dipping sheets of iron into molten tin. Tinplate became widely used for making everything from cookware to preserving food in cans—a technique patented by Peter Durand in 1810.

Today, tin is still widely used across the world with 80 billion tin cans produced every year. It continues to be a valuable and versatile metal with its ability to resist corrosion and its use in float glass production (a process that makes perfectly flat glass) for windows. Today, tin is also being used in energy-efficient glass coatings and thermal insulation. As new green technologies develop, tin is set to play a key role in making our world more sustainable!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Ordinary tin, or white tin, is a silver-white metal. It is soft, malleable, somewhat ductile, and has a highly crystalline structure. A bar of tin can be bent by hand, breaking its crystals and producing an audible “tin cry”—a high-pitched creaking sound.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Probably the best-known application of tin is the tin can. It is actually tin-plated steel; the tin prevents corrosion. However, tin is most useful when mixed into an alloy with other metals. Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. Solder, used for permanently binding metals together (including electrical contacts), is an alloy of lead and tin. Organ pipes are also lead and tin. Pewter, often used in metal dishes, decorative items, and jewelry, is an alloy of tin, antimony, copper, and bismuth (and sometimes silver).

A crystalline alloy of niobium and tin is superconducting at very low temperatures. (Currents flowing through ordinary conductors lose energy by generating heat. But superconductors conduct electricity with no energy loss.) This allows the construction of relatively small superconducting magnets, just a couple kilograms, that consume virtually no power. Yet they generate magnetic fields as strong as those of a multi-ton, high-power electromagnet.

Tin is also useful in glassmaking. Window glass is made by floating molten glass on top of molten tin to get flat, parallel surfaces. And tin salts sprayed onto a glass surface produce an electrically conductive coating. These can be used for panel lighting or frost-free windshields. And transparent, conducting films, like in liquid-crystal displays, are often made from tin oxide.

Finally, in organic chemistry applications, “organotin” compounds are especially valuable as PVC-plastic stabilizers and biocides. Biocides include pesticides, fungicides, algaecides, wood preservatives, and antifouling agents.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: At normal pressure, tin has two allotropes, or internal crystal structures that result in different physical properties and appearances. The element switches from one to the other at 13.2°C (55.8°F).

Gray tin, or alpha tin, exists below 13.2°C. It is a dull gray powder. It is also a nonmetal, held together internally by covalent chemical bonds (shared electrons between atoms). When heated above 13.2°C, it changes into white tin, or beta tin, the metal. While white tin has several uses, gray tin has few, other than some highly specialized semiconductor applications. To prevent white tin from degrading into gray tin at coolish everyday temperatures, small amounts of antimony or bismuth can be mixed into it. Other metal additives also help control the transition from white to gray.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Tin is found chiefly in the mineral cassiterite (tin oxide, or stannic oxide, SnO2). This and other tin-containing minerals are usually found with granite. Most of the world's supply of tin (from cassiterite) comes from Asia and South America. Tin is extracted from the oxide by heating cassiterite ore with coal in a furnace. The carbon in the coal peels off the oxygen to make CO2, leaving just tin behind.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The name “antimony” comes from the Greek words anti (meaning “against”) and monos (meaning “alone”). It is “a metal not found alone,” so named because it rarely occurs in its pure elemental form. Although it bonds readily with heavy metals such as copper, lead, and silver, antimony is a chalcophile at heart, meaning its preferred companion is sulfur. Thus, the most common form of antimony is the mineral antimony trisulfide (Sb2S3), also called stibnite. It is unknown who first isolated antimony in its pure, elemental form—or when—but as a mineral it has been part of human history for thousands of years.

Like many elements, antimony’s symbol (and our word for its sulfide form, stibnite) comes from its Latin name, stibium (Sb), which in turn comes from the ancient Greek word for “mark.” The name is a reference to the practice of using crushed stibnite as an eyeliner and mascara, both to accentuate the eyes and to protect them from diseases and the sun. This practice dates to 3000 BCE, when it was popular in the Middle East and much of Africa.

In the first century CE, Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder—who is often credited with first using the term “stibnite”—described its medicinal uses and offered a curious warning that heating stibnite for too long would produce the element lead. The product he was referring to was most likely pure antimony. In the Middle Ages and beyond (as late as the 1800s), antimony remained in vogue as a remedy for various ailments. In tablet form, it was commonly used as a laxative capable of being ingested, recovered, and re-ingested. Despite a long tradition of medicinal, cosmetic, and material use (in pigments, glazes, and pewter), we now know that antimony and many of its compounds are toxic, with health effects comparable to those of arsenic poisoning.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Pure antimony is brittle, flaky, and easily powdered. It is one of five elements that, like water, expands as it cools, and it lends this property to some of its alloys. Antimony is a metalloid, meaning its characteristics fall somewhere between those of metals (to which it is chemically most similar) and solid nonmetals (with greatest similarity to sulfur). It is a poorer conductor of heat and electricity than most metals.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Antimony is highly valued for its ability to increase the hardness and strength of metals. It is often paired with lead, an almost buttery-soft metal in its pure form. Lead-antimony alloys (or mixtures) are durable and corrosion-resistant, especially with the addition of tin, antimony’s neighbor to the left on the periodic table. The major uses of this alloy are for solder, bullet castings, cable sheathing, and, most commonly, the grid plates and terminals of lead-acid storage batteries.

Antimony in its pure form is a critical “doping agent” in the manufacture of semiconductor devices. Semiconductors are elements like silicon that fall near the middle of the electrical conductivity spectrum—a range of ability to conduct electricity. Adding antimony to a semiconductor, called doping, shifts the material’s electron configuration and can increase its conductivity by several orders of magnitude. Antimony-doped semiconductor devices include lasers, solar cells, and the microchips used in modern computing.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Antimony trioxide (Sb2O3) is a component of the flame-retardant compounds applied to everyday items like mattresses, toys, electronic devices, and car seat covers. These compounds account for more than half the annual consumption of antimony in the United States. Sb2O3 is also used to facilitate chemical reactions in the production of plastics and rubber and is added to some enamels, ceramics, and glass as an “opacifier” to reduce their transparency, making them harder to see through.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Besides the stable, grey, metallic form, there are three allotropes (or forms) of antimony that are only stable under certain conditions: black, yellow, and explosive white.
Black antimony forms when antimony vapor cools rapidly. It has no definite shape and is susceptible to spontaneous combustion. It transforms into the stable, metallic form of antimony above 100° C.
Yellow antimony is the most unstable allotrope and forms when the compound stibine (SbH3) oxidizes below -90° C. Above this temperature, it will transform to black antimony.

White antimony is a solid solution of antimony trichloride (SbCl3). It can be made to explode easily by scratching it with a sharp object; when it vaporizes, heat is released and a toxic cloud of SbCl3 is emitted as the elemental antimony returns to its stable, metallic form.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Antimony is almost always encountered as a component of mineral ores, mainly stibnite, from which it is extracted and purified. The first recorded discovery of naturally occurring pure antimony was not made until 1783 in Sweden. Today, more than 50% of the world’s antimony is mined in China. As an alternative to mining, it can be extracted from lead, copper, and silver ores during the smelting process.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In the early 1780s, Austrian chemist Franz-Joseph Müller von Reichenstein began investigating a gold ore that’d been found in a Romanian mine. The ore contained a strange substance that Müller thought must be bismuth sulfide. This turned out not to be correct, and Müller then declared that the substance was an unknown metal that was a lot like antimony.

After three years of research, Müller discovered that the new metal didn’t resemble antimony so much after all. For this reason, Müller took to referring to the substance as aurum paradoxium (paradoxical gold) and metallum problematicum (problem metal). Even the best chemists get frustrated now and then!

Müller published a paper in a journal, announcing the discovery of a new element. But because the journal wasn’t well known, the announcement didn’t get much attention. In 1796, Müller sent some of the gold ore to famed German chemist Martin Klaproth. Klaproth confirmed that the metal (which would turn out to be a metalloid rather than a true metal) was a new element. Klaproth chose the name tellurium for the element, from the Latin word tellus, meaning Earth.

This name was in keeping with the supposed correspondence of certain metals with the planets. For example, the Moon was associated with silver, Mars with iron, Saturn with lead, Mercury with mercury, and so on. When Klaproth discovered uranium in 1789, he named the element after Uranus. So the name “tellurium,” which connected the new element with the Earth, made sense!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Tellurium is a semi-metal that’s commonly processed into a grey powder. The element has two allotropes, or forms. One of these allotropes is crystalline, silvery, brittle, and easily crushed. The other allotrope is an amorphous black-brown powder. Tellurium is a chalcogen, meaning it shares qualities with oxygen, sulfur, selenium, polonium, and livermorium.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Today, most tellurium is used in cadmium telluride photovoltaic cells. Tellurium is helping make the transition to renewable energy possible!

Previously, most tellurium was used in steel alloys. By adding tellurium to steel, steel becomes a lot easier to machine. Tellurium has also been used to catalyze reactions in oil processing, in vulcanizing rubber, and in the ceramics that make certain electronic devices function.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Tellurium suboxide has been used in some types of CDs and DVDs. When tellurium bonds with halogens like chlorine, tellurium can take on the electron configuration of xenon.

Gold and silver are often found compounded with tellurium. Cadmium telluride, a compound of cadmium and tellurium, is used in photovoltaic cells. Other tellurium compounds have been used as brown or blue ceramic pigments. Diphenyl ditelluride can be used to remove oxygen from, or reduce, certain organic compounds.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, tellurium is found in eight isotopes. Six of these—tellurium-120, tellurium-122, tellurium-123, tellurium-124, tellurium-125, and tellurium-126—are stable (non-radioactive). Tellurium-128 and tellurium-130 are unstable (radioactive), but they both have very long half-lives. In fact, tellurium-128 has the longest known half-life of any radioactive element: its half-life is 160 trillion times the age of the known universe!
Researchers have created 31 other tellurium isotopes. All these isotopes have half-lives of 19 days or less.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most tellurium is extracted from the byproducts of copper ore processing. Tellurium prices have gone up in recent years as demand has increased, especially as the metal has been used in solar cells. The United States, Canada, and Peru are the top tellurium producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Iodine has a colorful history—literally! It was discovered in 1811 by Bernard Courtois, a French chemist, whose family produced saltpeter, a key ingredient in gunpowder. While prepping one of the ingredients necessary for saltpeter, Courtois accidentally added too much sulfuric acid, causing a cloud of violet vapor to appear! When the vapor cooled, dark crystals formed. Courtois knew he was onto something new, but he didn’t have the resources to keep investigating.

Several scientists began studying the substance, including Charles Desormes, Nicolas Clément, and Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Gay-Lussac confirmed that the mysterious violet substance was a new element, calling it "iodine", from the Greek word for violet, iodēs. Around the same time, British chemist Sir Humphry Davy also identified it as a new element. There was some debate over who figured it out first, but everyone agreed that Courtois had been the first to isolate iodine.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Iodine is a bluish-black, lustrous solid, volatizing at ordinary temperatures into a blue-violet gas with an irritating odor; it forms compounds with many elements, but is less active than the other halogens, which displace it from iodides. Iodine exhibits some metallic-like properties. It dissolves readily in chloroform, carbon tetrachloride, or carbon disulfide to form beautiful purple solutions. It is only slightly soluble in water.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Iodine is an essential element for life. It plays an important role in thyroid function, helping to control the body’s growth rate. To make sure people get enough iodine, it is often added to table salt, called iodized salt.

Iodine is also used in sanitation systems and as topical antiseptic to kill germs and bacteria. In its radioactive form, it can help visualize the inside of the body, helping doctors diagnose medical issues and disease. Other applications include cloud seeding, dyes, and photography.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Iodine is fairly rare but is found in both the Earth's crust and in ocean water. There is a higher concentration of iodine in the ocean than in the Earth's crust. Some ocean plants such as seaweed have a high concentration of iodine. It is also found in underground brines (concentrated salt water) near oil and natural gas reserves.
Ultrapure iodine can be obtained from the reaction of potassium iodide with copper sulfate but several other methods of isolating the element are known.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: After William Ramsay and Morris Travers successfully collected neon, argon, and krypton from liquid air in 1898, they wondered if other gases were in the atmosphere. One day, they received a high-tech gift from wealthy businessman Ludwig Mond—a new liquid-air machine that was able to collect larger amounts of Krypton. After repeating the process several times, they eventually collected a heavier gas that glowed a beautiful blue color when isolated in a vacuum tube. This gas did not react during their experiments, so they concluded that they had found another member of the inert gas group and named it xenon after the Greek word xénos, meaning 'foreign(er)', 'strange(r)', or 'guest'.

As decades passed, scientists continued to study xenon, all contributing to our modern understanding of the noble gas. In the 1930s, Harold Edgerton studied the light created by sending electricity through xenon gas. From1939 to 1951, Albert R. Behnke Jr., Nikolay V. Lazarev, and John H. Lawrence, investigated the anesthetic properties of xenon. In 1962, Neil Bartlett was able to combine xenon and hexafluoride and created the first known compound. Most recently, in the 1980s, IBM scientists used new technology to position xenon atoms on chilled crystal nickel, marking the first time atoms were purposefully positioned on a flat surface.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Though xenon can form some compounds, it is mostly nonreactive and therefore considered inert and a member of the noble gas group. Xenon is about 4.5 times denser than the Earth's atmosphere at sea level. It absorbs red light when metallized, turning a bright sky-blue color, and it turns lavender when combined with electricity.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because xenon can emit a bright blue color, it is useful in some light sources like high-speed light bulbs used for photography, tanning beds, lamps used for food preparation and processing, and lamps used in ruby lasers. It can also be used to keep satellites and some spaceships in orbit by accelerating the high-mass ions. For example, NASA's Xenon Ion Drive engine fires a small number of xenon ions at high speed (146,000 km/hour for the Deep Space 1 probe). In addition, xenon is used in when producing 5-fluorouracil, a drug used to treat certain types of cancer. Finally, xenon is used as an oxidizing agent in nuclear energy fields.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Before 1962, most scientists assumed xenon was unable to form compounds like most other noble gases. In recent years, new discoveries have shown that xenon, as well as other members of zero valance elements, do form compounds. Among the compounds of xenon now reported are sodium perxenate, xenon deuterate, xenon hydrate, difluoride, tetrafluoride, and hexafluoride. Xenon trioxide, which is highly explosive, is another compound that has been achieved.
Xenon can also combine with fluorine to create three fluorides (XeF2, XeF4, and XeF6), oxygen to create three oxides (XeO3, XeO4, and XeO2), and other less electronegative compounds like carbon.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Natural xenon is composed of nine stable isotopes. In addition to these, 20 unstable isotopes have been characterized.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Xenon is available in very small amounts in Earth’s atmosphere. Like other noble gases, it is obtained through evaporating liquid air, but can also be found in the gas emitted by mineral springs.
Xenon can also be found in space—though limited on Earth, the Sun, and some asteroids, it is found in large quantities on Jupiter. It is also formed during supernova explosions.
Finally, nuclear fission produces some stable and long-lived isotopes of xenon.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Robert Bunsen (the German chemist who invented the Bunsen burner) and Gustav Kirchhoff (a German physicist best known for his work on electrical circuits and “blackbody” radiation from heated objects) discovered cesium together by flame spectroscopy.

Spectroscopy is a method of chemical identification based on the specific colors (wavelengths) of light emitted or absorbed by an element. It was done with a spectroscope, which Bunsen and Kirchhoff invented one year earlier. Their spectroscopic observations of flames from evaporated mineral water from Dürkheim, Germany, included a combination of several prominent blue lines (specific shades of blue) that had not been seen by spectroscopy before. Bunsen and Kirchhoff concluded that there was a new element present and named it after the latin word caesius, which means bluish gray. Cesium was the first element to be discovered by spectroscopy.

While spectroscopy made it possible for Bunsen and Kirchhoff to identify cesium, their efforts to isolate the element were unsuccessful. It was first isolated in 1882 by Swedish chemist Carl Setterberg.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Cesium is a shiny alkali metal with a pale gold color. Alkali metals form the first column of the periodic table. Like the other alkali metals, cesium is ductile (stretchable) and soft enough to be cut with a knife.

Unlike most other metals, cesium has a very low melting point; it is a shiny metallic liquid above 28.5°C, slightly above room temperature. Only five metals are liquid at or near room temperature. The other four are gallium, mercury, rubidium, and francium. Rubidium and francium sit immediately above and below cesium on the periodic table.

Cesium is extremely reactive. It reacts explosively with water, especially cold water, sometimes shattering the water container. It is so reactive because it is the most electropositive element. That means it is the most likely of all the elements donate an electron to another element, making that element into a negative ion and making cesium into a positive ion so the two can form an ionic bond between them.
It is also the most alkaline (highest pH) element. It is a strong enough base that it eats through glass.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The most well-known application of cesium is the atomic clock. The most accurate clock—indeed, the most accurate measurement of any kind—relies on electromagnetic transitions between two states in the cesium atom, using the cesium-133 isotope. Modern cesium atomic clocks are so accurate that they would only lose or gain one second every 20 million years. In fact, the behavior of cesium forms the basis for the modern definition of one second.
The compound cesium formate is widely used as an environmentally friendly well-drilling fluid in oil extracting.

Cesium metal is used in photoelectric cells and as a catalyst in the hydrogenation of certain organic compounds. Cesium is also used in a variety of scientific instruments and other electronic, industrial, and medical applications.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Cesium comes primarily from a whitish mineral called pollucite. A particularly rich source of pollucite is located at Bernic Lake, Manitoba. The deposits are estimated to contain 300,000 tons of pollucite, averaging 20 percent cesium. The cesium can be isolated by electrolysis (chemical separation via electric current) and other methods.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: “Bologna stones” or lapis solaris—smooth pebbles of the barium-containing mineral baryte—can be found in volcanic rock near Bologna, Italy. Alchemists in the Middle Ages were fascinated by the baryte’s natural phosphorescence: when exposed to light, it would glow for years!

But it wasn’t until 1772 that Carl Scheele, a Swedish chemist, determined that baryte contained a new element. He was able to isolate barium oxide, but not barium itself. Barium is very reactive and is always bound to something when found in nature. Barium was first isolated by British chemist Sir Humprey Davy in 1808. Davy succeeded because he used the new process of electrolysis—using an electric current to drive the chemical separation. This method is still used to isolate barium today.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Barium is a soft metallic element and, when pure, is silvery white. It is also moderately heavy; in fact, it comes from the Greek word barys, which means heavy.
Barium loses electrons, or oxidizes, very easily. To keep it from oxidizing, it must be kept within oxygen-free liquids, such as petroleum.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Barium metal is present in many alloys, such as the barium-nickel alloy commonly used in automobile spark plugs. Barium compounds have many uses, too. Barium sulfate is a high-quality, permanent, white pigment that is used in paint, paper, and glassmaking. It is also used in medical imaging to boost contrast in x-ray diagnostics. “Barium meals” and “barium enemas” help visualize your digestive tract, often in real-time!

While barium sulfate is used safely in the medical field, other barium compounds have a dark side, like barium carbonate that is used as rat poison. But on the light side, barium nitrate is used to create yellow and apple-green colors in fireworks!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: The most important compounds are barium peroxide, chloride, sulfate, carbonate, nitrate, and chlorate.
All barium compounds that are soluble in water or acid are poisonous.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Naturally occurring barium is a mixture of seven isotopes. However, in all, barium has a whopping 40 known isotopes (only cesium, xenon, and mercury have about as many). The others are artificial (human-made) and usually unstable (radioactive). The naturally occurring isotopes are all stable except for one, barium-130, which is almost stable because it has a half-life of a billion trillion years! That’s about a hundred billion times longer than the current age of the universe. So even though barium-130 is radioactive, naturally occurring barium (which contains barium-130) is generally quite harmless.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Barium is found only in combination with other elements, usually barium sulfate (baryte). It is separated from the sulfate by electrolysis—using electricity to separate the elements.
Though not a major source—in fact, a very rare one—barium can also be found in a blue, fluorescent, precious gemstone called benitoite. It is the state gem of California.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Lanthanum was discovered by Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander in 1839, in a sample of a mineral called cerite. But this discovery took a lot of patience!

In the 1820s, Mosander suspected that a sample of cerite he’d gotten from his mentor, legendary Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius, might contain a new element. However, in the early 1820s, there was only one known source of cerite—a mine in Bastnäs, Sweden—which meant that supplies of the mineral were limited. Unfortunately, Mosander ran out of the mineral, which meant that he had to give up his quest for the new element for more than a decade.

In 1839, Mosander acquired more cerite and resumed his research. Ultimately, he succeeded in finding a new element in the mineral. But he was reluctant to announce his discovery, because he didn’t want to embarrass his mentor, Berzelius, who’d failed to find the element first. Finally, Mosander overcame his shyness and told Berzelius about the discovery. Berzelius suggested calling the new element “lanthan,” which came from the Greek word lanthanein, meaning “to lie hidden.”

Mosander still wasn’t sure that he’d completely separated the new element from his cerite, so he waited until 1840 to publish his results. By the time he officially announced lanthanum’s discovery, he’d further broken down the cerite into oxides that later yielded the new elements praseodymium and neodymium. In chemistry, it pays to be thorough!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Lanthanum is a rare earth metal that’s soft, silver, and ductile (meaning that it can be stretched) and malleable (meaning it can be hammered or shaped). Lanthanum is a lot more reactive than the other lanthanides—douse it with water, and it will give off hydrogen gas. Lanthanum metal is soft enough to be cut with a knife!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Hollywood owes lanthanum a thank you: Because the element produces an emissions spectrum like sunlight, it’s often used in photographic and film studio lighting.

Camera lenses also often contain lanthanum, which can improve the glass’s color spectrum. Because lanthanum nickel absorbs hydrogen gas—as a powder the compound can absorb up to 400 times its own volume in hydrogen—lanthanum nickel can be used to store hydrogen, which can make it useful for things like hydrogen-powered cars.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Lanthanum nickel does a great job of absorbing hydrogen, which makes it useful in things like hydrogen-powered cars. Hybrid cars also use lanthanum in their batteries. Up to 40% of all lanthanum oxide gets mixed into optical glass, which is in turn used in things like cameras and binoculars. Mischmetal alloy, which contains lanthanum, can be used to create sparks in lighters.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find lanthanum either as lanthanum-139 or lanthanum-138. But you’d have to look hard to find lanthanum-138. More than 99.9% of naturally occurring lanthanum is lanthanum-139. Both isotopes are stable (non-radioactive). Synthetic lanthanum radioisotopes generally have a half-life of less than one minute (although lanthanum-137 has a half-life of around 60,000 years).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: It’s a lot easier to find lanthanum today than it was in Mosander’s day! Most lanthanum comes from monazite and bastnäsite, which can be up to 25% and 38% of the mineral, respectively. Most lanthanum ores come from the United States, Brazil, India, Sri Lanka, and Australia. About 12,500 metric tons of lanthanum are produced each year.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Some elements were discovered at the same time by different people! One such element is cerium, which was discovered in 1803 by Swedish chemists Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger, and almost simultaneously in Germany by chemist Martin Heinrich Klaproth.

Hisinger had found a strange rock on his father’s estate, which he initially suspected of containing the newly discovered element tungsten. When this turned out not to be the case, he brought the mineral to Berzelius and together they identified the new element. Berzelius and Hisinger named the new element cerium, after Ceres, a recently discovered asteroid (which had been named in turn after the Roman goddess of agriculture).

However, something of a controversy ensued when, a few months after Berzelius and Hisinger published a paper about their discovery, Klaproth published a paper in the same journal, claiming to have discovered the element. In the end, it was decided that Berzelius and Hisinger found the element first. But the discoveries happened near enough to each other that it is still impossible to talk about cerium’s history without mentioning Klaproth.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Cerium is a silvery metal that’s about as hard as silver. It is ductile, meaning that it can stretch without breaking. Because cerium is electropositive, tending to lose its electrons easily, it combusts rapidly, which is why the element has applications as a fire starter.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Cerium is one of two elements that make sparks when struck (the other is iron). For this reason, cerium is commonly used in lighters and fire starters.

During the Manhattan Project—the World War II-era effort concentrated at Los Alamos National Laboratory to create the world’s first atomic bomb—scientists used cerium to create crucibles for casting plutonium metal. Cerium continues to be an important part of nuclear energy research at the Lab today.

Today, automakers use cerium in catalytic converters, which make certain exhaust chemicals from motor vehicles less toxic. Cerium is also used in television screens, in LED lightbulbs, and in chromium plating, which helps make metal shiny! Cerium is used as a glass polish, too.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Cerium oxide is by far the most used cerium compound. It’s used for polishing things and for making glass colorless. Adding cerium to pigments can make the pigments less likely to fade.
Although cerium sulfide was used to make crucibles for casting plutonium during the Manhattan Project, the compound has been used rarely for this purpose since.
Cerium is a major component of mischmetal, an alloy that also contains other rare earth elements, and that is commonly used in lighters to make sparks.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find cerium in four stable (non-radioactive), isotopes: cerium-136, cerium-138, and cerium-142. Cerium-140 is by far the most common (around 88% of cerium is found in this isotope).

Thirty-five radioactive cerium isotopes have been observed. The longest-lived, cerium-144, has a half-life of 285 days. Most of the other radioisotopes have far shorter half-lives, often of less than 10 minutes.
Cerium(III) and cerium(IV) are the element’s two most common oxidation states. For this reason, cerium tends to be in one of these forms when it makes a compound with other elements.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Cerium is the most common of the lanthanide, or rare earth, elements. Despite the name of this group of elements, the rare earths aren’t really all that rare. In fact, cerium is only slightly less abundant in the Earth’s crust than copper. It’s much more abundant than lead and tin.
The rare earth elements are sufficiently alike that they’re difficult to separate from each other (although among lanthanides, cerium is the easiest to separate).
It wasn’t until 1875 that American chemists William Hillebrand and Thomas Norton isolated cerium metal for the first time.
Cerium can be found in many minerals, but commercially produced cerium comes from monazite and bastnäsite. Most cerium comes from the United States, Brazil, India, Sri Lanka, Australia, and China.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Praseodymium is one of those elements that just can’t stand to be alone. That’s why you’ll only ever find praseodymium in nature alongside other rare earth metals, such as cerium, lanthanum, or praseodymium’s sister element, neodymium. In fact, praseodymium and neodymium are so similar that for decades, scientists couldn’t tell them apart!

In 1841, Swedish chemist Carl Mosander found what he thought to be two new elements in a sample of the mineral cerite. He called these two supposed elements “lanthanum” and “didymium.” However, in 1885, Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach succeeded in splitting didymium up into two elements.

Von Welsbach was a student of German chemist Robert Bunsen, who, in addition to inventing the Bunsen burner, helped develop the technique of spectroscopy (which involves burning a substance and examining the light emitted in the process to determine what the substance was made of). Using spectroscopy, von Welsbach was able to prove that the two elements he’d separated out from didymium were indeed distinct. He named the elements neodidymium (meaning “new didymium”) and praseodidymium (meaning “green didymium,” after the element’s oxide’s color). The name “praseodidymium” was then modified to “praseodymium,” which is what we call the element today.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, praseodymium looks like silver. Praseodymium is moderately soft, ductile (meaning it can be stretched without breaking), and malleable (meaning that it can be hammered or shaped without breaking). Because rare-earth metals share many similar properties, praseodymium can often be substituted seamlessly in most applications involving rare-earth metals.
Praseodymium is reactive enough that it needs to be stored in mineral oil or sealed in plastic, or else it will form a greenish layer of oxide.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Praseodymium can be used in a ceramic glaze called Praseodymium Yellow, which is remarkably bright in color—think of banana-flavored Laffy Taffy! Praseodymium can also be mixed into zirconia to give inexpensive jewelry a greenish tint.

Praseodymium is used in praseodymium-neodymium magnets, which are in everything from electric or hybrid cars and wind turbines to computer hard drives, cell phones, and more. Alloyed with magnesium, praseodymium can help create very strong metals that are used in things like aircraft engines. Mixed with its sister element neodymium, praseodymium is often used in glasses designed to protect the eyes of welders or craftspeople, or of people in tanning beds.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Praseodymium-nickel metals can be used in magnetic refrigeration. In fact, these magnets have been used by scientists to approach absolute zero—the coldest temperature imaginable!

Other praseodymium compounds, such as praseodymium(III) oxalate, are used to give ceramics, glass, and other substances a yellow color. Mixed with other elements, praseodymium oxide can help catalyze oxidation (when an element loses electrons during a chemical reaction).

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Praseodymium only has one naturally occurring isotope, praseodymium-141, which is stable (non-radioactive). Scientists have produced around 40 praseodymium radioisotopes. Praseodymium-143 has a half-life of nearly 14 days, while all the other isotopes have half-lives of less than one day, and most have half-lives of less than one minute.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, most praseodymium comes from monazite and bastnäsite ores. China is the top producer of these ores, so it’s the top producer of praseodymium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce praseodymium. Praseodymium also occurs as a product of fissioning uranium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The mid-1800s was a period of intense activity in the search for new elements. This was especially the case for scientists working with the elements that we now call the lanthanides, or rare earth metals. But the process of discovering these elements was challenging because the rare earth metals all behave so similarly! These similarities made it hard for researchers to split the elements apart, and to tell if they’d found a new element, or two, or even more!

Identifying the elements got a lot easier after 1859, when Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff invented the spectroscope. Bunsen and Kirchhoff figured out that by burning a substance and examining the light produced in the process (like a colorful fingerprint), it was possible to figure out what the substance was made of.

Back in 1841, Swedish chemist Carl Mosander had found what he thought to be two new elements in a sample of the mineral cerite. He called these two supposed elements “lanthanum” and “didymium.” However, in 1885, one of Robert Bunsen’s students—Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach— succeeded in splitting up didymium into two elements. He then used spectroscopy to prove that these elements were in fact distinct, and he named the elements neodidymium (meaning “new didymium”) and praseodidymium (“green didymium”). The name “neodidymium” was then modified to “neodymium,” which is what we call the element today.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, neodymium looks like silver. However, neodymium is more reactive than other rare earth elements, which is why it tarnishes quickly in air. Neodymium is ductile (meaning it can be stretched without breaking) and malleable (meaning that it can be hammered or shaped without breaking).

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Neodymium often gets used in magnets, and not just the kind that holds receipts to refrigerators. Neodymium magnets are used in electric or hybrid cars or electric generators and wind turbines, in computer hard drives, cell phones, and more.

Neodymium is often used in lasers, especially lasers that operate at high temperatures. In manufacturing, these lasers can be used for engraving or etching, or in medicine—for example, to remove skin cancers. Mixed with its sister element praseodymium, neodymium is often used in glasses designed to protect the eyes of welders or craftspeople, or of people in tanning beds.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Compounds of neodymium, iron, and boron can be made into powerful magnets, and up to 70 percent of neodymium is used in this way. Neodymium acetate can be mixed into the kind of glass that’s used in welding goggles. Neodymium can make a compound with yttrium and aluminum to form yttrium aluminum garnet, which is used in lasers. Neodymium oxide can be used in glass, too, but for more decorative purposes: in daylight, this glass appears purple, but under fluorescent lighting the glass will look blue. It's not magic, it’s science!

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find neodymium in five stable (non-radioactive), isotopes: neodymium-142, neodymium-143, neodymium-145, neodymium-146, and neodymium-148. Neodymium-142 is the most common: about 27% of neodymium is in this form.

Naturally occurring neodymium also comes in two radioactive isotopes, although both have very long half-lives. Neodymium-144 has a half-life of 2.29×1015 years, while neodymium-150 has an even longer half-life, of 6.7×1018 years. Scientists have made 31 other neodymium radioisotopes that have half-lives ranging from around 11 days to seconds or less.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, most neodymium comes from monazite and bastnäsite ores. China is the top producer of these ores, so it’s the top producer of neodymium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce neodymium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Czech chemist Bohuslav Brauner predicted the existence of element 61 in 1902, speculating that there must be an unknown element between neodymium and samarium. In the ensuing four decades, researchers around the world tried to find this element without success.

But a massive breakthrough happened across the world in 1926! That year, teams in Italy and at the University of Illinois claimed to have found element 61. That same year, British chemist Charles James, who was one of the three researchers to have discovered lutetium, also claimed to have discovered the element.

Today, we know that James couldn’t have found element 61; although the element exists in nature, its short half-life means that it is practically impossible to find. Conclusive evidence of element 61’s discovery came only in 1945, when Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin, and Charles D. Coryell at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (then known as Clinton Laboratories) succeeded in separating element 61 from the byproducts of irradiating uranium in a reactor. The researchers named the element promethium, after Prometheus, who in Greek mythology stole fire from the gods!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Promethium is a silvery metal that, true to Bohuslav Brauner’s predictions, has qualities between those of neodymium and samarium. It is a lanthanide, or rare-earth, element. Not all the rare-earth elements are actually rare, but promethium is! All of promethium’s isotopes are radioactive. The longest-lived isotope, promethium-145, has a half-life of only around 18 years.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Promethium-147 is the most widely consumed isotope of the element. It’s often used to make paint glow. Promethium-147 has also been used in atomic batteries, which use the element’s radioactive decay to produce electricity that can be used in aircraft, watches, pacemakers, and more.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Few promethium compounds have been studied, largely because the element is so unstable. However, promethium compounds like promethium(III) chloride have been used in luminous paint, and other compounds are used in atomic batteries.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Researchers have found 41 promethium isotopes, all of which are unstable (radioactive). The longest-lived isotope, promethium-145, has a half-life of around 18 years. Promethium-147, the most used isotope of the element, has a half-life of around 2.6 years. Most other isotopes have half-lives of a few seconds or less!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Although promethium is produced in nature as a byproduct of fissioning uranium, promethium decays too quickly, and occurs in quantities too small, to be gathered from these sources. Some elements just don’t want to be found!

Today, promethium is produced in much the same way that it was at the time of its discovery—as a byproduct of fission in nuclear reactors. Like the saying goes, one person’s trash is another’s promethium! Russia is the only commercial producer of promethium today. Only a few hundred grams of the element are produced each year.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Samarium is one of the 17 rare earth elements. These elements have strikingly similar qualities, and as a result they took a long time to discover!
In 1803, the element cerium was discovered. Although it was thought that cerium might contain other elements as well, researchers were at a loss for a way to separate and characterize these elements.

In 1839, Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander found lanthanum and didymium, which he thought to be distinct elements, in cerium. However, other researchers came to suspect that this didymium wasn’t a pure element and suspected it was actually two or more distinct elements.

In 1879, French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran separated a sample of didymium from the mineral samarskite (which had been named after Russian mining engineer Vasili Yevgrafovich Samarsky-Bykhovets). Lecoq de Boisbaudran then separated the hydroxide of a new element from the didymium, which he named samarium, after the mineral in which it was found.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Samarium is a silvery metal that looks a lot like the other rare-earth elements. It is the second most abundant rare-earth elements. It is fairly stable in air, although it will oxidize slowly. Mixed with water, samarium turns into samarium hydroxide.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Alloyed with cobalt, samarium can be used in magnets that are incredibly powerful—up to 10 thousand times more powerful than iron magnets, in fact. These magnets are used in everything from motors to headphones (although neodymium magnets are more common nowadays).

Calcium chloride crystals with samarium mixed into them can be used in lasers. Hollywood uses samarium in lights that help illuminate movie sets. It’s not just genetics—samarium is what makes movie stars look good!
Because samarium is good at absorbing neutrons, it’s sometimes used in nuclear reactors, too. Samarium is also used as a catalyst (which helps make chemical reactions occur).

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Samarium oxide is used in ceramics and glassmaking. Samarium iodide (SmI2) is used to synthesize artificial substances that resemble natural ones. Few of the lanthanides form a monoxide, but samarium does.

Samarium(II) sulfide is an especially unusual compound: these black crystals function like semiconductors, but if you scratch them or expose them to high pressures, they turn a yellowish-gold color and conduct electricity like a metal!

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find samarium in five stable (non-radioactive) isotopes: samarium-144, samarium-149, samarium-150, samarium-152, and samarium-154. Naturally occurring samarium also comes in two radioisotopes, samarium-147 and samarium-148, which have very long half-lives (of 1.06 x 1011 years and 7 x 1015 years, respectively). Samarium-152 is the most abundant isotope: about 27% of naturally occurring samarium is in this form.

Altogether, researchers have characterized some 38 isotopes of samarium. The longest-lived synthetic, or artificial, samarium isotope has a half-life of 94.6 years. The shortest-lived have half-lives of mere microseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, most samarium comes from monzanite and bastnäsite ores. China is the top producer of these ores, so it’s the top producer of samarium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce samarium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The story of the rare earth elements is a story of ongoing discovery. And europium is a case in point!

In 1803, ceria—which was thought to be a new element—was discovered in ores from a mine in Bastnäs, Sweden. Although ceria did contain the element cerium, it contained other elements, too. In 1839, Swedish chemist Carl Mosander separated lanthanum and didymium from ceria as well.

Mosander thought that didymium was its own element, but this wasn't the case. In fact, didymium is made mostly of two elements, which Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach separated in the 1880s. These elements became known as neodymium and praseodymium.

But wait! There's more! In addition to neodymium and praseodymium, there were other elements in the didymium yet to be discovered. In 1879, French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran separated samarium from didymium—but the samarium wasn’t pure, either! In 1880, Swiss chemist Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac separated the element gadolinium from samarium. Like a Russian nesting doll, there appeared to be one more metal in the samarium, which French chemist Eugène-Anatole Demarçay at last separated in 1901. He named europium after—you guessed it—Europe. The name was fitting, given how many European scientists it took to find the element!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Europium is a relatively soft metal that is ductile (meaning that it can be stretched without breaking). It is the most reactive of the rare earth elements, which is why it tarnishes quickly in air.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: In the early 1960s, it was discovered that europium could be used in television sets to produce a vibrant red color, which caused demand for the element to soar. Europium(II) can also be used in televisions to produce the color blue. Europium is great at absorbing neutrons, so it’s also used in lasers and in nuclear control rods. All told, europium doesn’t have quite as many uses as some other rare earth elements do—but it’s still plenty useful!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Europium is unusual among the rare earth metals for its ability to form divalent compounds. Europium(II) oxide has been researched for potential use in magnetic refrigeration. That’s not a refrigerator with magnets on it; it’s the use of magnets to make things cold!

Europium(II) sulfide has also been researched for use in magnets, as well as in semiconductors. Europium(III) oxide is used in tubes in old-fashioned televisions, while europium-doped yttrium oxysulfide can used in light-emitting diodes (LEDs).

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, europium comes in the form of two isotopes. Just under 50% of naturally occurring europium is europium-151, while just over 50% of naturally occurring europium is europium-153. Europium-153 is stable (non-radioactive), while europium-151 is unstable, although the isotope has a very long half-life (of 5 x 1018 years).
Scientists have produced 35 other europium isotopes, all of which are radioactive. The half-lives of these isotopes range from around 37 years to mere nanoseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare earth elements, you won’t find europium by itself in nature. Instead, europium is something of a “buddy element” that’s extracted alongside other rare earth elements from ores such as bastnäsite and monazite.
The largest producers of europium, and of most of the rare earth metals, are China, Russia, and Malaysia.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Gadolinium was officially discovered in 1880, but it might have been found sooner! The element takes its name from gadolinite, a mineral that was in turn named after Johan Gadolin, a Finnish chemist and mineralogist. Gadolinite was named after Gadolin in recognition of the fact that he discovered the element yttrium from a sample of gadolinite in 1792. But Gadolin missed the other nine new elements that were also inside the mineral!

Element 64 was one of those hidden elements, but in fairness it's only present in gadolinite in very small amounts. Gadolinium was ultimately found in the mineral by Swiss chemist Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac in a sample almost 90 years later. De Marignac named the element after the gadolinite and, by extension, after Gadolin. Although Gadolin didn't discover element 64, he still ended up having the element named after him!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Gadolinium is a silvery white metal. It is malleable, which means that it can be easily shaped, and ductile, meaning that it can stretch without breaking. In moist air, gadolinium tarnishes quickly. The element is also highly magnetic.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Mixing gadolinium into metals like iron or chromium can make those metals easier to work with. Because gadolinium is great at absorbing neutrons, it’s often used in nuclear reactors. Gadolinium is also used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By injecting a gadolinium mixture into a patient’s bloodstream, doctors can more easily see inside a patient’s body. About one third of MRIs involve the use of gadolinium!
Gadolinium is also useful for making magnets and electronics like compact discs. Gadolinium yttrium aluminum garnets are a type of crystal that’s often used in lasers.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Gadolinium forms most of its compounds in its +3 oxidation state (meaning it loses three of its electrons). Many of these compounds are useful in MRI imaging.
In the past, other gadolinium compounds were used in television tubes. However, this use has declined because new televisions don’t use tubes.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, gadolinium is found in six stable (non-radioactive) isotopes—gadolinium-154, gadolinium-155, gadolinium-156, gadolinium-157, gadolinium-158, and gadolinium-160, along with one unstable, or radioactive isotope, gadolinium-152. About a quarter of naturally occurring gadolinium is in the form of gadolinium-160.

Altogether, 33 radioactive gadolinium isotopes have been observed. The most stable—naturally-occurring gadolinium-152—has a half-life of 1.08×1014 years. Most of the other isotopes have half-lives of less than 25 seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Gadolinium is a rare-earth element that’s found alongside many other rare-earth elements, such as monzanite and bastnäsite. Although the element is technically named after the mineral gadolinite, gadolinium is only a trace element in that mineral.
Most commercially produced gadolinium comes from China, the United States, Brazil, Sri Lanka, India, and Australia.
