sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Terbium is one of several rare-earth elements found in yttrium oxide. Because these elements come from the same source, they all have strikingly similar names (and qualities)—which can make them tricky to keep straight!

Terbium was first identified in its oxide form by Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander in 1843. Mosander was exploring yttrium oxide, which Swedish chemist John Gadolin had discovered in 1789. Yttrium oxide contained the element yttrium, but Mosander suspected that the oxide might contain other elements, too. He separated the yttrium oxide into the oxides yttria, erbia, and terbia (which contained the elements yttrium, erbium, and terbium).
Not long after this discovery, the names of terbia and erbia were confused—a mix-up that persisted for several decades. In the end, the elements switched names to the ones we recognize today!
Incidentally, the terbium and erbium that Mosander discovered later yielded other new elements, such as thulium and lutetium, as well.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Terbium is a silvery metal that is malleable (meaning that it can be hammered into shape) and ductile (meaning that it can be stretched without breaking). Terbium is soft enough to be cut with a knife!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Terbium doesn’t have all that many commercial uses, in part because it’s very expensive to produce (a gram of terbium costs four times as much as a gram of platinum!). When exposed to magnetic fields, terbium alloys can lengthen or shorten, which makes them useful in things like speakers, and also, potentially, in motors and pumps.
Like other rare-earth elements, terbium can be used as a component in lasers. It has also been used in lamps and color television tubes. Because terbium oxidizes easily, it’s often used for research.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Terbium oxidizes easily and has a number of oxides, some of which are used in fluorescent lamps, television tubes, and computer screens. Certain terbium compounds emit a bright green color, and these compounds have been used in medicine, making it possible to see whether specific reactions are taking place inside a patient’s body.
TbFe2-based compounds are magnetorestrictive—that is, they become smaller or larger when exposed to a magnetic field—which makes them useful in electronics.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find only one stable (non-radioactive) terbium isotope (terbium-159). In laboratory contexts, scientists have observed some 36 radioisotopes whose half-lives range from 180 years (terbium-158) to much less than one second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, most terbium comes from monazite and bastnäsite ores. China is the top producer of these ores, so it’s the top producer of terbium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce terbium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Dysprosium was discovered in 1886 by Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran, a French chemist who also discovered samarium, europium, and gallium. Lecoq de Boisbaudran was a self-taught scientist who began his career in a laboratory that he assembled on the second floor of his family’s home. He was a pioneer in the field of spectroscopy, which involved looking at the color of light emitted by burning a substance to determine what the substance was made of. Lecoq de Boisbaudran’s career shows that you don’t need an expensive laboratory to be a scientist! You just have to be passionately curious.

In 1886, Lecoq de Boisbaudran was analyzing a sample of erbium oxide when he noticed that the substance had an unusual spectrum. He proceeded to spend a lot of time trying to separate out the element—so much time, in fact, that he chose to name the element dysprosium, which comes from the Greek word dysprositos, meaning hard to get. Not to be confused with Despacito—though the process was as slow as the song’s title suggests!
It wasn’t until decades later, in 1950, that Frank Spedding at Iowa State University developed a technique to easily separate out dysprosium and other lanthanide elements.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, dysprosium is silvery white and soft enough to cut with a knife. Dysprosium has a high melting point, and it’s very good at absorbing neutrons. At room temperature, it’s stable in air. However, dysprosium is easily dissolved with certain kinds of acids, such as sulfuric acid. Dysprosium is one of the most magnetic elements there is, so it’s a good idea to make sure your keys are still in your pocket after you work with it!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The biggest use of dysprosium is in magnets. In fact, up to 95% of dysprosium is used in magnets. Dysprosium’s ability to be magnetized makes it useful in computer hard discs. Even at high temperatures, dysprosium stays magnetic, which makes it useful for the magnets used in wind turbines or electric car motors. Because more and more electric cars are being produced, demand for dysprosium is growing all the time.

Dysprosium also gets top marks for its ability to absorb neutrons, which is why it’s sometimes used in nuclear reactors. And dysprosium is sometimes used in dosimeters, which help scientists and other people who work with radioactive substances tell how much radiation they're being exposed to.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Dysprosium iodide gets used in metal halide lamps. Mixed in the right way with gallium, aluminum, or iron, dysprosium can be made into a kind of crystal called a garnet, which can be useful in lasers or in a process called magnetic refrigerating (which involves using magnets to make cold temperatures). Mixed with nickel, dysprosium oxide can be used in the control rods of nuclear reactors. Dysprosium oxide is highly magnetic, which is why it’s used in—you guessed it—magnets, among other things.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, dysprosium comes in a few different isotopes—seven of them, to be precise— dysprosium-156, dysprosium-158, dysprosium-160, dysprosium-161, dysprosium-162, dysprosium-163, and dysprosium-164. The most common are dysprosium-164 and dysprosium-162. Around 28% of naturally occurring dysprosium is dysprosium-164, while another 26% is dysprosium-162.
Scientists have made around 30 radioactive isotopes of dysprosium. These radioisotopes have half-lives that range from millions of years down to much less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most dysprosium comes from monazite sand, which is extracted using the ion exchange process developed by Frank Spedding’s team in 1950. Most dysprosium comes from China, although in recent years, Australia has begun producing more of the element.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In the history of chemistry, sometimes an element gets discovered simultaneously by different people. That’s the case with element 67, holmium!

In the late 1800s, scientists across Europe were studying an oxide called yttrium that came from an unusual stone in the town of Ytterby, Sweden. By the late 1800s, the oxide had already yielded several new elements, including yttria, terbium, erbium, and ytterbium. Ultimately, seven more elements would be discovered in yttria. Not bad for a single stone!

One of these elements, holmium, was discovered by researchers who were analyzing yttria. In 1878, Swiss chemists Jacques-Louis Soret and Marc Delafontaine noticed that a substance they took to be pure erbium oxide emitted unexpected spectrographic bands (like a visual fingerprint). They concluded that the erbium oxide must contain a new element, which they called “element X.”

Meanwhile, in 1879, Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve noticed that samples of erbium he was analyzing had varying weights depending on how the samples had been produced. This implied the existence of another substance in the erbium. Cleve named the new element holmium, after the Latin word for Stockholm, Holmia, which is what we call the element today (presumably because “element X” was too cool of a name to keep permanently).

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Holmium is a bright, soft, silvery metal that looks a lot like the other rare earth elements. It is malleable, meaning it can be hammered into shape, and ductile, meaning it can be stretched without breaking.

Holmium is a paramagnet, meaning that it becomes magnetic when exposed to a magnetic field. However, once it’s exposed to a magnetic field in this way, holmium becomes the most magnetic element of all. You’d better take off your jewelry before you work with holmium!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Holmium doesn’t have all that many uses. Yttrium-iron garnet—a synthetic crystal that’s used in lasers—sometimes includes small amounts of holmium. These lasers can be used in everything from cleaning teeth to zapping cancerous tumors!
Holmium has unique magnetic properties, which is why it’s also used in certain magnets. Because holmium can absorb neutrons, it’s sometimes used in nuclear reactors, too.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Holmium oxide is among the most powerful paramagnetic substances known (meaning that the substance becomes magnetic when it’s exposed to an external magnetic field). Holmium oxide is also useful for calibrating spectrophotometers, which can help researchers determine what elements are inside a given substance.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, holmium is found in one stable (non-radioactive, isotope)—holmium-165. Scientists have made 35 synthetic radioisotopes of holmium that have half-lives ranging from some 4,500 years to much less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most holmium comes from China—specifically, from the rare earth mines in Inner Mongolia, which are the source of most of the world’s rare earth elements. Holmium is extracted chiefly from the minerals monazite and bastnäsite. Russia and Malaysia also produce holmium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Look at the periodic table, and you’ll notice that some of the elements have awfully similar names—ytterbium, yttrium, terbium, and erbium. That’s because these elements were all discovered in minerals found near the village of Ytterby, Sweden. If you have a hard time keeping these elements straight, you’re not alone!

These elements all have similar properties, so discovering many of them was a long and sometimes confusing process. That was certainly the case with erbium, which Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander discovered in a piece of gadolinite from Ytterby. Mosander thought that this chemical sample was an oxide (a compound of oxygen and some other element) called yttria. From the sample, he also separated out two other oxides, which he called “erbia” and “terbia.”

It turned out that giving these oxides such similar names wasn’t the best idea. Not long after Mosander’s discoveries, another chemist confused erbia with terbia. That mix-up caused scientists problems for more than two decades! That confusion wouldn't be cleared up until the oxides, and the elements erbium and terbium that they contained, were finally renamed.

In addition to erbium and terbium, the gadolinite that Mosander analyzed ended up containing five other new elements—ytterbium, scandium, thulium, holmium, and gadolinium. Now just try to keep the names straight!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, in metallic form, erbium is soft, malleable (meaning capable of being shaped), and silvery white. In compounds such as erbium oxide, erbium had a distinct pink color. Erbium has very sharp and specific absorption bands, which means it absorbs and emits light at very precise wavelengths. This makes it especially useful in technologies like lasers and fiber optics (think high-speed internet and medical equipment), where accurately controlling light is important.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Erbium is often used in lasers, especially in medical applications. Dentists use erbium lasers to clean teeth, dermatologists use erbium lasers to make skin look younger, and surgeons use erbium lasers to conduct laser surgery.

Erbium is also commonly used in fiber-optic cables. By incorporating erbium into fiber optics at regular intervals, it’s possible to amplify the laser signals that travel along the cables’ length. You might have erbium to thank (or blame) for making it possible to read this article!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Erbium oxide is the form of erbium first obtained by Carl Mosander in the 1840s. Erbium oxide has a pink-lemonade color, which is why it’s sometimes used in cheap jewelry or sunglasses.

Erbium tetraboride, which is hard and has a high melting point, has many applications, so it’s used in applications that range from semiconductors to the nozzles of rocket engines. Erbium fluoride is used in fiber optics and for other optical applications.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Naturally occurring erbium comes in six stable (non-radioactive) isotopes—erbium-162, erbium-164, erbium-166, erbium-168, and erbium-170. About one third of natural erbium is erbium-166, the most common isotope, followed by erbium-168 (which makes up about 27% of naturally occurring erbium).
Scientists have made around 30 radioactive erbium isotopes. Their half-lives range from around 9 days to several seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Like other rare earth metals, most erbium comes from monzanite and bastnäsite ores. China is the top producer of these ores, so it’s the top producer of erbium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce erbium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Thulium is an element that took a lot of trial and error to discover. Its discovery can be traced back to 1789, when Swedish chemist Johan Gadolin discovered the element yttrium (in the form of yttrium oxide, or yttria) in an ore from near the village of Ytterby, Sweden. However, Gadolin’s yttria wasn’t pure yttrium.

In 1843, Swedish chemist Carol Gustaf Mosander discovered terbium and erbium in the oxide, too. But these oxides weren’t pure, either! In 1879, Swedish chemist Per Teodor Cleve discovered the elements holmium and thulium in a sample of erbium oxide. Cleve named element 69 “thulium” after the Latin word for Scandinavia, thule (which you might also recognize as a manufacturer of automobile roof racks).

Thulium was difficult to discover in part because it’s a rare-earth element. The rare-earth elements all have similar qualities, and they’re difficult to separate from each other. In fact, it wasn’t until 1911 that American chemist Theodore William Richards succeeded in obtaining a pure sample of thulium. He did this by painstakingly recrystallizing thulium bromate 15,000 times! In recognition of his efforts, Richards was awarded the Nobel Prize for chemistry in 1914.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, thulium is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife. It is malleable (meaning it can be shaped by hammering) and ductile (meaning it can be stretched without breaking). Thulium tarnishes slowly in air. The element interacts with water to make thulium hydroxide.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Thulium isn’t one of those elements that has a million uses, partly because the element is so expensive to produce. Other rare-earth elements are far cheaper and similar enough to thulium that in most cases, they can be used instead of thulium.

Thulium has been added to yttrium aluminum garnet—an artificial crystal that’s in the kinds of lasers that doctors use in laser surgery. Thulium-170, an isotope that is produced in laboratories, can be used in portable X-ray devices.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Thulium forms just one oxide (Tm2O3), and this substance is often referred to as “thulia” (in keeping with the names of other rare-earth oxides, such as yttria, erbia, and terbia). While thulium does form compounds such as chlorides, fluorides, and bromides, none of these have major commercial uses. However, thulium iodide has been used to add a bluish green color to lamps and lights.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find thulium in just one stable (non-radioactive) isotope—thulium-169. Scientists have characterized some 25 radioactive thulium isotopes. The longest-lived of these, thulium-171, has a half-life of nearly two years. The shortest-lived have half-lives of mere nanoseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most thulium comes from China—specifically, from the rare earth mines in Inner Mongolia, which are the source of most of the world’s rare earth elements. Thulium is extracted chiefly from the minerals monazite and bastnäsite. Russia and Malaysia also produce thulium.
Not all the rare-earth elements are in fact rare, but thulium is! Thulium occurs in tiny amounts in rare-earth minerals, which is why it’s one of the most expensive elements in the world.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, discovering ytterbium was a long process!

Ytterbium’s story goes back to 1789, when Swedish chemist Johan Gadolin discovered the element yttrium (not to be confused with ytterbium) in an ore sample from the town of Ytterby, Sweden. It turned out, though, that the sample of yttrium oxide that Gadolin had extracted wasn’t pure. In 1843, Swedish chemist Carl Gustaf Mosander found the new elements terbium and erbium in yttrium oxide as well. But these elements weren’t in their pure form, either.

It wasn’t until 1878 that Swiss chemist Jean Charles Galissard de Marignac found ytterbium, a new element, in a sample of erbium. The rare-earth elements are so similar that it was hard to separate out the ytterbium, but after a lot of hard work, de Marignac succeeded. Sometimes, persistence pays off!

As it happens, at around the same time that de Marignac found ytterbium, so too did Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach. Von Welsbach named the new element aldebaranium, but it was de Marignac who wound up getting credit for finding the element, and de Marignac’s name for the element—ytterbium, after the Swedish town—is the one that stuck.
Incidentally, in 1907, French chemist Georges Urbain succeeded in splitting the ytterbium that de Marignac had discovered into two elements: ytterbium and a new element that he called lutetium.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Ytterbium is a soft, silvery-white metal that, like other rare-earth elements, is malleable (meaning it can be hammered into shape) and ductile (meaning it can be stretched without breaking). Ytterbium is more reactive than some rare-earth elements, which is why it will tarnish in air.
Some metals are hard to work with, but ytterbium is fairly cooperative. But powdered ytterbium does pose a fire risk—see below!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Ytterbium doesn’t have all that many uses. It has been mixed into stainless steel alloys to make the metal stronger. It has also been used as a radiation source in commercial X-ray machines, and it’s been used in bubble memory devices (a type of computer memory), too.
In other contexts, ytterbium is used as a catalyst, helping to make certain chemical reactions occur. Ytterbium has been incorporated into certain kinds of laser devices as well.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Like other rare-earth elements, most ytterbium compounds form in the +3-oxidation state. Unlike other rare-earth elements, ytterbium also forms compounds in its +2 state. Those oxidation states indicate how many electrons the element has lost during a chemical reaction.
Ytterbium oxide is the only widely used ytterbium compound, and it’s sometimes used in glass and ceramics.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll find ytterbium in seven stable (non-radioactive) isotopes: ytterbium-168, ytterbium-170, ytterbium-171, ytterbium-172, ytterbium-173, ytterbium-174, and ytterbium-176. Most naturally occurring ytterbium is ytterbium-174: about a third of natural ytterbium is this isotope.

Scientists have also observed some 27 radioactive ytterbium isotopes. The most stable of these, ytterbium-169, has a half-life of around 32 days, while the shortest-lived have half-lives of much less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most ytterbium comes from monazite ores. Like other rare-earth elements, it’s also found in the mineral bastnäsite, although ytterbium occurs in bastnäsite in small enough quantities that it’s not commonly extracted from this mineral. Some rare-earth elements are indeed rare, but not ytterbium—it’s the 44th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust!
China is the top producer of bastnäsite ores, so it’s the top producer of ytterbium, too. Russia and Malaysia also produce ytterbium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Lutetium was the last of the lanthanide elements to be identified, but the time was ripe for its discovery. Most elements on the periodic table were discovered by one researcher at a time, and some elements were discovered by two researchers simultaneously. But lutetium has the distinction of having been discovered by three different scientists at once!

At the end of the 18th century, researchers began discovering the 15 elements that are now referred to as the lanthanide elements. This process was complicated by the fact that the lanthanide elements all have similar properties, and by the fact that at the time, nobody was sure how many lanthanides there were.

In 1794, yttrium was discovered, but the sample of yttrium oxide that researchers isolated turned out not to be pure yttrium. Over the next century, researchers would find that the supposed yttrium contained the elements ytterbium, erbium, terbium, holmium, thulium, and lutetium as well.

In 1907, French chemist Georges Urbain found lutetium in a sample of ytterbium oxide. He named the element lutecium after the Latin name for Paris, Lutetia (the element’s name was changed to lutetium in 1949). However, at the same time that Urbain discovered lutetium, so too did Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach and, separately, British chemist Charles James. A conflict ensued over who the element’s true discoverer was. In 1909, the International Commission on Atomic Weights, which was then the authority on naming the elements, gave credit for the discovery to Urbain.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Lutetium is a hard, silvery metal that resembles the other rare earth elements. As the last element in the lanthanide series, lutetium has the highest melting point and density of the lanthanides, and it is the hardest of these elements. In air, lutetium tarnishes slowly.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: So far, researchers have found few uses for lutetium, partly because it is so expensive to produce. It has been used in oil refining and as an additive in gadolinium gallium garnet—a type of artificial crystal that has been used in magnetic-bubble memory devices (a type of computer memory). Researchers are exploring the possibility of using the radioactive isotope lutetium-177 to help diagnose and treat cancers. New uses for lutetium are being found all the time!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Lutetium reacts with the halogens to form lutetium(III) halides. In water, lutetium reacts to form lutetium hydroxide and hydrogen gas. Few lutetium compounds have attained widespread non-research use, although some of its compounds have been used in x-ray phosphors and optical lenses.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, you’ll fine lutetium in two isotopes: lutetium-175 and lutetium-176. Lutetium-175 is stable ( non-radioactive). Lutetium-176 is radioactive, but the isotope has a very long half-life (of 3.78 x 1010 years). Researchers have produced 39 lutetium radioisotopes, and their half-lives range from over three years to much less than one second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Lutetium is one of the rarest elements on Earth! It is found alongside other rare earth elements, especially yttrium, in certain ores (chiefly monazite). The biggest producer of lutetium, as of the other rare earth elements, is China, followed by Russia and Malaysia.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1911, French chemist Georges Urbain claimed to have discovered element 72, which he called “celtium.” Although Urbain was right about finding a new element, his descriptions of the element were mostly wrong, so he didn’t truly “discover” the element. In science, it’s important to get the details right!

It wasn’t until 1923 that George Charles de Hevesy and Dirk Coster separated hafnium from zirconium at the University of Copenhagen, officially discovering the element. The two scientists dubbed element 72 “hafnium,” after “Hafnia,” the Latin name for Copenhagen.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Hafnium is a silvery metal that is ductile, meaning it can be stretched without breaking. It’s also resistant to corrosion and acids. Hafnium and zirconium are a lot alike. However, hafnium is denser and a lot better at absorbing neutrons than zirconium is.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because hafnium resists corrosion and is great at absorbing neutrons, it’s often used in nuclear reactors. Hafnium also gets used in gas-filled and incandescent lamps. It’s also useful as a semiconductor, which can be used in computers. When alloyed with other metals, hafnium metals can be made into spacecraft components and other useful objects.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Hafnium oxide gets used in semiconductors, which are important in electronics. Hafnium carbide has the highest melting point—more than 3900 °C—among known compounds, but this compound is too expensive to be very useful. At high temperatures, hafnium reacts with carbon, boron, nitrogen, oxygen, silicon, and sulfur.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: More than 40 hafnium isotopes have been observed, but only five of those isotopes (hafnium-176, -177, -178, -179, and -180) are stable (non-radioactive).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most hafnium comes from zirconium ores, which are usually about 5% hafnium. Hafnium and zirconium are quite difficult to separate from other elements. Splitting them from each other can be a real headache, too!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1802, Swedish chemist Anders Ekeberg discovered element 73, but he didn't get credit for this during his lifetime. Other researchers questioned the discovery and thought that the “new” element was the already-discovered element columbium (now known as niobium).

Forty years later, in 1846, German chemist Heinrich Rose concluded that Ekeberg had discovered a new element. But it would be another twenty years before the differences between tantalum and niobium were definitively confirmed by Christian Wilhelm Blomstrand, Henri Etienne Saint-Claire Deville, and Louis J. Troost.

In what may be the ultimate irony, Ekeberg named element 73 after Tantalus of Greek mythology. According to legend, Tantalus was punished by the gods to stand in a pool whose waters would forever recede when he tried to drink, beneath a fruit tree whose branches would forever be out of reach. Ekeberg probably felt a little like Tantalus when he tried to prove his discovery to other scientists.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Tantalum is a blue grey, heavy, and very hard metal. It is ductile, meaning it can stretch without breaking. At low temperatures, it’s resistant to acids and corrosion. At higher temperatures, tantalum becomes more and more likely to react with other substances.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Tantalum has many uses. Because it isn’t irritating to bodily tissues, it’s often used for medical implants and surgical tools. It’s also used in electronic components for cell phones, computers, cars, and cameras. In particular, tantalum is often used in capacitors, which store electrical charge and control the flow of current in electronic devices.
Tantalum alloys can be strong and have high melting points, which makes them useful for things like rocket nozzles or in nuclear reactors, both of which can get quite hot!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Tantalum pentoxide is used in electronics. Tantalum carbides are hard and brittle, which makes them useful in tool bits. Tantalum oxide can be used to make special kinds of glass that can be turned into camera lenses.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, tantalum can be found in two stable (non-radioactive) isotopes: tantalum-180 and -181.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: In nature, tantalum is relatively rare. It’s found mainly in the mineral columbite-tantalite, also known as coltan, which often contains niobium, too. You can find tantalum ores in Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Mozambique. In Malaysia and Thailand, tantalum is produced as a byproduct of tin mining and smelting.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Tungsten was first used more than 350 years ago, when Chinese porcelain makers used the element to give their ceramics a warm, peachy color. But tungsten wasn’t known to the Western world until 1783, when Spanish chemists (and brothers) Juan José and Fausto Elhuyar extracted the element from the mineral wolframite, calling the discovery wolfram.

Today, in most European languages, element 74 is still called wolfram. But in English, French, and other languages, element 74 is called “tungsten,” which means “heavy stone” in Swedish. That’s because in 1781, two years before the Elhuyar brothers isolated tungsten, Swedish-German chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele suggested that an acid derived from scheelite—a mineral that was then called tungsten—might be reduced into a new metal.
Since then, element 74 has gone by both names. But everyone agrees that the element’s symbol is the letter W!

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Tungsten is a steel-grey to tin-white metal. Impure tungsten is brittle and hard to work with, but pure tungsten is soft enough to be cut with a hacksaw.

Tungsten has the highest melting point and the highest tensile strength of all metals. The element is non-reactive, too, meaning that it doesn’t interact with water, acids, or oxygen at room temperature.
Mixing tungsten into steel can make the steel much tougher.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, tungsten and tungsten alloys were used as lightbulb filaments. But because these lightbulbs aren’t very energy efficient, they’ve been gradually phased out.

Tungsten can also make alloys stronger, and its high melting point means that it can be used to manufacture things like rocket nozzles, which must be able to withstand getting extremely hot without melting.
Tungsten carbide is applied to cutting and drilling tools that are used for metalworking, mining, woodworking, construction, and petroleum manufacturing.
Tungsten can also be made into contact points in electronics, or the metal can be used as components in electrical furnaces.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Tungsten is a relatively rare element. In nature, you’ll find tungsten in four stable (non-radioactive) isotopes (tungsten-182, -183, -184, and -186).
One naturally occurring radioisotope, tungesten-180, has an extremely long half-life, of about 2 quintillion years (1.8×1018).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most tungsten comes from the minerals scheelite and wolframite—the same minerals that Scheele and the Elhuyar brothers analyzed more than two hundred years ago! Today, China, Russia, Canada, Bolivia, Vietnam, Portugal, Australia, Rwanda, Spain, and Brazil are all major tungsten producers.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: When Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev rolled out his groundbreaking periodic table of the elements in 1869, element 25—manganese—was the only element with two gaps below it, leaving room for elements that Mendeleev predicted would exist. One of those elements was eventually found to be element 43, technetium. The other was element 75, which would come to be known as rhenium.

In 1908, Japanese chemist Masataka Ogawa claimed to have found element 43, which he called nipponium, after one of the Japanese words for Japan. But no one was able to replicate his work and his claim was rejected. Later, another Japanese chemist, Kenjiro Kimura, figured out why Ogawa’s work had never been replicated; Ogawa had actually discovered element 75! Because the elements are in the same group, they are a lot alike—so Ogawa had good reason to be confused!

German chemists Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke, and Otto Berg rediscovered the element in 1925, extracting it from platinum ore and columbite. Rhenium was exceedingly hard to isolate; the team had to process 660 kilograms of the mineral molybdenite to get 1 gram of rhenium! Rhenium is one of the rarest elements there is!
The Noddack team named the new element “rhenium” after the Latin word Rhenus, for the Rhine River—an important waterway in Germany.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Rhenium has the third-highest melting point (and the second-highest boiling point) of any element. When it isn’t molten, rhenium is a silver metal that’s often sold as a powder.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Most rhenium—up to 80%—is alloyed with the metals that make up turbine blades for airplane and industrial turbine engines. That’s because rhenium has one of the highest melting points of all metals. With a melting point of nearly 3200°C, rhenium can withstand a lot of heat!
Other uses for rhenium include fossil-fuel refining and, experimentally, in cancer treatments.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: The rhenium compound (Re2Cl8)2 is important in the history of chemistry. This rhenium compound showed that it was possible in nature for two atoms to have a quadruple bond. Good luck trying to pry those atoms apart!
Rhenium forms in lots of oxidation states. Rhenium dioxide is often used as a catalyst. Rhenium(VII) oxide is an important compound, serving as the basis of all rhenium compounds.
Commercially, you’ll often find rhenium in the form of perrhenate salts.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: In nature, rhenium has just one stable isotope, rhenium-185. A little less than 40% of rhenium is found in this form, while the rest is rhenium-187—a radioactive isotope of the element with a very long half-life (4.16×1010 years). That’s a lot of zeroes!
Scientists have created around 30 radioactive rhenium isotopes.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most rhenium comes from copper-porphyry ores. Both molybdenum and rhenium are produced as byproducts from processing these ores.
Chile is the biggest producer of rhenium, followed by the United States and Poland.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1803, Smithson Tennant and William Hyde Wollaston identified osmium as a new element while analyzing an insoluble residue of platinum that was dissolved in aqua regia (a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids). Tennant named the element osmium after the Greek word osme, meaning “a smell” because of the ash and smoke produced by one of the isolated residues (osmium tetroxide).

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: At room temperature, osmium is a hard, brittle, shiny, bluish-white metal. It is highly durable when combined with another metal. Osmium is very reflective in ultraviolet light and absorbs hydrogen when in powdered form.
In small quantities, it can spontaneously form volatile and poisonous osmium tetroxide at room temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Osmium alloys are used in high-wear applications where durability is important. Some example uses are fountain pen tips, instrument pivots, electrical contacts, and phonograph needles.
Osmium tetroxide is used in fingerprint detection and potassium osmate is an oxidant in organic synthesis.
An alloy of osmium is used in pacemakers and heart valves.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Osmium is the least abundant stable element in the Earth’s crust. It is found as a pure element or in iridium-osmium alloys. Within the crust, osmium is present in igneous deposits, impact craters, and nickel-copper deposits. South Africa, Russia, and Canada have significant sources of osmium.
Osmium is also produced as a by-product of the processing of platinum and nickel ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Smithson Tennant, an English chemist, discovered iridium in 1803 in the residue of crude platinum, after dissolving it in aqua regia, a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids. Because of the bright colors of iridium’s salts, Tennant named the element after the Greek goddess Iris—who was known for leaving behind a rainbow.

Much like its supernatural namesake, iridium does not appear naturally on the Earth’s surface. Iridium has extraterrestrial origins and only a very thin layer of iridium exists in the Earth's crust. The iridium on earth was likely caused by a large meteor or asteroid hitting the Earth, because meteors and asteroids contain such high levels of iridium.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Iridium is white and looks like platinum but has a slight yellow tinge. Because of its brittleness, hardness, and high melting point, solid iridium is difficult to shape and mold, so it's often used in its powder form instead.

If elements had personalities, iridium would be the queen of chill. Iridium is unbothered by acids (including aqua regia), unchanged by air, and unconcerned with water (it's the most corrosion-resistant metal!).

But when there’s oxygen around and at high temperatures, iridium does react with cyanide salts, halogens, and oxygen itself. Iridium also reacts directly with sulfur (at atmospheric pressure) and creates iridium disulfide.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Iridium is used for coating optical lenses to reduce glare and improve clarity in certain lighting conditions. It also helps reduce the amount of scratching that might appear on camera and telescope lenses. But don’t get this element in your eyes: it can cause irritation!

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Important compounds of iridium are chlorides and iodides that are used as industrial catalysts. Catalysts help speed up chemical reactions, but unlike other chemicals in the reaction, a catalyst is not used up.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Iridium is mostly used in alloys. Osmium-iridium alloys are used for fountain pen nibs and for compass bearings. Iridium appears in solid form, also, but it is very brittle and difficult to work with.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Iridium is mostly found in igneous deposits (volcanic) and asteroid impact craters. The largest known iridium reserves are located in South Africa (near the largest known asteroid impact site, the Vredefort impact structure). There are other deposits in large copper–nickel deposits in Russia and an asteroid impact crater in Canada. Smaller reserves are found in the United States.
Iridium is also found in small deposits with platinum in alluvial (running water) deposits.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Platinum has long since been a prized possession across the globe. An artifact made of worked platinum was found in an Egyptian casket from the 7th century BCE and early inhabitants of Ecuador and Colombia also valued this silvery-white metal, using it in ornaments and as cladding on other precious objects.

Because platinum’s melting point is so high (around 1770°C, compared to gold at 1065°C), ancient people had to get creative to work it. Many ancient artifacts were made from large platinum nuggets or tiny grains that were bound together with a more malleable metal, such as gold.

In the 1500s, Spanish explorers encountered platinum while searching for gold in South America. They found a strange, shiny metal mixed with the gold, which they called “platina,” meaning "little silver." Because it was so hard to melt, they didn’t think it was valuable.

In 1735, Spanish explorer Antonio de Ulloa definitively described the metal, publishing the results 13 years later. In the meantime, British metallurgist Charles Wood sent samples of the metal to William Brownrigg for investigation in 1741. Brownrigg was the first person to recognize platinum as a new element. Soon after, chemists across Europe began characterizing the properties of platinum.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Platinum is a beautiful silvery-white metal when pure. It’s malleable, ductile, and does not oxidize in air. The metal is ultra-resistant to corrosion, but can be affected by halogens, cyanides, sulfur, and caustic alkalis.
It is insoluble in hydrochloric or nitric acid, but dissolves when they are mixed as aqua regia.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Platinum is an incredibly versatile metal used in everything from jewelry and dental crowns to cutting-edge technology. Its ability to withstand high temperatures makes it perfect for turbine blades, missile nose cones, and jet engine fuel nozzles. Plus, it's essential in producing high-quality glass for TVs and computers.

Platinum’s true superpower lies in its role as a catalyst—boosting the efficiency of chemical reactions. Platinum is a catalyst in catalytic converters (the car part that helps control pollution). Platinum is also a key component in fuel cells—a more resilient, emission-free way to power vehicles.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Platinum occurs naturally but is extremely rare. Miners unearth far more gold and silver than platinum. The ore is usually accompanied by small quantities of iridium, osmium, palladium, ruthenium, and rhodium.
Platinum is primarily found in western Russia, Colombia, and parts of the United States, especially Montana. Dozens of other countries have platinum, but in extremely small quantities.
Sperrylite, a mineral that’s mainly mined in Ontario, Canada, is primarily composed of platinum.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Gold is one of the first metals ever used by humans. We were making jewelry with it as early as 4600 BCE, with the rise of civilization. Unlike other metals, gold often appears in nature in its pure form, making it easy for early civilizations to spot and use. Across the world, ancient cultures were fascinated by this shiny metal.

It’s known as the Bronze Age, but gold artifacts first appeared in Ancient Egypt in 5000 BCE. While ancient man was developing the wheel, humans were also crafting bracelets, rings, and necklaces from the precious metal. Gold became a symbol of wealth and power, spreading across the ancient world and enabling trade far beyond Egypt, reaching as far as the Indus Valley, Anatolia, and the Balkans.

Early civilizations hammered and shaped naturally occurring gold into jewelry and ornaments. But as smelting techniques developed around 4000 BCE, goldsmiths were able to separate the metal from ores, enabling more intricate work. The Egyptians, in particular, mastered the art of alloying gold with other metals to improve its strength and alter its color, allowing for a wider variety of uses in ceremonial objects, jewelry, and even furniture. By 1200 BCE, the Egyptians were using lost-wax casting to create intricate gold sculptures, a method still used today!

Early innovations in goldsmithing laid the foundation for how we manipulate gold and other metals today. While ancient people prized gold for ceremonial and artistic purposes, modern science has expanded gold’s role far beyond decoration. Gold’s unique properties, like excellent conductivity and resistance to corrosion, make it crucial in high-tech fields for electronics, space exploration, and medicine. From circuit boards in smartphones to life-saving medical equipment, gold plays an essential role in the cutting-edge technologies of modern life. Gold's role has evolved from a symbol of beauty to a critical component of cutting-edge innovations and scientific breakthroughs.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Gold is one of the densest of all metals, is highly malleable and is a good conductor of heat and electricity. It is one of the few elements found in a natural state, as a soft metal with a characteristic yellow color. But, when finely divided, gold's color may shift to be black, ruby, or even purple.

The Purple of Cassius is a test to detect gold. Gold is inert, meaning it is chemically unreactive, but it will dissolve in in aqua regia (a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids). The purple pigment of the test's namesake comes about when the dissolved gold mixes with tin(II) chloride, turning the solution purple and creating a type of auric gold. Auric gold atoms have lost three electrons, giving them a positive charge. That charge determines how gold interacts with other atoms. Like a magnet, positively charged auric gold is strongly attracted to negatively charged atoms (or ions), making gold more reactive and easier to form compounds. These compounds are typically used in specialized chemical reactions, industrial processes, and sometimes in medicine, rather than in the familiar metallic form of gold used for jewelry or coins.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Around half of all gold mined today is used to make jewelry, which is still the single largest use for gold. It is used in coinage and is a standard for monetary systems in many countries. You'll even find gold in dental work and for coating things to protect them. Gold is used to coat satellites because it reflects heat well and doesn’t react with other materials, making it perfect for outer space!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Gold is found in veins of rock or in loose deposits, like sand or gravel, called alluvial deposits. To get gold out of the ground, people mine for it or use a method called panning, where they wash the dirt away to find bits of gold—you may have seen this in old Gold Rush movies with people sifting through rivers. Once the gold is collected, it’s separated from other materials through processes like cyaniding, amalgamating, and smelting (basically, heating it up to melt away impurities). Sometimes, gold is refined further using electrolysis, a process that uses electricity to purify it.

Although there’s some gold in seawater (around 4 grams in 1,000,000 tones of water), no one has figured out a way to collect it in a way that would be profitable. Almost 15,000 tons of gold is floating around in the ocean!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: This type of Mercury doesn’t go into retrograde, but it was associated with the Swift Planet (a nickname for the planet Mercury) by alchemists trying to transform the element and other metals into gold. (Spoiler: It didn’t work.)

Mercury was among one of the first metals known by humankind, with its chemical symbol (Hg) coming from the Greek word hydrargyrum—meaning liquid silver or quicksilver. It perfectly describes mercury’s shiny, liquid properties—the only metal on earth that is liquid at room temperature. Alchemists and early scientists were drawn to mercury's ability to flow like water, but behave like a metal.

Alchemists believed mercury was the "First Matter," the substance from which all metals were created. They thought you could change, or transmute, mercury into gold. They obviously weren’t successful, but their experiments laid the foundation for modern chemistry! These experiments led to the development of distillation and sublimation, techniques still used in research today.

The unique metal was highly prized by ancient cultures, believing it to have healing powers and grant immortality. China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, drank a potion of mercury and powdered jade seeking to live forever; he promptly died. Despite mercury’s toxicity, the element would continue to be used in medicine for centuries, even being used to treat syphilis as recently as the 1950s.

Beyond medicine, mercury was the key to unlocking basic science. It was key to developing barometers (which measure air pressure) and blood pressure cuffs because it reacts consistently to pressure changes. Mercury was also perfect for thermometers because it expands and shrinks predictably with temperature. Today, we use safer materials for most of these tools, but mercury is still used for more advanced things, like electrodes, coulometers (a way to measure chemical reactions), and high-powered microscopes.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Mercury is a heavy, silvery-white liquid metal. It is so heavy that stone, iron, and even lead can float on its surface. While it is a poor conductor of heat, as compared with other metals, mercury is a fair conductor of electricity. It is also unreactive and highly resistant to corrosion.

Mercury is highly toxic and can be absorbed through the respiratory tract, the gastrointestinal tract and through unbroken skin. It is very important to handle mercury with care, in a well-ventilated hood.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Despite its toxicity, mercury has several applications across different industries. It is used for laboratory work in thermometers, barometers, diffusion pumps and many other instruments. It is used in making mercury-vapor lamps and advertising signs, etc., and is used in electrical switches and other electronic apparatus.
Amalgams used in dental fillings once contained tin and/or silver dissolved in mercury. Mercuric chloride is still used as a disinfectant and in antifungal skin ointments.
The compound mercuric sulfide can be red and is used in coloring material. Mercuric oxide is a component of batteries that support space exploration.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Mercury easily forms alloys with many metals—such as gold, silver, and tin—which are called amalgams. Mercury amalgamates easily with gold and is used to help recover the precious metal. Mercury also forms important salts that act as everything from poisons to paints.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are seven stable isotopes of mercury, with mercury-202 being the most abundant. The half-life of the isotopes ranges vastly, from 444 years and to less than a day.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Mercury rarely occurs freely in nature. Rather, it stems from the ore Cinnabar, which can be ground up and heated via high temperature air flow and then condensed using vapors.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1861, British chemist William Crookes (inventor of the Crookes tube) was busy examining the leftovers from producing sulfuric acid. He used flame spectroscopy, a technique that had just been approved for identifying minerals after improvements by scientists like Robert Bunsen (yes, the guy behind the Bunsen burner!). Crookes was hoping to find tellurium, but instead, he spotted something totally new—a bright green line in the flame. This had never been seen before and meant he had a new element on his hands. He named it thallium, after the Greek word thallos, meaning "green twig" because of that distinctive green color.

But Crookes wasn't the only one on the trail of thallium! Around the same time, Claude-Auguste Lamy in France was also using flame spectroscopy to study materials from sulfuric acid production. Lamy noticed the same green spectral line and realized he, too, had found a new element. While Crookes was first to announce the discovery, Lamy was the first to purify thallium, producing a small nugget of the shiny new metal in 1862.

There was a bit of drama between Crookes and Lamy about who should get the most credit for discovering thallium. While Crookes made the initial find, Lamy was the first to isolate it in larger quantities, which helped scientists learn more about the element’s properties. Ultimately, both scientists were recognized for their work.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Thallium is a soft, heavy, silvery-gray post-transition metal. It can be cut with a knife at room temperature. It tarnishes very quickly when exposed to air, forming a layer of blue-gray thallium oxide. It is the heaviest of the boron group elements, and is found in group 13, period 6 of the periodic table. It can be identified by the brilliant green flame it produces in a Bunsen burner.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Thallium sulfate was commonly used as a rat poison, until people realized just how toxic it was to humans and other animals. In 1972, it was banned in the United States (after 50 years of use), when it was discovered that about one quarter of sick/dead bald eagles had been poisoned by thallium. Household use is now banned in most countries.

Thallium oxide is used to make a special glass with a high refractive index that is used in optical measuring devices. Thallium is also used in low temperature thermometers and switches, because when alloyed with mercury, it lowers its melting point by 20°C.

Thallium-201 is proving to be an excellent isotope for cardiovascular imaging, because it has a half-life of 73 hours and emits x-rays as it decays. That short half-life means that it leaves the body quickly and is less risky for patients.
Thallium compounds are also used to produce green fireworks and color artificial gemstones.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Several minerals containing thallium occur in nature as sulfide/selenide complexes with antimony, arsenic, copper, lead, and silver.
Thallium oxide, bromide, iodide, and sulfate are produced for industrial uses. Thallium usually takes a +3 or +1 oxidation state in these compounds, reflecting the number of electrons it has lost.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are currently 41 known isotopes of thallium, with atomic masses ranging from 176 – 216. Only thallium-203 and thallium-205 are stable, and the only isotopes found naturally. Thallium-203 makes up 29.5% of naturally occurring thallium, with thallium-205 accounting for 70.5%. The most stable radioisotope of thallium is thallium-204, which has a half-life of 3.78 years.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Thallium is not found in its free form in nature, but thallium compounds do exist. The main naturally occurring ones are crookesite, hutchinsonite, and lorandite. Thallium is also found in manganese nodules on the ocean floor. Thallium is estimated to exist in the earth’s crust at an abundance of 0.7 ppm. It is mostly obtained as a by-product of sulfuric acid production from pyrites, and from refining of copper, lead, and zinc from their ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Lead has been used by humans for thousands of years, dating all the way back to 7000 BC! Some of the earliest lead artifacts, like beads, have been found in Asia Minor, where ancient people discovered how to melt lead from rocks. Although lead wasn’t very useful on its own because it’s soft, it was often found alongside silver. This made it valuable to early civilizations, who used lead for things like fishing sinkers, cosmetics, and even writing materials. The ancient Egyptians were some of the first to explore lead’s many uses, and soon, lead became popular across the ancient world.

By the time of the Roman Empire, lead production was booming. Romans mined huge amounts of lead. They used it for water pipes, which is actually where the word "plumbing" comes from—plumbum is the Latin word for lead! Romans also used lead to make coins, sling bullets, and even wine sweeteners (clearly not a healthy decision). In fact, lead was so important to Roman society that some historians call this period the Lead Age. While lead poisoning was a problem, especially for the wealthy who used lead vessels, the metal remained essential for everyday life.

During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, lead continued to be widely used. It was a key material for creating stained glass windows, and alchemists believed that lead could be transformed into gold. Lead even found its way into cosmetics, with Queen Elizabeth I of England famously using lead-based makeup to achieve a pale complexion. Unfortunately, the lead in these cosmetics caused serious health issues, and many believe it contributed to Elizabeth’s death.

The Industrial Revolution in the 18th and 19th centuries saw an explosion in lead production. Lead became crucial for plumbing, paint, and printing presses. This increased exposure to lead also led to more cases of lead poisoning. Scientists began to understand the dangers of lead fumes and dust, and in the late 1800s, the first laws were passed to protect workers from lead poisoning.

In the 20th century, lead was still widely used, especially in lead-based paints and as an additive in gasoline. However, as we learned more about the harmful effects of lead, countries began to phase it out. In the 1970s, the United States and Europe started passing laws to reduce lead exposure, and leaded gasoline was eventually banned. Today, lead is mainly used in batteries, but its long history reminds us of how much this metal has shaped human civilization.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Lead is a bluish-white metal of bright luster. It is very soft, highly malleable (easy to shape), ductile (able to be made into a wire), and a poor conductor of electricity. It is very resistant to corrosion.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: For years, lead was widely used in a variety of products, including cosmetics, glazes for pottery, paint, pipes, and in gasoline. All these uses have now been banned, replaced, or discouraged as lead is known to be detrimental to health, particularly for children. However, many pipes in our homes today are still made of lead.

Lead is very effective as a sound absorber, is used as a radiation shield around x-ray equipment and nuclear reactors and is used to absorb vibration. Lead is still widely used for car batteries, pigments, ammunition, cable sheathing, weights for lifting, weight belts for diving, lead crystal glass, radiation protection, and in some solders (melted metal used to fuse objects together). It is used to line containers for corrosive liquids (such as sulfuric acid). It is also sometimes used in architecture, for roofing, and in stained glass windows.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Lead is present in a variety of compounds such as lead acetate, lead chloride, lead chromate, lead nitrate, and lead oxide.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Natural lead is a mixture of four stable isotopes: lead-204 (1.48%), lead-206 (23.6%), lead-207 (22.6%), and lead-208 (52.3%). Lead isotopes are the end products of each of the three series of naturally occurring radioactive elements: lead-206 for the uranium series, lead-207 for the actinium series, and lead-208 for the thorium series. Twenty-seven other isotopes of lead, all of which are radioactive, are recognized.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Lead is obtained mainly from galena (PbS) ore by a roasting process. Anglesite, cerussite, and minim are other common lead minerals.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Bismuth has been a part of human history since ancient times. It was one of the first ten metals to be discovered, but no one knows who actually discovered it. The name bismuth likely comes from an old German word, Wismut, meaning “white mass.” Miners used to call it tectum argenti, or “silver being made,” thinking the earth was turning the substance into silver. Bismuth was confused with other elements for centuries.

In the 1500s, famous scientist Georgius Agricola noted that bismuth was different from tin and lead, based on its physical properties, but it took a while for people to realize just how distinct it was. In 1753, Claude François Geoffroy showed bismuth was chemically different from lead, getting credit for proving it was a unique element. Still, bismuth would continue to be confused with both lead and tin until modern analytical methods became available.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Bismuth is a white, crystalline, brittle metal with a pinkish tinge. Its thermal conductivity is lower than any metal, except for mercury. Of all metals, it is the most strongly repelled by a magnetic field.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Bismuth might seem a lot like lead, but it’s actually heavier and, most importantly, nontoxic. Since the 1990s, bismuth has been used as a safe replacement for lead. It's also been important in medicine. One of its most famous uses is in the pink stomach medicine, Pepto-Bismol—the active ingredient, bismuth subsalicylate, helps treat indigestion and other stomach issues. Bismuth is even used in cosmetics, giving makeup products like powders and eyeshadows a smooth, shiny finish.

Bismuth is highly versatile. It’s also used in fire sprinklers because it melts easily, which helps trigger the sprinklers when it gets too hot. That low melting point is also important for casting. Bismuth expands when it solidifies, which makes it perfect for creating sharp castings of objects that might be damaged by high heat.
Bismuth also plays a role in nuclear reactors, where it’s used as a coolant, and in thermoelectric devices, where it helps turn heat into electricity.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Bismuth is stable in air and water at ordinary temperatures. At high temperatures, it reacts with water to make bismuth(III) oxide. And when heated in air, it burns with a blue flame, forming yellow fumes of bismuth oxide. Bismuth sulfide forms naturally in bismuth ores. Bismuth oxychloride is used extensively in cosmetics. Bismuth subnitrate and subcarbonate are used in medicine.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Bismuth occurs naturally in the Earth’s crust at about twice the rate of gold. Its most important ores are bismuthinite and bismite. Peru, Japan, Mexico, Bolivia, and Canada are major bismuth producers. Much of the bismuth produced is obtained as a byproduct of refining lead, copper, and tungsten ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Gregor Mendeleev, who is sometimes called the “father of the periodic table,” predicted an element with polonium’s qualities in 1891. His pioneering periodic table had made it possible to predict the existence of elements that hadn’t yet been discovered—a kind of chemical crystal ball!

Seven years later, in 1898, French chemists Pierre and Marie Curie were investigating pitchblende—a radioactive mineral that contains uranium and thorium. They discovered that even with the uranium and thorium removed, the pitchblende was still highly radioactive. Eventually, the Curies found the elements polonium and radium in the pitchblende. They opted to name element 84 polonium after Marie Curie’s homeland, Poland—which was at that time under Russian, German, and Austro-Hungarian control—in part to raise awareness of the country’s lack of independence.

Polonium was first used in textile mills and in factories to reduce static electricity. During the Manhattan Project (the World War II-era effort to produce the world’s first nuclear weapon), polonium was used in some weapon designs. But polonium became notorious when, in 2006, it was used in the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko, a former Soviet intelligence officer who had defected to the United Kingdom. Only a few micrograms of polonium-210 were sufficient to cause Litvinenko’s death from radiation sickness.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Polonium’s most notable quality is its radioactivity. It is the most radioactive naturally occurring element: and less than one microgram of polonium-210 can be lethal! Although it’s usually handled in quantities that are too small to be visible to the naked eye, polonium is a silver-grey semi-metal that dissolves in dilute acids.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Polonium’s radioactivity is such that it generates heat, which is why it has been used in space. For example, the Soviet Union used polonium-210 as a heat source in moon rovers and satellites to prevent freezing.

Polonium is also used in antistatic devices, which are used in factories or industrial manufacturing (rather than to keep people from getting shocked by light switches!). However, polonium is so radioactive that researchers have increasingly looked for other substances that can remove static.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Almost all polonium compounds are made in laboratories, although you’ll find PbPo in nature (because polonium decays to form lead). Polonides are compounds of polonium and one other element. For example, polonides of calcium, barium, thulium, and others have been produced.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Researchers have identified 42 polonium isotopes. Polonium has no stable (non-radioactive) isotopes. Polonium-210 is the most common isotope, with a half-life of around 138 days. Polonium-209 has the longest half-life of any polonium isotope: its half-life is around 125 years. The shortest-lived polonium isotopes have half-lives of mere microseconds (a microsecond is one millionth of a second!).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Historically, polonium was extracted from uranium ores. However, this is a difficult process, because polonium is found in nature only in trace amounts. Today, all the world’s polonium is produced at the Ozersk nuclear reactor near Chelyabinsk, Russia. Only around 100 grams of polonium are produced each year. (For context, most apples weigh between 150 and 250 grams!)

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: On the periodic table, the space below iodine, reserved for element 85, sat empty for decades. Many scientists claimed to have found and isolated the elusive element, but none of these results were repeatable. In 1940, D.R. Corson, K.R. MacKenzie, and Emilio Segrè were able to create element 85 in a particle accelerator (called a cyclotron) at the University of California, Berkeley. The team bombarded bismuth-209 with alpha particles, causing the bismuth to emit two neutrons and, in doing so, become astatine-211. They chose the name astatine for their discovery, inspired by the Greek word astatos, meaning “unstable.”

Aptly named, astatine is highly radioactive, meaning it decays rapidly. The scientific community was reluctant at the time of its discovery to accept synthetically made, highly radioactive isotopes as legitimate elements. Fortunately for astatine, which has no stable isotopes, this changed in 1946 when the element was formally recognized.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: The most stable astatine isotope, synthetically produced astatine-210, has a half-life of only 8.1 hours. Most other isotopes of astatine have half-lives of a few seconds or less, decaying rapidly into polonium, bismuth, or radon. Because of its short half-life, the properties of astatine are difficult to discern. A weighable sample of the pure element is nearly impossible to assemble for study. Any visible portion of astatine would immediately vaporize itself because of its extreme radioactivity. Therefore, physical properties of this element are mostly speculative, either derived from theory or extrapolated from the properties of other halogens (those elements in column 9 of the periodic table).

Mass spectrometers have been used to confirm that astatine behaves chemically very much like other halogens, particularly iodine (although astatine is thought to be more metallic). Like iodine, astatine accumulates in the thyroid gland.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: The only isotope with an identified potential for use is astatine-211. Research in the field of nuclear medicine has shown that its short half-life and limited penetration through tissue offer advantages over current radiation therapies (such as iodine-131) for cancer treatment when a tumor is very small or in close proximity to important non-cancerous tissue.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Astatine is known to form compounds but is the least reactive of the halogens. It is most often studied in combination with iodine to ensure a sufficient quantity of substance to perform tests.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Astatine is continuously forming in the Earth’s crust as a decay product of the radioactive elements uranium and thorium. Its half-life is so short (a matter of seconds for most isotopes), that it does not accumulate, decaying rapidly into other elements. It is present on Earth in quantities of less than 30 grams at any given time. The isotopes astatine-209, -210, and -211 can be produced in small quantities in a cyclotron by bombarding bismuth with energetic alpha particles.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Observations of radon are recorded as far back as 1899. In separate experiments that year, Ernest Rutherford and Robert B. Owens, and Marie Curie and Pierre Currie observed a radioactive gas emitting from thorium and radium. A year later, Friedrich Ernst Dorn also saw a gas emanating inside tubes of radium. All five scientists were observing radon!

Rutherford went on to investigate the new gas and condensed it to a liquid in 1900. Finally, in 1908, William Ramsay and Robert Whytlaw-Gray at University College, London, gathered enough radon to learn more about it and even discovered that it was the heaviest gas known.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Radon is colorless, odorless, chemically nonreactive, and radioactive. Radon is gaseous when it decays, and therefore dangerous if inhaled. It is considered a contaminant and constantly monitored in air quality measurements.
When radon is cooled below freezing, it changes colors from yellow to orange red the more the temperature is lowered.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Once thought to cure various maladies, radon’s ionizing radiation is now known to cause cell damage, potentially leading to cancer. Still, some hospitals tried to use radon’s radiation to treat tumors directly by sealing the gas in small tubes and implanting the tubes into the tumors. These methods have been replaced with safer options. But some evidence suggests that radon can help improve some autoimmune diseases, like arthritis.
Meteorologists can also use measurements of outdoor radon to track air masses and gather information about moving weather systems.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Radon is expensive and very radioactive, so it is not used in many experiments. Not much is known about its chemical compounds, but there are a few reports of compounds made with fluorides or oxides.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Radon has 39 unstable isotopes. Radon-222 is the most common and the most stable with a half-life of only 3.8 days!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Radon is found naturally in rocks, uranium ores, phosphate rock, shales, igneous and metamorphic rocks and in some common rocks like limestone. This radon comes from the radioactive decay of radium-226. We can also detect a small amount in Earth’s atmosphere and a larger amount in areas where mining takes place.

Because radon is naturally produced in rocks, some can enter homes in the areas where the building touches soil. Scientists estimate that one gram of radon is in every square mile of soil! Radon is also industrially produced by processing uriniferous ores.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Chemists of the late 1800s expected another alkali metal, with atomic number 87, to exist below cesium on the periodic table. But its discovery proved extremely elusive until 1939. Marguerite Perey, of the Curie Institute in Paris (where she had been mentored by Marie Curie), identified francium after purifying a sample of the radioactive isotope actinium-227. The actinium decayed into something with an unexpected energy, and she wanted to identify what it could be.

After eliminating various possibilities (thorium, radium, lead, bismuth, and thallium), she concluded it might be the long-sought element 87. She correctly surmised that some of the actinium-227 underwent alpha decay to produce an isotope of the new element—francium-223. She later named the element francium, after her home country.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: It is very difficult to measure the properties of francium because it decays so fast. No weighable quantity of the element has been prepared or isolated, so even the atomic mass is difficult to quantify. Chemists report an atomic mass of 223 to match that of its longest-lived and naturally occurring isotope. The other chemical properties of francium are expected to resemble those of cesium, which is an extremely reactive metal that melts to a liquid around room temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because of the remarkable radioactive instability of francium, it does not stick around long enough to have any practical uses beyond scientific research.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: The only francium naturally occurring on Earth is in tiny amounts in uranium minerals. The isotope uranium-235, which comprises less than 1% of uranium in nature, undergoes a series of radioactive decays that includes francium-223. However, francium-223, though the longest-lived francium isotope, has only a 22-minute half-life! Francium-223 is the only francium found in nature. At any given time, it has been estimated that there is probably only about 30 grams (1 ounce) of francium in the entire crust of the earth.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Radium was discovered by physicist Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie. They found it in a large sample of uraninite, a radioactive mineral ore rich in uranium. This was incredibly difficult work because there is so little radium in uranite—only about one gram of radium in seven tons of uranite. After removing all the uranium and then a few other elements, the remaining material was still radioactive! This made the Curies curious and they suspected that they had found something new.

The Curies tried flame spectroscopy to identify what they had found, measuring the exact colors present in a flame when they burned the material. Each element has a unique color signature, but the specific deep-red shades that they saw when they tested their mystery material didn’t match any known element.

In 1898, the Curies reported their discovery of a compound containing a new element and named it radium for the intense radioactive rays it emits. Their samples produced a faint blue glow that could be seen in the dark because of the radioactivity affecting the surrounding air!

In 1911, Marie Curie and French chemist André-Louis Debierne isolated pure radium metal, using electrolysis (using an electrical current to drive the chemical separation), by splitting apart radium chloride. The process also required mixing the radium with mercury and then boiling off the mercury.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: The pure metal is silvery-white, shiny, and soft when freshly prepared, but it blackens upon exposure to air. With other metals, such tarnishing is usually caused by the oxygen in air, causing the metal to oxidize. But for radium, it’s the nitrogen in air that forms radium nitride on the metal’s surface.
All isotopes of radium are radioactive; none are stable. As a result, radium is quite dangerous to human beings and can cause cancer and other problems if touched, eaten, injected, or inhaled.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Radium has few uses. As of 2015, the total worldwide supply of purified radium was only a few kilograms. What little radium exists is primarily used in advanced physics research and as a cancer treatment. Cancers that get into the bone can be treated with radium-223, which emits alpha radiation. (The cancer-killing “bullets” of alpha radiation are helium nuclei: tiny bundles containing two protons and two neutrons. These helium nuclei get shot out of the radium nucleus.) Because radium is in the same group (periodic table column) as calcium, the two are chemically similar. Therefore, radium can be made to go where calcium goes—into the bones.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Radium is rare. It makes up only about one trillionth of the earth’s crust. But it is found in uranium deposits. Originally, radium was obtained from uranite ore from Bohemia (now the Czech Republic). This was Marie and Peirre Curie’s source. But since 2011, radium compounds are taken from spent fuel coming out of nuclear reactors. Now, chemists react radium oxide with aluminum at high temperatures to isolate the radium metal.
