sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Actinium is the first non-primordial radioactive element to be isolated. That means it’s the first radioactive element discovered that has only existed since after the Earth was formed.

First discovered in 1899 by French chemist Andre-Louis Debierne, actinium was named after the Greek word aktinos, meaning ray or beam, because of its bluish glow. Despite the discovery, he later lost interest in the element and the torch was taken up by Friedrich Oskar Giesel, a German organic chemist. Giesel originally thought he discovered another new element in 1902, but after comparing the half-lives of his material and actinium, it became apparent that he had become the first person to isolate the element.
Giesel continued his research on actinium and produced the first pure sample of the element. That’s why he gets credit for identifying its atomic number.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Actinium is the first element of the actinides and gave the set of 15 elements its name. It is a soft, silver-colored metallic element that sometimes has a golden cast. Yes, it glows in the dark with an eerie blue light. The blue color comes from the radioactive ionization of gases in the air.

In metal form, it is a good conductor of both heat and electricity. It has chemical properties that are similar to lanthanum, the element located directly above actinium in the periodic table. It has a density of 10.07 grams per cubic centimeter. Actinium’s melting point is 1050.0°C and the boiling point is 3200.0°C. It tarnishes easily in the air, forming a white coating of actinium oxide layer.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Right now, actinium doesn’t have a lot of uses. It’s used primarily in radiological research because it is a very powerful source of alpha rays and a good neutron source. Actinium-225 shows promising results as a radiation therapy to treat cancer.

The stable isotope actinium-277 has a half-life of 21.77 years, which makes it useful in modeling the slow, vertical mixing of oceanic waters. Researchers evaluate the concentration depth-profiles for actinium isotopes, which allows them to estimate the mixing rates and model the mixing behavior in the deep ocean. It also may be used for thermoelectric generators in spacecraft.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Actinium is intensely radioactive, so it has a limited number of known compounds. These compounds include actinium fluoride (AcF3), actinium chloride (AcCl3), actinium bromide (AcBr3), actinium oxyfluoride (AcOF), actinium oxychloride (AcOCl), actinium oxybromide (AcOBr), actinium sulfide (Ac2S3), actinium oxide (Ac2O3), actinium phosphate (AcPO4), and actinium nitrate Ac(NO3)3. They all contain actinium in the oxidation state.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Actinium is observed to form oxides, halides, oxyhalides, and oxophosphates. All isotopes of actinium are radioactive. Naturally occurring actinium is composed of two radioactive isotopes, actinium-227 (from uranium-235) and actinium-228 (from thorium-232).

Thirty-six radioisotopes have been identified, with the most stable being actinium-227 (half-life 21.772 years), actinium-225 (half-life 10 days), and actinium-22c (half-life 29.37 hours). All the remaining radioisotopes have half-lives shorter than 10 hours, with most being shorter than one minute.
The shortest-lived known radioisotope is actinium-217 (half-life 69 nanoseconds).

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Even though actinium is a rare element, it is found naturally in uranium ores, where it forms from radioactive decay of uranium. Actinium has a very small natural concentration, which makes separation of the element difficult and impractical. In fact, complete separation of actinium from uranium can never be achieved!

To get pure actinium, researchers bombard radium with neutron radiation in a nuclear reactor. However, only small amounts—meaning milligrams—can be made. After the actinium is synthesized, scientists can separate the actinium from any remaining radium or contaminants with a chemical solution and mild acid. Scientists can also separate actinium with resins and nitric acid.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1828, Norwegian amateur mineralogist Morten Thrane Esmark found an interesting black mineral on an island in Norway. In 1829, Jöns Jakob Berzelius of the Royal Karolinska Institute, Stockholm extracted thorium from the rock specimen sent to him by Esmark and realized that it had not previously been reported. The mineral turned out to be thorium silicate, now known as thorite. Berzelius produced a sample of metallic thorium by heating thorium fluoride with potassium, and confirmed it as a new metal.
The radioactivity of thorium was first demonstrated in 1898 by Gerhard Schmidt and confirmed by Marie Curie. Thorium, like uranium, survives on Earth because it has isotopes with long half-lives.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Thorium is a bright silvery metal that tarnishes olive gray when it is exposed to air; it is moderately soft and malleable and has a high melting point. It is nearly half as dense as uranium and plutonium, but is harder than both. It is about as hard as soft steel and can be rolled into sheets or pulled into wire. Its properties vary widely with the amount of impurities in the sample.
Thorium is highly reactive and tarnishes quite easily, becoming gray and finally black at the surface. Small bits of thorium can spontaneously ignite in air. It burns with a brilliant white light.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Thorium is used as an alloying agent with other metals such as magnesium to improve high-temperature strength.

Thorium was used to make ceramics, welding rods, camera and telescope lenses, and fire brick. It was also used in commercial photoelectric cells, added to glass for a high-refractive index, formerly a component of mantles for gas and kerosene lamps, and has been used in the manufacture of tungsten filaments for lightbulbs and vacuum tubes.
It is used in heat resistant paint and metals for the space industry.
Thorium can be used heavy water reactors, high-temperature gas-cooled reactors, light water reactors, and molten salt reactors. It is also used in scientific research.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Thorium can form alloys with many other metals, such as magnesium, chromium, and uranium. Thorium forms hydrides, dioxides, acids, fluorides, nitrides, halides, iodides, borides, carbides, silicides, and salts. The salts are quite acidic and are highly soluble in water. Thorium can also form perchlorates, sulfates, stultifies, nitrates, carbonates, phosphates, vanadates, molybdates, and chromates, and their hydrated forms.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are 32 characterized isotopes of thorium. All known thorium isotopes occur in nature and are unstable. They range in mass number from thorium-207 to thorium-238. The most stable isotope, thorium-232, has a half-life of 14.05 billion years—three times the age of the earth, and just slightly longer than the age of the universe. Thorium-232 is the only isotope that occurs in quantity in nature. The rest of the half-lives range from 75,380 years to less than 10 minutes.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Thorium is the 41st most abundant element in the Earth’s crust. It is found in trace quantities in virtually all rock, soil, water, plants, and animals.

Thorium is found as the minerals thorite, uranothorite, and thorianite. It is also found in monazite, a phosphate mineral, which is the most common source of thorium. It occurs in igneous rocks and other large deposits worldwide—principally India, South Africa, Brazil, Australis, and Malaysia. Thorium also occurs as a minor part of most minerals. It can be mined and refined from naturally occurring ores in rock or sands, and can be found in waste products such a mill tailings.
Man-made thorium is rare.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table predicted that an element existed in between thorium and uranium. The actinide series was not known at that time, but the search for the element was on!

Many experiments were conducted without success. Element 91 was finally identified in 1913 by Kazimierz Fajans and Oswald Helmuth Göhring, when they encountered it during their studies of the decay chains of uranium. They named the element “brevium” because of the short half-life of 1.16 minutes (protactinium-234). In 1917-1918, a more stable isotope (protactinitum-231) was discovered by Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn in collaboration with Frederick Soddy and John Cranston. They chose the name protactinium because they were looking for the “parent” of actinium.
In 1949, the IUPAC chose the name “protactinium” and confirmed Hahn and Meitner as the discoverers. The discovery completed one of the last gaps in early versions of the periodic table.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Protactinium is a very rare, dense, silvery-gray metal. It is malleable and radioactive. It reacts with oxygen, water vapor, and acids. It is a highly toxic and radioactive rare earth metal that requires special handling. Protactinium is a solid. At room temperature it crystallizes in a body-centered tetragonal structure, which can be seen as a distorted lattice.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because of its scarcity, protactinium is used only in basic scientific research. One isotope, protactinium-231, can be combined with thorium-230 and used to date marine sediments.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Protactinium can form oxides, hydroxides, halides, hydrides, fluorides, bromides, chlorides, iodides, nitrides, and sulfides. Since its oxides are basic, it can easily convert to various salts, such as sulfates, phosphates, and nitrates.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Protactinium has 29 isotopes whose half-lives are known, none of which are stable, with mass numbers 211 to 239. Its longest-lived isotopes are protactinium-231, with a half-life of 32,760 years, protactinium-233 with a half-life of 26.967 days, and protactinium-230 with a half-life of 17.4 days. The remaining isotopes have half-lives shorter than 1.6 days, with the majority of these having half-lives less than 1.8 seconds. All of the isotopes are highly radioactive.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Protactinium occurs naturally in very small amounts in all uranium ores, especially pitchblende. It is also produced as a by-product of uranium processing in nuclear reactors. In its natural state, it is one of the rarest and most expensive naturally occurring elements.
It is found mostly in two isotopes—protoactinium-231 and protoactinium-234. Nearly all naturally occurring protactinium is protactinium-231 (approximately 99.9999%).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1789, a German chemist named Martin Heinrich Klaproth was working on an experiment in his laboratory in Berlin. He was able to precipitate a yellow compound by dissolving pitchblende in nitric acid and neutralizing the solution with sodium hydroxide. He heated the substance with charcoal and produced a black powder, which he thought was a newly discovered metal. Turns out the powder was a uranium oxide. He named the newly discovered element uranium. In 1841, Eugène-Melchoir Péligot, a French chemist, isolated the first sample of uranium metal.

In 1896, Henri Becquerel, a French physicist and engineer, discovered the radioactivity of uranium in one of the most well-known accidental discoveries of physics. He unintentionally left a sample of uranium salt on top of an unexposed photographic plate, noting later that the plate had become fogged. He determined that a form of invisible light or rays emitted by uranium had exposed the plate. Serendipitously, radioactivity was discovered.

During World War I, there was a shortage of molybdenum to make artillery gun barrels. As a substitute, ferrouranium was used instead. In 1916, the US government requested that several prominent universities research the use of uranium in manufacturing and metalwork. Then, in 1942, came the Manhattan Project and the world would never be the same. Uranium became part of fission research and weapon development. The rest, as they say, is history.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Uranium is a silvery white, weakly radioactive metal that corrodes to a black oxide in air. Uranium is a solid at room temperature and is hard enough to scratch glass. It is malleable, ductile, and a poor electrical conductor. It reacts with almost all non-metal elements and their compounds. Uranium is highly soluble so it can be easily dissolved, transported, and precipitated within groundwater.

Uranium is the heaviest naturally occurring element and is actually more abundant than silver. It has the largest energy density of any of the world’s fuels used for generating electricity. Uranium is fissile and fissionable, describing how easily the atom can be split.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Uranium was first used in the year 79 CE to add a yellow color to ceramic glazes. That use continued into the Middle Ages. More recently, it was used to produce a ceramic glaze for Fiesta® ware, brightly colored dishware, from the 1930s to 1970s. This use was discontinued for health reasons.

Uranium continues to be used in nuclear reactors and nuclear weapons. It is also used in inertial guidance devices, gyro compasses, as counterweights for aircraft control surfaces, and ballast for missile reentry vehicles. It has many military uses. Uranium is also used for x-ray targets in the production of high-energy x-rays.
Uranium is used in scientific research, i.e., estimating the age of igneous rocks and other types of radiometric dating. It is also used for diagnosis and medical research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Uranium has 28 isotopes that have been identified, ranging in mass number from 214 to 242. Naturally occurring uranium is composed of three isotopes. Of the three, uranium-238 makes up 99.28%, uranium-235 makes up 0.71%, and uranium-234 makes up 0.0054%.

Uranium's most stable isotope, uranium-238, has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. Uranium-235, with a half-life of 704 million years, is the only naturally occurring isotope, and the only naturally occurring fissile material. It is also rare in nature.

Uranium-236 has a half-life of about 23 million years. It is not found in significant quantities in nature. Uranium-235 has a half-life of 245,500 years. Uranium-233 has a half-life of 160,000 years and, like 235U, is fissile.

Uranium-232 has a half-life of 68.9 years and is actually considered a nuisance; its decay products emit dangerously high gamma radiation. It won’t turn you into the Hulk, but this radiation is a huge safety concern and it complicates handling and processing. All other uranium isotopes have half-lives shorter than one hour.
Depleted uranium is the main by-product of uranium. It is the form of uranium that happens when most of the highly radioactive isotopes are removed. It is highly dense.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Uranium is a common element found in soil, rock, water, food, and animals. It is also found in numerous natural minerals such as pitchblende, uraninite, carnotite, autunite, uranophane, and tobernite; and in phosphate rocks, lignite, and monazite sands.
It is found in the Oklo natural nuclear fission reactor in West Africa.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Early in 1934, Enrico Fermi began an experiment that bombarded uranium with neutrons. He was trying to produce elements 93 and 94. His team was initially reluctant to publicize the claim that they might have found element 93, but they did publish a paper entitled "Possible Production of Elements of Atomic Number Higher than 92" in June 1934. Many theoretical objections were quickly raised. Several other experiments attempted to create element 93, but they all failed.

In 1939, physicist Edwin McMillan began an experiment bombarding uranium with neutrons in the 60-inch cyclotron at the University of California, Berkeley. He found a fission product whose half-life of 2.3 days was unknown. He took the sample to Emilio Segrè to isolate the source of the radioactivity. The two scientists believed that the unknown half-life was simply another fission product of uranium.

However, early in 1940, McMillan and Philip Abelson, another chemist, tried again to find out what was causing the unknown half-life. Abelson noticed that whatever was producing this half-life did not have a chemistry like any other known element but that it was similar to uranium. After bombarding another sample, they proved that a new element had been discovered.
Neptunium is one of three elements that are named for planets (or Roman gods, if you prefer). Because uranium was named for Uranus, neptunium was named for Neptune, the next planet beyond Uranus.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Neptunium, like most actinides, is a ductile, silvery, radioactive metal that tarnishes when exposed to air. It has a low melting point. Its boiling point is not empirically known but is guessed at from its vapor pressure. It has the largest liquid range of any element. It is the densest element of all the actinides and the fifth most dense of all naturally occurring elements. It can exhibit magnetic behavior.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Neptunium is used in neutron detectors and basic scientific research. It is also used to produce plutonium.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Neptunium forms a variety of compounds such as halides, hydrides, fluorides, chlorides, bromides, sulfides, nitrides, and oxides (where known).

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Neptunium exists in three crystalline forms: orthorhombic, tetragonal, and body-centered cubic. It is a man-made metal.

There are 24 characterized isotopes of neptunium, and all are radioactive; the most stable is neptunium-237 with a half-life of 2,144,000 years, and among the most unstable is neptunium-225 with a half-life of little more than 2 microseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Neptunium is present in nature in extremely small amounts. Trace amounts of neptunium are found as decay products in uranium ores. Most neptunium that is found in the environment came from atmospheric nuclear explosions.
Neptunium is obtained as a by-product from nuclear reactors, extracted from the spent uranium fuel rods.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1934, Enrico Fermi and a team of scientists at the University of Rome reported that they had discovered a new element, element 94. Fermi called the element hesperium. However, the sample of material actually contained products of nuclear fission, primarily barium and krypton. Nuclear fission was unknown at the time and not discovered until 1938 (by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassman).

Plutonium was first made in December 1940 at the University of California, Berkeley, by Glenn Seaborg, Arthur Wahl, Joseph Kennedy, and Edwin McMillan in a 60-inch cyclotron, a type of particle accelerator. They produced plutonium by bombarding uranium-238 with alpha particles (two protons and two neutrons, like helium but without the electrons). Within a couple of months, element 94 had been identified and its basic chemistry characterized. However, the discovery announcement was delayed until a year after the end of World War II because of security concerns.

McMillan had recently named the first transuranic (after uranium) element neptunium after the planet Neptune. He suggested that the new element be named for the next planet, Pluto, which was still considered a planet at the time (and remains so in our hearts).

At first, the amounts of plutonium produced were so minuscule that they were invisible to the naked eye. But by August 1942, there was enough to see—just three millionths of a gram. By 1945, enough plutonium was produced to make three atomic bombs: the Gadget, Fat Man, and Third Shot.

The Gadget was detonated in the world's first nuclear test—Trinity—on July 16, 1945, marking the beginning of the atomic age. Fat Man was one of two atomic bombs used against Japan during World War II; it was detonated above Nagasaki on August 9, 1945, killing over 40,000 people. Third Shot was another Fat Man-style bomb that was disassembled, with its plutonium core kept for testing, after Japan surrendered.
Had the war continued, the US had enough plutonium to make a new bomb about every ten days.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Plutonium is a radioactive metal with a silvery-gray appearance. It tarnishes when exposed to air and forms a dull coating with a gray, yellow, or olive-green color when oxidized. It is about as hard and brittle as cast iron, unless it is alloyed with another metal to make is soft and ductile. A large piece can feel warm to the touch. Large pieces will produce enough heat to boil water because of radioactive decay. It is highly radioactive.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Plutonium is used as an explosive ingredient in nuclear weapons and is a key material in the development of industrial nuclear reactors and nuclear power. It is also used as a power and heat source for instruments left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts, weather satellites, interplanetary probes, thermoelectric generators for spacecraft and extra-terrestrial rovers, and some medical equipment. It is also used in basic scientific research.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Plutonium can form alloys and intermediate compounds with most other metals. Gallium, aluminum, americium, scandium, and cerium can stabilize plutonium metal. Nuclear fuel pellets can be formed by alloying plutonium with various metals such as aluminum, zirconium, cerium, cerium-cobalt, uranium-titanium, uranium-zirconium, and uranium-molybdenum.

Plutonium also forms compounds with a variety of other elements. Plutonium reacts with pure hydrogen, forming plutonium hydrides. It also reacts readily with oxygen, forming PuO and PuO2. The metal reacts with the halogens, giving rise to trivalent Pu compounds with the general formula PuX3 where X can be F, Cl, Br, or I, and tetravalent plutonium compounds, such as PuF4.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Plutonium metal is man-made and has six crystal structures, or allotropes, at atmospheric pressure—more than any other element! At room temperature, it takes the alpha form; the other forms are beta, gamma, delta, delta prime, and epsilon. That range is exceptionally weird and unusual for a pure element!

Twenty isotopes have been characterized—all radioactive. The longest-lived are plutonium-244, with a half-life of 80.8 million years, plutonium-242, with a half-life of 373,300 years, and plutonium-239, with a half-life of 24,110 years. The remaining radioactive isotopes have half-lives that are less than 7,000 years.

Plutonium-244 has been found in interstellar space and has the longest half-life of any non-primordial radioisotopes. The known isotopes range from -228 to -247. Plutonium-244 is the most stable isotope.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Plutonium has the highest atomic number of any element to occur in nature. Trace quantities are found in natural uranium deposits and in the natural nuclear fission reactor in Oklo, Gabon. It is the heaviest primordial element in existence. There is also evidence of spontaneous fission of extinct plutonium in meteorites.
For the most part, plutonium is produced as a by-product in nuclear reactors. It can also be found in Earth’s atmosphere due to atmospheric weapons testing in the 1950s and 1960s.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Americium was first intentionally produced and identified in late 1944 at the University of California, Berkeley as part of the Manhattan Project by Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, and Albert Ghiorso. It was chemically identified at the Metallurgical Laboratory of the University of Chicago. Although it is the third element in the transuranic series, it was the fourth transuranic element to be discovered. Its discovery was kept secret and wasn't released to the public until November 1945.

Americium is a man-made radioactive chemical element. It is a transuranic (meaning beyond uranium) member of the actinide series. In the periodic table, it is located under its twin lanthanide element, europium. Matching its twin, it was named americium by analogy and because it was first produced in the United States.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Americium is a highly radioactive, silvery-white, man-made element. It slowly tarnishes in dry air at room temperature. Americium is less dense than both curium and plutonium; but has a higher density than europium—mostly because of its higher atomic mass. Americium is relatively soft and easily deformable. It readily reacts with oxygen and dissolves in aqueous acids. Its melting point is 1176°C, its boiling point is 2011°C, and its density is 12 g/cm3.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Americium can be produced in kilogram quantities and has few practical uses. Americium is commonly used in smoke alarms, keeping us firesafe.

Americium is used in smoke detectors for its alpha particles. Alpha particles ionize air molecules creating negatively and positively charged particles. There is a constant flow of the charged particles inside the smoke detector, and when broken by smoke, the alarm is triggered.

Americium can also be used as a portable source of gamma rays for medical and industrial uses, such as spectroscopy, radiography, and the creation of flat glass. It has the potential to be used in spacecraft batteries in the future, but that use is hindered by the scarcity and high price of this element ($1500/gram).

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Americium reacts with oxygen to form the dioxide AmO2. It reacts with halogen elements to form compounds such as tetrafluoride (AmF4). It reacts with hydrogen to form the hydride AmH2. It has four oxidation states in acidic aqueous solutions: Am3+ (pink), Am4+ (rose colored and very unstable), AmO2+ (yellow), and AmO22+ (light tan).

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are at least 19 radioactive isotopes. The longest-lived and most common isotopes of americium, americium-241 and -243, have half-lives of 432.2 and 7,370 years, respectively. Because of the length of these half-lives, any americium that was present during the formation of the earth should have decayed by now. Americium-241 produces about three times as much alpha radiation as radium.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Americium is produced by bombarding uranium or plutonium with neutrons in nuclear reactors. It also is concentrated in areas that were used for atmospheric nuclear tests and nuclear accident sites, such as Chernobyl.
Americium has also been theoretically detected in stars. It may occur naturally in extremely small trace amounts in uranium minerals because of nuclear reactions.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Curium was first made in the 60-inch cyclotron at the University of California, Berkeley, by the team of Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, and Albert Ghiorso in 1944. They bombarded a piece of the newly discovered element plutonium with alpha-particles (two protons and two neutrons, like helium but without the electrons). They then sent the piece to the Metallurgical Laboratory at the University of Chicago where a tiny sample of curium was separated and identified. However, like actinium, the discovery was kept secret until after the end of World War II. The news of the discovery was released to the public in November 1947.

Curium was named after Marie and Pierre Curie, who discovered radium. In the informal naming tradition, it followed the naming example of the lanthanide element gadolinium, which was named after Johan Gadolin, the explorer of rare-earth elements.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Curium is a hard, dense, silvery metal. For an actinide, it has a high melting and boiling point. It has a weak magnetic attraction at ambient conditions until it cools. All known isotopes of curium are radioactive.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Curium is used primarily for scientific research and for making heavier actinides. Isotopes of curium are used in power generation industries such as thermo-electric and thermionic converters.

The metal is used in x-ray spectrometers for quantitative analysis of rock structures and composition on the surface of Mars or other planetary bodies. It can also be used as a power source in medical and spacecraft applications. It is not currently used a nuclear fuel because of low availability and high price.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Curium readily reacts with oxygen forming mostly oxides. It can also form fluorides, chlorides, sulfides, selenides, and tellurides. Most of the compounds are faintly yellow.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Curium has two crystalline forms, one with a hexagonal symmetry. It does not exist in any other form.

Curium has approximately 19 isotopes with half-lives ranging from 15.6 million years to 18.1 years. All isotopes undergo self-sustaining nuclear chain reactions. Curium-250 is unusual as it mostly decays by spontaneous fission.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Curium is a man-made metal produced in nuclear reactors. It is produced in small amounts for research purposes.
It is present as one of the waste products in spent nuclear fuel and is present in nature in some areas historically used for nuclear weapons testing.

Any naturally occurring curium would have decayed away long ago, because even the longest half-life of 15.6 million years is shorter than the age of the Earth. Its past presence as an extinct radionuclide is detectable in its long-lived daughter, uranium-235. It may have been present in Oklo, Gabon, Earth’s natural nuclear fission reactor site.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The first known discovery of berkelium happened in 1949 at the University of California, Berkeley. Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg bombarded americium with alpha particles (two protons and two neutrons, like helium without the electrons) for several hours in a 60-inch cyclotron—ultimately producing a new element. The isotope that they produced had a half-life of about five hours. It took another nine years before enough berkelium was made to see it with the naked eye (and the amount was only a few micrograms). It was named berkelium after Berkeley, California, the city of its discovery.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Berkelium is a soft, silvery-white, radioactive metal. It shares many qualities with the lanthanide terbium, it’s partner element in the lanthanide series. It is easily soluble in dilute mineral acids, and rapidly oxidizes in air or oxygen.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because berkelium is rare, there are no commercial uses. However, it is used in scientific research as a target to synthesize heavier elements by charged particle bombardment. It has the lowest resistance to bulk compression of the actinides.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Berkelium forms two oxides, one a brown solid and the other a yellow-green solid. It also forms halides such as berkelium fluoride and berkelium chloride. Both of these are yellow green in appearance. Another halide is berkelium bromide, which has two forms. One is, you guessed it, yellow green. The other is just yellow.

Other inorganic compounds are berkelium sulfide and berkelium hydroxide. Berkelium sulfide is brownish black, while berkelium hydroxide shows a strong fluorescence when put under a green light. Berkelium also forms numerous alloys.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Berkelium metal exhibits two crystal forms: a double hexagonal close packed, and a face-centered cubic.

Nineteen isotopes of berkelium are now known and have been synthesized from mass number 233 to 253. All of the isotopes are radioactive. The half-lives range from 1,380 years (berkelium-247) to microseconds, therefore none could have persisted since Earth’s formation. Berkelium could have occurred naturally in the natural nuclear fission reactor in Oklo, Gabon, but would have long since decayed away. The isotope that is easiest to synthesize is berkelium-249, which is produced in nuclear reactors.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: There are no natural sources of berkelium. It is artificially produced and only in small amounts. Most of the world’s berkelium is made at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in the High Flux Isotope Reactor, which was recently designated a Nuclear Historic Landmark.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Californium is a man-made element that was first produced at the University of California Radiation Laboratory at Berkeley by physics researchers Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street, Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg in February 1950. It was made by bombarding microgram quantities of curium with helium ions in the Berkeley 60-inch cyclotron. Californium was discovered almost simultaneously with berkelium. The discoverers named the new element after the university and the state. This was a break from the convention used for elements 95 to 97, which drew inspiration from how the lanthanide elements directly above them in the periodic table were named.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Californium is, like most actinides, a silvery-white metal. It is pliable and easily cut with a razor blade, but don’t—it’s radioactive. Californium metal can act like a magnet. It forms alloys with lanthanide metals, but little is known about those materials. It is extremely radioactive. Californium slowly tarnishes in air at room temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Californium is one of the few actinides that has practical applications. It is used to help start up nuclear reactors and is used as a source of neutrons in neutron diffraction and neutron spectroscopy. It is also used in treatments of certain cervical and brain cancers.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Californium forms water-soluble chlorides, nitrates, perchlorates, and sulfates. It precipitates as a fluoride, oxalate, or hydroxide. Compound colors include yellow, dark violet, yellow green, bright green, emerald green, lemon yellow, pale green, black brown, and just plain green. Californium is the heaviest actinide to exhibit electron sharing, as in californium borate. Only a few of the compounds have been studied. These compounds include californium oxide, californium trichloride, and californium oxychloride.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Californium exists in two crystalline forms under normal pressure and one crystalline form that exists under high pressure.

Californium has 20 known isotopes from mass number 237 to 256. Half-lives range from 898 years to less than 20 minutes. The most stable isotope is californium-251 (898 years). Californium is formed from the beta decay of berkelium-249.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Californium can be found in traces near facilities that use it in mineral prospecting and in medical treatments. It can also be found in radioactive dust collections from atmospheric nuclear weapons testing fallout. It is believed that it occurred naturally in the Oklo natural nuclear reactor but is no longer present.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Einsteinium was discovered in December 1952 by Albert Ghiorso and co-workers at the University of California, Berkeley, in collaboration with Argonne and Los Alamos national laboratories. The element was discovered in the fallout (or debris) from a thermonuclear device, which was exploded in the South Pacific. Because plutonium-244 was discovered on filter papers from a plane flown through the fallout, other filter papers were examined. Larger amounts of radioactive material were later isolated from the coral debris of an atoll.

The researchers were puzzled by the multiple neutron absorptions found when such a process was supposed to be extremely rare. Einsteinium, along with other actinide elements, was recovered. Its discovery was kept secret until 1955 because of the secrecy surrounding the nuclear test. It was named Einsteinium in honor of Albert Einstein.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Einsteinium is a soft, silvery, weakly magnetic, radioactive metal. It is among the heaviest elements that can be used in bulk studies.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Einsteinium has no commercial uses. It is used for basic scientific research in radiation damage, targeted radiation medical treatments, and accelerated aging.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Very few compounds are known, but include halogens (known as halides), oxygen (known as oxides), and hydrogen (known as hydrides).

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Einsteinium is believed to have a face-centered cubic crystal symmetry. There is a report of a room-temperature hexagonal crystal, which converts to the face-centered cubic on heating.

Einsteinium has 19 known isotopes with mass number from 240 to 257. All of the isotopes are radioactive. The most stable isotope is einsteinium-252, with a half-life of 471.7 days. The next most stable isotopes are einsteinium-254 (half-life 275.7 days), einsteinium-255 (39.8 days), and einsteinium-253 (20.47 days). The remaining isotopes have half-lives shorter than 40 hours, with most being shorter than 30 minutes.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Einsteinium does not exist in nature. It is only produced in small amounts in nuclear reactors, scientific laboratories, or nuclear weapons tests.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Fermium was first discovered in 1952 in the fallout from the “Ivy Mike” nuclear test (the first successful test of a hydrogen fusion bomb) in the South Pacific. Researchers identified a new plutonium-244 isotope on filter papers from a drone aircraft flown through the fallout. This discovery raised the possibility that the uranium nuclei could have absorbed still more neutrons, resulting in more new elements.

The researchers discovered einsteinium almost immediately on other filter papers but needed more material to see if there were any other new elements. Contaminated coral from the Enewetak Atoll was shipped to Berkeley for processing and analysis. About two months after the test, a new element was isolated, emitting high-energy particles with a half-life of about 20 hours. The discovery was kept secret on the orders of the US military until 1955 because of Cold War tensions.

From 1953 to 1954, the Berkeley team was able to prepare fermium in the lab by neutron bombardment of plutonium-239 in a cyclotron. They published their work in 1954 with a disclaimer that the results were not the first studies that had been carried out on the new element. The Ivy Mike studies were later declassified and published in 1955.

Meanwhile, a group of researchers at the Nobel Institute of Physics in Stockholm independently claimed discovery of element 100 by producing an isotope with a 30-minute half-life, publishing their work in May 1954. However, the historical precedence of the Berkeley team discovery was recognized and they got to name the new element. They named the element Fermium in honor of the recently deceased Enrico Fermi, who developed the first artificial self-sustained nuclear reactor.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Fermium is the heavy-weight champion of man-made elements that can be formed by neutron bombardment of lighter elements. It is highly radioactive. It is thought that fermium metal would have a silvery appearance; however, nobody knows much about this element.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because of the short half-lives of all fermium isotopes, and the fact that only very small amounts of fermium can be produced, fermium has no applications beyond basic scientific research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Fermium has 20 isotopes. Fermium-257 is the longest-lived, with a half-life of 100.5 days. Fermium-252 has a half-life of three days, fermium-252 and fermium-255 have half-lives of about one day (25.4 hours and 20.1 hours, respectively), while fermium-251, fermium-254, and fermium-256 have half-lives of a couple of hours (5.3 hours, 3.2 hours, and 2.6 hours, respectively). The remaining isotopes have half-lives ranging from 30 minutes to less than a millisecond.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Because of the short half-life of all fermium isotopes, any that may have been present from the beginning of the formation of the Earth have long since decayed away. Einsteinium and fermium did occur in the natural nuclear fission reactor at Oklo (Earth’s two-billion-year-old, only known natural nuclear reactor), but they no longer exist.

Fermium is produced by the bombardment of lighter actinides with neutrons in nuclear reactors or accelerators. The major source of fermium is the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1955, the same team from the University of California, Berkeley, that discovered many of the actinides (Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg, Greg Choppin, Bernard Harvey, and Stanley Thompson) were bombarding an einsteinium-253 target with alpha particles (two protons and two neutrons, like helium without the electrons) in the 60-inch cyclotron. They produced seventeen atoms of mendelevium-256. This discovery was part of a program that started in 1952 that bombarded plutonium with neutrons to change it into heavier actinides. This process came about because the previous method of using neutron capture was not working. Because the short half-lives of fermium isotopes limited the success of the neutron capture process, they could not produce isotopes of mendelevium through that method.

The team decided that because it was the first of the second hundred chemical elements, the new element would be named after Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table. Because the discovery happened during the Cold War, Seaborg had to get permission from the US government to propose naming the element after a Russian.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Mendelevium is mostly known in solution and can take on the +3 or +2 oxidation states (having lost either two or three electrons). It is believed that it could form insoluble hydroxides and fluorides, but none have been observed.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Mendelevium is only used for basic scientific research.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Mendelevium is thought to be a solid at standard room temperature; however, the color and other properties are unknown.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: It is predicted that mendelevium would have a face-centered cubic crystal structure.

Mendelevium has 17 known isotopes, all of which are radioactive. The longest-lived is mendelevium-258, which has a half-life of 51.5 days. Mendelevium-256, with a half-life of 1.17 hours, can be produced in larger quantities and therefore used in research. Other half-lives range from 31.8 day to less than 5 minutes.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: The only source of mendelevium is bombarding targets in a cyclotron. It is very rare and only a few atoms have ever been made.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Nobelium’s discovery was one of the most complicated processes with multiple claims by groups from Sweden, the United States, and Russia (the former Soviet Union). The first claim was announced in 1968 by physicists at the Nobel Institute in Sweden in 1957. They proposed the name nobelium for the new element, which was immediately approved by the IUPAC, a decision Russia said was hasty. The second claim came in 1958 from scientists at the University of California, Berkeley. The claims all revolved around the half-life of the isotope that was found. Sweden reported a half-life of 10 minutes; the United States reported approximately 3 seconds; and later in 1963, the Russians reported a half-life of approximately 50 seconds. The Russians were right.

While both the Swedish and US teams contributed valuable research, their experiments were ultimately clouded by background elements and misinterpretations. Finally, in 1994, the IUPAC credited the Russian team with the discovery, but ratified the name for element 102 on the basis that it was the name used in the literature for over 30 years. The element was originally named for Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist, engineer, inventor, businessman, and philanthropist.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Nobelium is highly radioactive. It is predicted to be a divalent metal. A lot of properties remain unknown. It is predicted to have a face-centered cubic structure. It is only known in an aqueous solution. It is predicted to be silver in color, just like the other actinides.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Nobelium has no uses beyond basic scientific research because only a few atoms have ever been made.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Nobelium can react with chlorine and result in nobelium chloride. Other compounds are predicted but are not known at this time.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Because only tiny amounts of nobelium have been produced, its structures are not well known.

A total of 13 isotopes are known to exist. The most stable is nobelium-259, which has a half-life of 58 minutes. Nobelium-255 has a half-life of 3.1 minutes, but it is the most common isotope to be used in research. We can make more of it than the other isotopes. There is a prediction that nobelium-261 has a half-life of 170 minutes, but this has not been confirmed. All of the remaining nobelium isotopes have half-lives that are less than a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Nobelium can only be produced in particle accelerators by bombarding lighter elements with charged particles. It does not exist in nature.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Lawrencium was synthesized in 1961 by Albert Ghiorso, Torbjørn Sikkeland, Almon Larsh, and Robert Latimer at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, California. It was the last member of the actinide series to be discovered. It is named after Ernest Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron particle accelerator.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Lawrencium is expected to be a silvery radioactive metal that easily oxidizes in air steam, and acids. It is expected to be rather heavy with a density of around 14.4 g/cm3. It is also predicted to have a melting point of around 1627°C.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Because of the scarcity of lawrencium, it has no uses beyond scientific research.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: In 1969, lawrencium was shown to react with chlorine to form a product that was a trichloride. At this time, other compounds are predicted but have not yet been identified.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Lawrencium has 14 isotopes whose half-lives are known. All of the isotopes are short-lived and radioactive. The longest-lived isotope is lawrencium-266 with a half-life of approximately 10 hours. It is not used in chemical experiments because it can only be produced as a final decay product of heavier and harder-to-make elements.

Lawrencium-264 (half-life of 4.8 hours), lawrencium-262 (half-life 3.6 hours), and lawrencium-260 (half-life of 2.7 minutes) are the next long-lived. All other known isotopes have half-lives shorter than five minutes. The shortest half-life is 24.4 milliseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Lawrencium does not occur naturally. It is produced in particle accelerators by bombarding californium with boron.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Rutherfordium belongs to a class of elements that have only been created in laboratories. You'd think credit for the creation of a synthetic element would be pretty straight forward, but the question of when and who first discovered rutherfordium remains controversial.

In 1964, a team led by Georgi Flerov (sometimes spelled Georgii Flyorov) was the first group to report discovering element 104. The team, based in then-Soviet Union at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR), bombarded atoms of plutonium-242 with atoms of neon-22, with the goal of causing the atoms to fuse and—presto!—create a new element. The team wanted to name the element kurchatovium, after Soviet physicist Igor Kurchatov—father of the Soviet atomic bomb. But the scientific community had doubts about the team’s research, and the element remained officially undiscovered.

In 1969, an American team led by Albert Ghiorso at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory published their efforts to synthesize element 104. The Berkeley team couldn't replicate the pathway that Flerov's team claimed, but they did discover three pathways to produce the new element—bombarding curium-248 with oxygen-18 and californium-248 and -249 with carbon-12 and -13, respectively. They proposed calling the new element rutherfordium, after New Zealander physicist Ernest Rutherford—father of nuclear physics.

Over twenty years later, in 1992, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) ruled that both teams deserved credit for discovering the element. However, IUPAC decided that the element should get the American name, rutherfordium.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Rutherfordium atoms have extremely short half-lives, and only a relatively small number of atoms of the element have ever been produced. For these reasons, scientists can only predict many of the element’s qualities. Rutherfordium is the first transactinide element (all of which have atomic numbers greater than 103). It’s thought that rutherfordium is a silvery metal like other group 4 elements, such as titanium, zirconium, and hafnium.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Rutherfordium has no known non-research uses.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: It’s thought that rutherfordium should make a very stable oxide. Rutherfordium also forms volatile chlorides.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: There are 16 known isotopes of rutherfordium, all of which are synthetic. The longest-lived rutherfordium isotope, rutherfordium-267, has a half-life of around 48 minutes, while the shortest-lived isotopes have half-lives of less than 50 microseconds. (A microsecond is one millionth of a second!)

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: You won’t find rutherfordium in nature, it exists only in laboratories with highly specialized equipment that allows researchers to bombard atoms—a kind of molecular bowling alley!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1968, lead researcher Georgy Flerov (sometimes spelled Georgii Flyorov) reported that his team at Russia’s Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) created a few atoms of element 105. They did so by bombarding amercium-243 with neon-22. The two nuclei combined, or fused, and a few neutrons popped out. The evidence that they created a new element was based on the analysis of emerging alpha particles (two protons and two neutrons, a helium nuclei), a common radioactive emission.

In 1970, an American team at the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory in California, led by Albert Ghiorso, bombarded californium-249 with nitrogen-15. Interestingly, their alpha-particle data conflicted with the JINR team's. The American team demonstrated that they produced an isotope of element 105 with a mass of 260. Their data indicated that JINR had not actually produced isotopes of mass 260. However, the JINR team had continued their research and published new results giving further evidence that they had produced isotopes of element 105 with a mass of 261, and possibly 260.

In 1997, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) decided that the credit for discovery should be shared, but the element should be named dubnium after Dubna, Russia, where JINR is located.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Research into the chemical properties of dubnium are limited. Given its short half-life, it is exceedingly difficult to work with this element and impossible to measure its properties. Even its atomic mass is unknown—there isn't enough of the element to weigh. It is simply listed as the mass number of its longest-lived isotope, 268.

With just a handful of atoms ever created, studies on dubnium have only been conducted on individual atoms. Still, the results generally align with theoretical predictions. Dubnium should behave like vanadium, niobium, and tantalum, which are directly above it on the periodic table.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Dubnium has no known uses beyond fundamental research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Like all synthetic, high-atomic-number elements, dubnium is extremely radioactive and has no stable isotopes. Of its 13 known isotopes, its longest-lived, dubnium-268, has a half-life of only 16 hours. Most of the others last only seconds or fractions of a second.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Dubnium is a purely synthetic element and does not occur in nature.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Element 106, seaborgium, was discovered by a team at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1974. Scientists bombarded molecules of californium with oxygen ions. But there was a twist—scientists at the Soviet Union’s Joint Institute for Nuclear Research claimed they’d found the element several months earlier!

It wasn’t until 1992 that an international committee decided the Soviet team’s research wasn’t convincing enough and gave credit for seaborgium’s discovery to the American team. The team named the element after Glenn Seaborg, an American chemist whose work helped redefine the scientific community’s understanding of the elements.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Seaborgium is an extremely radioactive element whose longest-lived isotope has a half-life of only around two minutes. Because seaborgium decays so quickly, scientists don’t know for sure what the element’s properties are. Analyzing seaborgium atoms is a little like watching for shooting stars—blink and you’ll miss them! However, scientists think that seaborgium has physical and chemical qualities comparable to tungsten, its neighbor in the periodic table.
It’s likely that in sufficient qualities, seaborgium would be silvery grey in color.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Seaborgium has no known non-research uses.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Despite its short half-life, several seaborgium compounds have been produced and studied, such as seaborgium oxyfluoride, seaborgium oxychloride, and seaborgium oxide.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Seaborgium has 13 have been reported isotopes. The longest-lived isotope, seaborgium-269, has a half-life of around two minutes. Many other seaborgium isotopes have half-lives of much less than one second!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Seaborgium is a synthetic element, meaning that as far as scientists can tell, it doesn’t occur in nature. In fact, only a few laboratories in the world can make seaborgium, and only a few atoms of the element have ever been produced. Seaborgium is made by bombarding the atoms of one element with the atoms of another inside a linear accelerator, like the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Bohrium was first observed by a team of scientists in Dubna, Russia, in 1975. Yuri Oganessian and his team published their results on creating an isotope of element 107 with a mass of 261, but they don't get credit for bohrium's discovery.

In 1981, a team from the German nuclear research institute, the Geselleschaft für Schwerionenforschung (GSI), confirmed the existence of bohrium with more evidence and received credit for the discovery.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Very few properties of bohrium have been measured because it decays so quickly and is expensive to make. A few chemistry-related properties have been measured here and there, but properties and compounds of bohrium are largely unknown and scientists have only theorized what those might be like.
Bohrium's most stable isotope is bohrium-270 and only has a half-life of about 1 minute! It decays into dubnium-266 (named after Dubna, Russia, where bohrium was first synthesized).

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Bohrium isn’t really used beyond scientific research of bohrium itself. It is only used to study its own physical properties and to synthesize isotopes of other elements. In a way, it’s a helper element by allowing scientists to understand other elements!

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: All known isotopes of bohrium are very radioactive. The most stable isotope has a half-life of only 2.4 minutes!
There is an unconfirmed isotope, bohrium-278, that may have a longer half-life of about 11.5 minutes.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Only a few atoms of bohrium have ever been produced. Bohrium is a synthetic element, meaning it is not found in nature. It is artificially created in particle accelerators by bombarding bismuth with chromium.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in the Soviet Union first attempted to create element 108 in 1978. They did this by bombarding radium-226 with calcium-48. Although the JINR team thought that they had discovered the new element, they weren’t sure of their results.

In 1984, a team at Germany’s Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung (GSI) proved the creation of element 108 by bombarding lead-208 with iron-58. Avid Baywatch fans, the scientists named the new element hassium, after David Hasselhoff. Just kidding! Hassium’s name was really inspired by Hesse, the state where GSI is located.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Hassium is an extremely radioactive element, with its longest-lived isotope having a half-life of a mere 10 seconds! Because hassium decays so quickly, scientists don’t know for sure what the element’s qualities are. However, it’s thought that hassium’s properties should be like those of osmium and the platinum group metals, given its placement on the periodic table. Hassium should have a high melting point. It should be a slightly noble metal, making it resistant to corrosion.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Hassium has no known uses beyond fundamental research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Thirteen hassium isotopes have been created, with mass numbers ranging from 263 to 277. None of these isotopes occur naturally and all of them are unstable (radioactive).
Many hassium isotopes have half-lives of only milliseconds—less time than it takes to blink! The element’s most stable isotope, hassium-269, has a half-life of only around 10 seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Hassium is a synthetic element, meaning that as far as scientists can tell, it doesn’t occur in nature. Hassium is made by bombarding the atoms of one element with the atoms of another inside a linear accelerator, like the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE).

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Meitnerium is a purely synthetic element. It does not exist in nature. Like other synthetic elements, it is highly radioactive and decays in seconds or fractions of a second.

The first meitnerium atom was created in 1982 at the Heavy Ion Research Laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany (then West Germany). A team lead by German physicists Peter Armbruster and Gottfried Münzenberg bombarded a target of bismuth-209 with accelerated iron-58 nuclei. This caused the two different nuclei to undergo fusion, merging into meitnerium-266. Then, 5 milliseconds after it appeared, it decayed!

Armbruster and Münzenberg recommended that the new element be named after Lise Meitner, an Austrian physicist who coined the term "nuclear fission." Working with colleagues in 1938, she found that bombarding thorium with neutrons caused the thorium to split into lighter elements. The following year, she and her nephew, physicist Otto Robert Frisch, figured out how the splitting occurs and published their findings. They named the process “fission.” Soon thereafter, the Experimental Breeder Reactor-1 (a collaboration between what is now Argonne National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory) generated the first usable electricity from atomic fission. Now, nuclear power is the nation's largest source of next-generation energy, providing high-efficiency electricity to modernize the nation’s energy infrastructure.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Very few meitnerium atoms have ever been made. Because they’re made one atom at a time and decay rapidly, it’s not possible to measure the element's basic properties, like density and boiling point. Even the atomic mass is unknown. Like other synthetic elements, its mass number is simply assigned from its longest-lived isotope, meitnerium-287. It is expected to have similar properties to the metals directly above it on the periodic table (cobalt, rhodium, and iridium). It should be solid at room temperature, but none of this can be confirmed!

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Meitnerium has no uses beyond fundamental physics research.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Meitnerium is a synthetic element and can only be produced in a laboratory. It decays almost immediately after it forms.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Darmstadtium is one of the newest elements in the periodic table. It is a highly radioactive element that’s only made in a laboratory. In 1994, scientists at the GSI Heimholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research bombarded a lead-208 target with nickel-62 nuclei, creating four atoms of the new darmstadtium element.

Darmstadtium is named for the city where it was discovered, Darmstadt, Germany, but creating the element was truly an international effort. The GSI team built on the attempts of scientists in the Soviet Union and had collaborated with scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Because darmstadtium decays very quickly—the longest-lived darmstadtium isotope has a half-life of only 13 seconds—scientists cannot measure any of the element’s properties.

Scientists hypothesize that darmstadtium has similar properties to the periodic table’s platinum group metals, such as nickel, palladium, and platinum. It is expected to be dense, heavy, and a noble metal—being resistant to chemicals, acids, and corrosion.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Scientists have produced 11 different darmstadtium isotopes. However, darmstadtium is so unstable that its atoms often stay intact for just a fraction of a second or less. The longest-lived isotope, darmstadtium-281, has a half-life of only 13 seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Darmstadtium is produced by bombarding the nucleus of a heavier atom with the nucleus of a lighter atom, combining the two atoms into one. Only a handful of darmstadtium atoms have ever been made!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Roentgenium isn’t the sort of element you’ll find just anywhere. In fact, only a few molecules of this element have ever been created!

In 1969, researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in the United States tried to find elements 110 to 114 in mineral samples. Despite all their searching, they turned up empty-handed. In the mid-1980s, scientists at the Russian Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (better known as JINR) tried to make element 111 by bombarding bismuth-290 with nickel-64. The idea was that by fusing the nuclei of the two atoms, a new element would result. But they weren't successful either. In 1994, a team of 13 physicists at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany, succeeded in making a few atoms of element 111 using the same process that the JINR team had tried.

After its discovery, the new element was given the temporary name unununium, based on the Latin roots for its atomic number. Ten years later, in 2004, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry accepted a name for the element proposed by the Darmstadt team: roentgenium, after Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen, the German physicist who discovered the x-ray in 1895.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Because so little roentgenium has ever been made (and because the atoms decay quickly), scientists can only speculate about the element’s properties. It’s thought that roentgenium should be a silvery noble metal that is quite dense.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Roentgenium has no known non-research uses.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: As far as scientists can tell, roentgenium isn’t found in nature. It has only been created in lab settings.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 1996, man-made copernicium came to life at the Heavy Ion Research Laboratory in Darmstadt, Germany. Like smashing pieces of clay together to make a new color, a team of scientists used a heavy ion accelerator to fuse zinc-70 with lead-208. The fusion was achieved by bombarding lead with zinc atoms traveling at 30,000 km per second, and the result was a single atom of copernicium-277.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Copernicium is considered one of the heaviest elements and is a highly radioactive metal. One of its most interesting properties is its short lifespan—the first production of Copernicium-277 decayed in just .24 milliseconds! Copernicium’s most stable isotope has an atomic weight of 285 and a half-life of 34 seconds.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: This element has no uses beyond scientific research because it decays so quickly.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Copernicium has only been created in lab settings and is not known to exist in nature.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Nihonium is one of the newest elements to be discovered. Don’t try to find nihonium anywhere in nature, though—it only exists in laboratories!

In the second half of the 20th century, scientists around the world were working to synthesize new elements. They did this primarily by bombarding “targets” of one element with atoms of another element, hoping to cause the nuclei to fuse and make a third, entirely new element. In 2003, a team of scientists at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Russia, working in collaboration with the United States’ Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, claimed to have discovered element 113 by this method.

However, the IUPAC/IUPAP Joint Working Party—which includes scientists from the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) and the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP)—felt that the JINR team hadn’t provided sufficient evidence that they actually created element 113. Instead, in 2015, credit for the discovery was awarded to a team from the Japanese research institute Riken, which had synthesized the element in 2004. The Riken team named element 113 after Nihon, one of two Japanese words for Japan.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Because so little nihonium has ever been created, and because nihonium is highly radioactive—meaning that its molecules decay quickly—scientists can’t say for sure what the element’s properties are. It’s thought that nihonium is a noble metal that has qualities in common with elements in the same periodic column—indium, boron, and aluminum—and that is denser than thallium.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Nihonium has no known non-research uses.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Nihonium isn’t naturally occurring. Eight nihonium isotopes have been reported, all of which are highly radioactive: nihonium-278, nihonium-282, nihonium-283, nihonium-284, nihonium-285, nihonium-286, nihonium-287, and nihonium-290.
The most stable (non-radioactive) of these is nihonium-286, which has a half-life of around nine seconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Nihonium is only produced in laboratories and is not known to exist in nature.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Flerovium is a radioactive element named after the Flerov Laboratory of Nuclear Reactions (or its founder, physicist Georgy Flerov, according to some) at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia. A team of Russian scientists at the institute produced the first observed flerovium atom in a particle accelerator in 1998. The discovery became official the following year with the team’s observation of a second and third flerovium atom. In both cases, the flerovium products were formed by fusion of a plutonium-244 and calcium-48. The newly discovered element was called ununquadium, based on the Latin roots for its atomic number. But in 2012, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) accepted the name flerovium in honor of JINR's founder.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Because so few atoms have been observed, the chemical and physical properties of flerovium remain largely unknown. Recent experiments suggest it may be a metal, though it has also exhibited properties consistent with noble gases.

sections.heading: Compounds
paragraphs: Flerovium compounds have not been observed and at this time are only predicted based on its proximity to lead on the periodic table.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Most observed flerovium atoms have been created by fusion within a particle accelerator. Others have occurred as transient decay products of heavier elements. To synthesize flerovium, a plutonium target is bombarded with calcium-48 atoms in the form of a high-speed beam. Producing the first flerovium atom took 40 days of bombarding plutonium-244 with billions of particles, at which point a calcium atom happened to fuse with an atom of plutonium. The resulting flerovium atom decayed 30.4 seconds later!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: In 2004, scientists from the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia, together with scientists from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, announced that they had successfully synthesized four atoms of element 115. The new element was originally named ununpentium based on the Latin root for its atomic number but was renamed moscovium in honor of the ancient land of Moscovia (present-day Russia), where the atom was first synthesized.

Although the atoms had decayed within milliseconds, the scientists were able to detect the predicted decay products that they had expected. As group leader Yuri Oganessian explained, the first five alpha decay reactions (where two protons and two neutrons [a helium nucleus] are spontaneously emitted from an unstable atom) occurred within 20 seconds...and then there was a pause. They didn’t see the next product until the following day! Because they were unsure of the exact pathway that had been followed, the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemists (IUPAC) decided that they didn’t have enough evidence to certify the existence of a new element.

The existence of moscovium was finally certified in 2016. JINR scientists determined that there had been a spontaneous fission decay event. Scientists independently observed the same thing in laboratories in Germany and California, supporting JINR's hypothesis.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Moscovium is one of the p-block transactinides. It is a member of group 15, the pnictogens, along with nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony and bismuth. Researchers predict that it should be a dense, reactive metal that is a solid at room temperature. It is thought to be most like bismuth.

So far, only about 100 atoms of moscovium have been produced, so no chemical properties have been confirmed. Scientists hope that moscovium is volatile enough, meaning it can easily become vapor, to study the element further. Many chemistry techniques use elements in their vaporized or gas state to analyze their properties.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Moscovium has no uses beyond scientific research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Currently there are five known isotopes of moscovium (moscovium-286, -287, -288, -289, and -290). Their half-lives range from 20 milliseconds to 650 milliseconds, with moscovium-290 being the most stable.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Moscovium is not found naturally anywhere on Earth. It has only been made in minute quantities in the laboratory. It is produced by using a particle accelerator to shoot Ca-48 atoms, traveling at one tenth the speed of light, into americium–243 atoms. When these two atoms fuse, moscovium is created.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The search for element 116 began in 1977, but it wasn’t until 2000 that scientists actually created the element, and not until 2011 that the element was officially recognized! Researchers from the Joint Institute of Nuclear Research (JINR) in Russia, the Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung (GSI) in Germany, and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) in California were all working towards creating and confirming the new element. LLNL scientists successfully created the element and earned naming rights by bombarding calcium-48 and curium-248.

Studies on the element continue today. In the summer of 2024, researchers at Lawrence Berkely National Laboratory in California created livermorium by a different pathway—fusing titanium-50 and plutonium-244. Hiromitsu Haba, leader of the Superheavy Element Research group at Japan's RIKEN, Nishina Center for Accelerator-based Science, said the new pathway was "truly groundbreaking" and will "greatly advance mankind towards the discovery of elements 119 and 120,"—elements that Haba's group is striving to discover.

Livermorium was first called ununhexium (Uuh), based on the Latin roots for its atomic number. The name Livermorium was chosen in 2012, to honor the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory scientists for their dedicated work on superheavy metals.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Livermorium is a highly radioactive, superheavy element. We can only make predictions about its properties because it decays so quickly. It is a chalcogen, or ore-forming element, and is found in group 16 of the periodic table. It's in the same family as oxygen, sulfur, and selenium, but is predicted to be me more like polonium. This would make it a volatile metal or metalloid that is probably solid at room temperature.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Noone has been able to identify any uses for livermorium yet. It doesn’t hang around long enough to test it!

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Four isotopes of livermorium are currently known to exist, with mass numbers of 290-293. But there may be a fifth one! The longest lasting isotope, livermorium-293, has a half-life of about 60 milliseconds, while livermorium-290 has a half-life of only 9 milliseconds.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Livermorium has only ever been created in a laboratory. It is not found in nature. It was made by blasting atoms of curium–248 with calcium–48 in a particle accelerator to create a nuclear fusion reaction. Only one atom of livermorium was made in this experiment, and it only existed for about 50 milliseconds–but they found it!

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The creation of element 117 took a team of international researchers. Elements 114, 115, 116, and 118 had already been synthesized and the periodic table had a gap for element 117. Russian physicist Yuri Oganessian developed the method that led to the discovery of the surrounding elements, and he reasoned that using that same “hot fusion” method but with a berkelium-249 target would lead to element 117. He would need a lot of it. Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the only place in the world with enough berkelium-249 to support the experiment.

In 2004, Yuri Oganessian proposed the collaborative experiment between the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Dubna, Russia and Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. By January 2009, Oak Ridge had produced enough berkelium-249 for the experiment—a whopping 22 milligrams!

Because of berkelium-249’s 330-day half-life, researchers had to work fast to process, transfer, and bombard the berkelium isotope. The US team sent the isotopes to Russia in what is still the fastest actinide transfer between the two countries. After further preparation at the Research Institute of Atomic Reactors in Ulyanovsk Oblast, Russia, the isotope finally arrived in Dubna on July 28, 2009, to begin bombardment. After 150 days of being irradiated with a beam of 6 trillion calcium-48 ions per second, the berkelium target produced six atoms of element 117.

The team announced the discovery on April 9, 2010 and replicated the results with subsequent experiments in 2012 and 2013. Independent researchers from across the world collaborated to confirm the experiment, independently verifying the discovery of element 117 in May 2014.

In December 2015, the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) and the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) confirmed the discovery. A year later, in November 2016, the element was officially named tennessine, in recognition of Oak Ridge National Laboratory and contributions by Vanderbilt University and the University of Tennessee.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Tennessine has no known non-research uses. The element is used for fundamental research to advance our basic understanding of the elements.

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Tennessine is a man-made (or synthetic) element, created using a particle accelerator.

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Once the noble gas group was discovered, scientists soon wondered about the possibility of a seventh gas that would fill in gaps on the periodic table. Even in 1895, the year after argon was discovered, Danish chemist Hans Peter Jørgen Julius Thomsen hypothesized that a group of unreactive gases (now known as the noble gases) would end with an element at an atomic weight of 292—a near-accurate prediction of oganesson-294, the first and only isotope of oganesson.

Though many scientists claimed possible discoveries of the hypothesized element over the years, it wasn’t until 2015 that oganesson was discovered by a group of scientists from the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR) in Russia and the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California.

sections.heading: Properties
paragraphs: Oganesson is highly radioactive and has an extremely short half-life (0.69 milliseconds!). Not much else is known about this gas, however, scientists can make educated guesses, or hypotheses, based on the characteristics of its neighbors in the periodic table. For example, like other noble gases, it is predicted to be a diatomic molecule, meaning it only pairs with itself.

sections.heading: Uses
paragraphs: Oganesson has no uses beyond scientific research.

sections.heading: Forms
paragraphs: Oganesson-294 is the only isotope of oganesson. It is extremely unstable with a half-life of 700 microseconds!

sections.heading: Sources
paragraphs: Oganesson is not found in nature, so we can only study it in a laboratory setting. Like any synthetic element, making oganesson is tricky. Using a heavy ion accelerator, a beam of energy launches calcium-48 into a target made of californium-249, californium-250, and californium-251. Scientists must then find the oganesson isotopes in the fallout of the collision.
